en: The first question:

We shall explain the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the seventh year, a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year. One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn.

During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion—especially one with a masculine name—he should serve food to an even number of Brāhmaṇas. Having caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Prosperity! Success!", he should have the hair of the boy who has eaten shaved. Then, having bathed him and adorned him, he should dress him in a new garment. On a site that slopes toward the east, or toward the north, or toward the northeast, or on level ground, he should dig up the earth, sprinkle it with water, prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with sand, scratch lines upon it, churn out the fire, or bring in common (secular) fire.

Having established [the fire], he kindles it. He strews around [the fire] with *darbha* grass whose tips point eastward; alternatively, they may have their tips pointing northward, being behind and in front [of the fire]. If they have tips pointing both east and north, he makes those on the south side upper and those on the north side lower. Having strewn *darbha* grass in the seat of the Brahman to the south of the fire with the two verses, "I take into myself that Agni who is ours... and "May our Agni...", he takes the fire into himself. Then, having strewn *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he arranges his ritual materials there.

An unworked stone, a garment, and an antelope skin; a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass for a Brāhmaṇa, a bowstring for a Rājanya, and one made of wool for a Vaiśya; a staff of bilva or palāśa wood for a Brāhmaṇa, one of nyagrodha wood for a Rājanya, and one of udumbara wood for a Vaiśya; a sacrificial fuel (idhma) of twenty-one sticks, or a quantity measured by the number of oblations—this he says. Upon this [altar], he binds the yoke-pins as enclosing-sticks (paridhi) together with the fuel.

Having sprinkled the ladle (*darvī*), the grass-bundle (*kūrca*), the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the water-vessel for the *praṇītā* waters, and whatever else is used for sprinkling—sprinkling all these only once, or as may be convenient—at this time the Brahman priest, having placed his sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), having sipped water, having passed behind the fire to the south, having cast away a blade of grass from the Brahman’s seat, and having touched water, sits down facing the fire.

Having made two *pavitra* strainers from two *darbha* blades with unbroken tips and a length of one span (*prādeśa*), having cut them with another [blade] rather than with the fingernails, and having wiped them with water; then, having poured water into a vessel over which the *pavitra* are placed and filled it up to the rim, having purified it three times by scooping upward with the two *pavitra* whose tips point north, and having set it down on *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he covers it with *darbha* blades. Having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters through the *pavitra*, and having placed them as before in upturned vessels with openings, he spreads out the fuel and sprinkles it three times with all the waters.

Having heated the ladle, wiped it, and heated it again, he sets it down. Having sprinkled the tips [of the grass blades], he places them on the fire. Having melted the clarified butter, poured the butter into the butter-pot over which a strainer has been placed, drawn out embers toward the north, and placed [the pot] upon them, having illuminated it, cast two *darbha* blades into it, carried fire around it three times, and removed it from the fire toward the north, having pushed the embers back, and having purified the butter three times by moving the strainers back and forth with their tips pointing north, he places the two strainers into the fire.

He encloses [the fire] with the *śamyā*-stakes as boundary-poles. To the west of the fire, he places the middle stake with its notch facing north. Having touched it with the middle one, he places the middle stake to the south of the fire with its notch facing east; having touched it with the middle one, he places the middle stake to the north of the fire with its notch facing east. To the west of the fire, he sits down facing east. To the south, the youth, wearing the sacrificial cord over his left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) and having sipped water, sits down and takes hold [of the teacher]. Then he sprinkles [water around the fire].

With "O Aditi, give your consent," he sprinkles from the south toward the east; with "O Anumati, give your consent," from the west toward the north; with "O Sarasvatī, give your consent," from the north toward the east; and with "O God Savitṛ, impel," he sprinkles all around clockwise. Having anointed the fuel-stick with clarified butter, he places it upon the fire.

"This fuel is your self, O Jātavedas; with it, kindle yourself and grow. As you grow, cause us to grow with offspring, cattle, Vedic splendor, and the enjoyment of food. Svāhā! Having thus spoken, he then offers with the wooden spoon. Having brought it down along the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, while meditating mentally on "To Prajāpati, the restrainer, svāhā," he offers straight, continuous oblations toward the south, east, and north.

Having brought [the ladle] along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks, he pours the two *āghāra* libations straight forward and upward with the formula, "To Indra, svāhā! Then he offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions: with "To Agni, svāhā! in the eastern part of the northern half; and with "To Soma, svāhā! in the eastern part of the southern half. He offers the other oblations between these two. "Yoked, O Jātavedas, carry [the offering] from the front; O Agni, know this rite as it is being performed. You are the physician, the maker of the remedy; through you, may we obtain cattle, horses, and men for all time, svāhā!"

"You who lie across, saying 'I am the supporter'—you, with a stream of clarified butter, I worship in Agni for the sake of prosperity, svāhā! To the goddess Saṃrādhinī, svāhā! To the goddess Prasādhanī, svāhā! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā! This is the ritual procedure for all offerings made with a ladle (darvī-homa). 1.

At the end of a mantra, the word *svāhā* is always used; for those [mantras] that are without a mantra, one says, "Svāhā to such-and-such [deity]. One offers oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*—*bhūr*, *bhuvas*, and *svar*—both individually and collectively, according to the respective deity. This [offering] is accompanied by the verse: "O Agni, giver of life... [and] "O divine Agni, giver of life, being praised as you reach old age, you whose face is ghee and whose back is ghee; drinking the ghee and the lovely nectar of the cow, lead this [person] to old age like a father his son, svāhā!"

To you, O Varuṇa, I approach with this truth. O Agni, be for us; be for us, O Agni. You, O Agni, are the Unswerving One (Ayāsya), established by the unswerving mind. As the Unswerving One, you have carried the oblation; as the Unswerving One, bestow upon us healing medicine. Svāhā! "To Prajāpati"—this is the formula. Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all of that well-sacrificed and well-offered for me.

"To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the well-offered, the well-sacrificed, the all-sacrificed, the fulfiller of the desires of all expiatory oblations—svāhā! With these words, he offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire], so that it does not touch the other oblations. At this point, some offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* before the *sviṣṭakṛt*. He offers the *jayas* with: "Consciousness, svāhā! Perception, svāhā! Or alternatively: "To consciousness, svāhā! To perception, svāhā!"

"May Agni, the lord of beings, protect me"—with these words he offers the *abhyātāna* oblations. To the *abhyātāna* verses, he adds the formula: "In this sacred power (*brahman*), in this sovereign power (*kṣatra*)... Wearing the sacrificial cord over his right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he offers and worships with the verse: "The fathers, the grandfathers, those beyond and those below... He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations with the verse: "The upholder of Truth, whose abode is Truth... Having recited each section in succession, he offers the first oblation with "To him, svāhā! and the second with "To them, svāhā!"

Having placed a stone at the front of the junction of the northern enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), he makes the boy step upon it with his right foot, [saying] with this [verse]: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, be thou firm. Crush those who wish thee ill; overcome those who attack thee. He causes him to put on an unwashed garment, having first laid it down [with the verse]: "The goddesses who spun, who wove, who stretched [the warp], and who, as goddesses, gave the ends on both sides—may those goddesses clothe thee for old age. Long-lived, put on this garment."

"Put on, clothe him with this garment; make him live for a hundred years, grant him long life! Bṛhaspati gave this garment to King Soma that he might put it on. You shall reach old age; put on the garment and become a protector against the curses of the people. Live for a hundred autumns, full of luster, and clothe yourself in the increase of wealth. Having clothed him, he addresses him: "This garment has been put around you for well-being; you have become a protector against the curses of your kinsmen."

"May you live for a hundred long autumns; living, may you distribute the riches of the noble. With these words, he girds him with the girdle three times from left to right. According to some, twice. "She who comes to us, driving away misfortune, purifying our protection and shelter, bringing strength through out-breath and in-breath—this auspicious girdle is the sister of the gods. Having made a triple knot to the north of the navel, he draws it across to the south of the navel. Then he makes an antelope skin his upper garment.

"May Mitra’s eye, the supporting, powerful, glorious, renowned, and anciently kindled brilliance; the unwearied, enduring garment—this skin, O vigorous one, put on as your armor. May this Aditi bind your girth for the sake of speaking the Veda, for wisdom, for faith, for not rejecting what has been recited, and for sacred knowledge and spiritual luster. A black antelope skin is for a Brāhmaṇa, a Ruru deer skin for a Rājanya, and a goat skin for a Vaiśya. Then he hands it over to him.

"O Indra, we place this man around for the sake of great sacred knowledge (*brahman*) and for hearing, so that he may long remain awake for hearing throughout his life"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa. "O Indra, we place this man around for the sake of great sovereignty (*rāṣṭra*) and for the kingdom, so that he may long remain awake for the kingdom throughout his life"—thus for a Rājanya. "O Indra, we place this man around for the sake of great nourishment (*poṣa*) and for prosperity, so that he may long remain awake for prosperity throughout his life."

Having thus seated the Vaiśya facing north in front of the fire, he makes him eat the remains of the oblation with these [formulas] joined together: "May Agni bestow wisdom upon you, offspring upon you, and splendor upon you. Some have him eat the *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter) with [the verses]: "In every endeavor, the most powerful one... and "O Agni, make this man fit for long life and luster. He gazes at him as he eats. Some have him eat [the clotted butter]. Having had him rinse his mouth and touch water, he addresses him with the mantra: "A hundred autumns are before us, O gods, within which you have ordained old age for our bodies."

"Where sons become fathers, do not harm our life-span in its course. (2) "We have come together with the coming [of the teacher]; ward off death for us. May we move about unharmed; may we move safely here from our homes with well-being. With these words, he addresses him as he circumambulates the fire from left to right. Then he causes him to recite: "I have come for the life of a student (*brahmacarya*); lead me near. Be a student, impelled by the god Savitṛ. He asks him: "What is your name? He replies, "I am so-and-so," using whatever name he has.

"May there be well-being! O God Savitṛ, I [shall study] such-and-such a verse," thus he announces his name. "May the divine waters be for our aid, may they be auspicious for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and happiness"—with these words, he purifies himself with water. 3.

Then, having touched his right shoulder with his right hand and his left shoulder with his left hand, he initiates him by placing his right arm around him while reciting the *vyāhṛtis* and the *Sāvitrī*. And [he says]: "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I initiate you, O so-and-so! Then, with his right hand, he takes hold of his right hand, including the thumb, [reciting]: "Agni has taken your hand; Soma has taken your hand; Savitṛ has taken your hand."

"Sarasvatī has taken your hand; Pūṣan has taken your hand; Bṛhaspati has taken your hand; Mitra has taken your hand; Varuṇa has taken your hand; Tvaṣṭṛ has taken your hand; Dhātṛ has taken your hand; Viṣṇu has taken your hand; Prajāpati has taken your hand. With these mantras, he takes the boy's right hand, including the thumb, with his own right hand, reciting each mantra in turn.

"May Savitṛ protect you; you are Mitra by virtue of his protection; Agni is your teacher. Impelled by the divine Savitṛ, become a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) under Bṛhaspati, [O so-and-so]. Drink water, eat with restraint, perform your duties, and do not sleep during the day"—thus he instructs him. Then, having touched his right shoulder repeatedly from above with his own right hand, he touches the region of the student's heart, saying: "May my heart be your heart; follow my mind with your mind."

"Delight in my speech with a one-pointed mind. May Bṛhaspati join you to me; follow me alone. Let your thoughts be in me; let your devotion be toward me. Entrust your speech to me. Thus [he says]. "You are the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen from me," [with this he touches] the region of the navel. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through offspring; rich in heroes through heroes; rich in luster through luster; rich in nourishment through nourishment; rich in wisdom through wisdom; and rich in sacred knowledge through those who practice sacred study."

Having thus consecrated him with the mantra: "Bhūḥ! In the Ṛg-verses, in Agni, on the earth, in speech, in Brahman, I take thee, O [Name]! Bhuvaḥ! In the Yajus-formulas, in Vāyu, in the intermediate space, in breath, in Brahman, I take thee, O [Name]! Svaḥ! In the Sāman-chants, in Sūrya, in heaven, in sight, in Brahman, I take thee, O [Name]! May I be dear to thee as Viṣṇu; may I be dear to thee as Anala. Here we two shall dwell. We two shall dwell in breath and in life-force. O [Name], do thou dwell in breath and in life-force!"—thus he speaks.

Then, with his own right hand, he takes hold of [the student's] right hand together with the thumb using five formulas beginning, "Agni is long-lived. Having whispered, "May he bestow life upon you from every side," into the right ear; and "O Agni, giver of life," into the left ear; he then attaches [the following] to both ears: "Be established in Agni, in the earth; in Vāyu, in the atmosphere; in Sūrya, in heaven. That well-being which Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Candramas, and the Waters follow—that well-being do you follow, O [Name]! You have become the *brahmacārin* of Prāṇa, O [Name]! He attaches this to both ears.
May Indra grant me wisdom; may the goddess Sarasvatī grant me wisdom;
may both the Aśvins, adorned with lotus garlands, bestow wisdom upon me.

Thus, placing his mouth close to the boy’s mouth, he mutters: "I entrust you to Kaśaka; I entrust you to Antaka; I entrust you to Aghora; I entrust you to Yama; I entrust you to Gada; I entrust you to Makha; I entrust you to Vaśinī; I entrust you to Pṛthivī together with Vaiśvānara; I entrust you to the waters; I entrust you to the plants."

I entrust you to the trees; I entrust you to all beings; I entrust you to all the gods; I entrust you to all the deities. Here he causes him to recite the Sāvitrī, if he has already been initiated previously; if he has not been initiated, after three days have passed. According to Puṣkarasādin, it is immediate.

Having placed a grass-bundle (kūrca) with its tips pointing north using the *apreṇa* formula, he sits upon it facing east, [saying]: "Thou art the Rāṣṭrabhṛt; thou art the teacher’s seat; may I not harm thee. Having made an añjali toward the sun and having clasped the feet of the teacher, the boy sits down to the south, says, "Recite, sir! and then, "Sir, please recite the Sāvitrī for me. Having consecrated him with the verse, "We invoke thee, the Lord of hosts, the leader of hosts," he then recites it to him first quarter by quarter, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally continuously.

Bhūḥ! That most excellent splendor of the Savitṛ, Bhuvaḥ! We meditate upon the radiance of the divine; Svaḥ! May he impel our thoughts. Bhūrbhuvaḥ! That most excellent splendor of the Savitṛ, we meditate upon the radiance of the divine; Svaḥ! May he impel our thoughts. Bhūrbhuvaḥ Svaḥ! That most excellent splendor of the Savitṛ, we meditate upon the radiance of the divine; may he impel our thoughts. (Three times)

Then he causes seven fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood—fresh, with unbroken tips, a span in length, and anointed with clarified butter—to be placed upon the fire, [reciting]: "To Agni, the great Jātavedas, I have brought a fuel-stick. As you, O Agni, are kindled by the fuel-stick, so do you cause me to prosper with wisdom, insight, offspring, cattle, Vedic splendor, and the enjoyment of food; Svāhā!"—thus for one stick. "To Agni, two fuel-sticks"—thus for two. "To Agni, four fuel-sticks"—thus for four.

Then he sprinkles water around as before; he completes the formulas with the words, "Thou hast consented; do not turn away. Then he pays homage to the deities: to Agni with the formula, "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall observe the vow"; to Vāyu with "O Vāyu, lord of vows"; to Āditya with "O Āditya, lord of vows"; and to the Lord of Vows with "O Lord of vows, lord of vows. At this point, he gives a choice gift to the teacher.

Having raised him up with the words, "O long-lived one," and having entrusted him with the words, "This is your son, O Sūrya; I entrust him to you," he worships the sun with the mantra: "That eye, beneficial to the gods, which shines white in the east—may we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns; may we rejoice for a hundred autumns; may we delight for a hundred autumns; may we prosper for a hundred autumns; may we hear for a hundred autumns; may we proclaim for a hundred autumns; may we remain unconquered for a hundred autumns; and may we long behold the sun."

"May Agni extend your life further; may Agni bestow prosperity upon you more abundantly. May Indra, together with the Maruts, grant it to you here; may the Ādityas, together with the Vasus, establish it for you. Having thus given the staff, he hands over the alms-bowl. Then he says, "Go on your rounds for alms. He should first beg from his mother. After that, having brought alms from other households that give with pleasure, he announces: "We take from you this first garment; may all the gods protect you."

"May many brothers, well-grown, follow after you as you grow, O well-born one! With these words, he takes the first shaving from it. When food is available, having taken portions of boiled rice, cakes, and groats, and mixing them with clarified butter, he offers them, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Agni, the eater of food, svāhā! To Agni, the lord of food, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, svāhā! To all the deities, svāhā!"

"To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"—in all cases where no deity has been specifically assigned, one offers thus: "To such-and-such, svāhā! To such-and-such, svāhā! For those for whom a deity has been assigned, it is according to that deity. Having taken portions from these very offerings together, he makes an offering on *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, saying: "To Vāstupati, svāhā!"

Having served the Brahmins with threefold food and having caused them to pronounce "an auspicious day," "well-being," and "success," he observes the vow for three days, eating food that is not pungent, not salty, and not consisting of unhusked grain; sleeping on the ground, drinking from a vessel other than one made of clay, avoiding the remnants of a Śūdra's meal, honey, and meat, and not sleeping during the day; fetching water in a jar and a piece of wood every day at both times [of dawn and dusk]; and placing fuel sticks on the fire at both times, or every evening.

As it is said: "O Vasus, this is your Gaurī"—having thus wiped around the fire from left to right, he sprinkles water around it as before. He places the fuel-sticks one by one with the *vyāhṛtis* and also with all of them together: "This is your fuel, O Agni; through it may you grow and swell, and may we grow and swell. *Svāhā!* May Indra bestow intelligence upon me; may the goddess Sarasvatī bestow intelligence; may the two Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, bestow intelligence upon me. *Svāhā!*"

"May that wisdom which is among the Apsarases, and that mind which is among the Gandharvas—may that divine wisdom, born of man, the fragrant wisdom, attend me! Svāhā! May the fragrant, all-formed, golden-colored wisdom, moving through the world and accessible to all, swelling with milk and full of vigor—may that wisdom of beautiful countenance attend me! Svāhā! Having wiped [the vessel] in the same manner, he sprinkles water around it as before.

He worships with these mantras, "O Agni, that splendor which is thine... and "In me be wisdom, in me be offspring. When three days have passed, having likewise served the Brāhmaṇas with food prepared from three kinds of grain, and having caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", he releases the vow with these mantras: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow... From this point forward, while residing in the teacher's household, he eats only such food as is prescribed for his vow—excluding pungent substances, salt, and unhusked grain.

He should carry a staff, wear matted hair, a girdle, or have his hair tied in a top-knot. He wears either saffron-colored cloth or an antelope skin and does not approach a woman for forty-eight years, or until he has mastered [the Veda], or at least twelve years; however, he must never be without his vow. At the commencement of a section and at the conclusion of a section, [he recites]: "The wonderful Lord of the Assembly, the beloved and desirable friend of Indra."

"Desiring gain and wisdom, I have approached [thee], svāhā!"—thus [he recites] the second [verse] for the *kāṇḍarṣi*. Then he recites: "This [oblation] to me, O Varuṇa," "That I implore thee," "Do thou, O Agni, for us," "So do thou, O Agni, for us," "Thou, O Agni, art the path," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess. Now some offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* as before. [The verses beginning with] "Upagantṛ," "We have come together," and "Ayaśca"—these are four.

Thus ends the first chapter in the first book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra. The second chapter: On the appearance of plants during the fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, or on the full moon day of the month of Hasta, the commencement of the term (upākarma) for Vedic study takes place. Having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers oblations to the five Ṛṣis of the sections (*kāṇḍa-ṛṣis*): "To Prajāpati, the Ṛṣi of the section, svāhā! To Soma, the Ṛṣi of the section, svāhā! To Agni, the Ṛṣi of the section, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, the Ṛṣis of the sections, svāhā! To Svayambhū, the Ṛṣi of the section, svāhā! Thus he offers.

Having offered oblations with the names of the sections—namely, the Sāvitrī, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, and Sadasaspati—and having observed a break for either three days or one day, they say that one should study according to the [specific] section. Now, therefore, the sections are stated: the Pauroḍāśika, the Yājamāna, the Hotṛ, the Hautra, and the Pitṛmedha; these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, belong to Prajāpati.

The duties of the Adhvaryu priest, the cups (*graha*), the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) formulas, the Vājapeya, the *śukriya* hymns, and the *sava* offerings—these belong to Soma, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas. The establishment of the fires (*āgnyādheya*), the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), the Agnihotra, the worship of the fires (*agnyupasthāna*), the Sāvitra, the Nāciketa, the Cāturhotrīya, the Vaiśvasṛja, the Āruṇaketuka, and the Āgnika—these belong to Agni, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas.

The Rājasūya, animal sacrifices (paśubandha), iṣṭis, nakṣatreṣṭis, Divaśyenayas, Apāghas, Sātrāyaṇa, upahomas, sūktas, ānuvākyās and yājyās, the Aśvamedha, Puruṣamedha, Sautrāmaṇī, the Acchidra rites, the Paśuhautra, and the Upaniṣads—these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, constitute the Vaiśvadevas. The Svāyaṃbhuva is the injunction recited in the Svāṅkāṅka; here the deity is Svayaṃbhū, the Lord of all beings.

Now, regarding the Kārīrī-vow: for four nights, one should eat on the ground like an animal, avoiding pungent and salty food and non-śamī grains. Then, reciting the *Oṣadhi-anuvāka* beginning with "The Maruts, the gods who bestow wealth; O Agni, the Maruts... and "The gods who grant protection," one should not eat here like an animal. Now, regarding the Kārīrī-vow: starting from the first verse of the *Oṣadhi-anuvāka*, reciting that very first portion, one should not eat on the ground like an animal; or alternatively, if one is reciting [the entire text] in its proper sequence.

The formal dismissal (*utsarga*) takes place under the asterism Rohiṇī in the month of Taiṣa, or on the full moon day. Having gone out toward the east or the north with their attendants, they enter water that is pleasant and easy to bathe in; having entered it, they perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and they purify themselves with their hands holding *pavitra* blades, reciting the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," the four verses beginning with "Golden-hued, pure, and purifying," and this entire section beginning with "Pavamāna, the one who dwells in light."

Having bathed, they exchange darbha grass with one another as if wishing to give it to each other; then, on a pure and level spot sloping toward the east, they prepare seats with the tips of the darbha grass pointing eastward and arranged so that they terminate toward the north.

To Brahmā, Prajāpati, Agni, Vāyu, Soma, Sūrya, Candramas, the Nakṣatras, Indra the king, Yama the king, Varuṇa the king, Soma the king, Vaiśravaṇa the king, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Ṛbhus, the Bhṛgus, the Maruts, the Atharvans, and the Aṅgirases—thus for the groups of deities.

Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kāśyapa—these are the seven sages (*ṛṣis*). Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*nivītinaḥ*), they prepare seats on the northern side of the altar, which is sloping toward the north, using *darbha* grass with the tips pointing north and arranged so that they end toward the east, for Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kāśyapa. Between Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa, they prepare a seat for Arundhatī. On the southern edge of the single altar (*ekavedi*), they prepare a seat for Agastya.

To the north, [offerings] for Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Jatukarṇa, Tarukṣa, Tṛṇavindu, Varmin, Varūthin, Vājin, Śravas, Satraśravas, Suśravas, Stutaśravas, Somaśuṣmāyaṇa, Sanatvāna, Bṛhaduktha, Vāmadeva, Vājarājña, Haritarājña, Udaman, Gautama, Ṛṇañjaya, Ṛtañjaya, Kṛtañjaya, Dhanañjaya, Satyañjaya, Babhru, Trivarṇa, Trivarṣa, Tridhātu, Parāśara, and Viṣṇu.

"To Rudra, to Skanda, to the Lord of Kāśī, to Old Age, to Dharma, to Artha, to Kāma, to Krodha, to Vasiṣṭha, to Indra, to Tvaṣṭṛ, to the Maker, to the Sustainer, to Dhātṛ, to Vidhātṛ, to Mṛtyu, to Savitṛ, to Sāvitrī, to the Ṛgveda, to the Yajurveda, to the Sāmaveda, to the Atharvaveda, and to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Thus [they offer]. To the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), they prepare seats on ground sloping toward the south with darbha grass blades pointing southward, arranged so that they end toward the west.

To Vaiśampāyana, Phaliṅgu, Tittiri, Ukha, Ātreya the author of the *pada-pāṭha*, Kauṇḍinya the author of the *vṛtti*, the authors of the *sūtras*, to Satyāṣāḍha the author of the *pravacana*, to the teachers, to the seers, to the forest-dwellers, to those whose vital energy is drawn upward, and to those who have but one husband.

"I prepare [this] for my own father, grandfather, mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother; for my maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather; for my maternal grandmother, maternal great-grandmother, and maternal great-great-grandmother. With the seat [he says], "I prepare for so-and-so, I prepare for so-and-so, I prepare for so-and-so"; with water, "I satiate so-and-so, I satiate so-and-so"; with scents, flowers, incense, and lamps, "Homage to so-and-so, homage to so-and-so"; with the oblation, "Svāhā to so-and-so, svāhā to so-and-so."

With the formula "Svāhā!", he satiates [the ancestors] with food, saying, "I satiate so-and-so; I satiate so-and-so; I satiate so-and-so"; and with fruit-water, having performed the ritual salutation (upasthāna) with the formula "Homage to so-and-so; homage to so-and-so; homage to so-and-so," he prepares a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the west of the altar, kindles the fire, performs the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, and offers oblations to the five *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis.

Having offered oblations with the names of the *kāṇḍas*, or with the verses beginning "Sāvitrī, Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, Sadasaspati," he recites the first and last sections (*anuvākas*) or all the opening sections of the *kāṇḍas*. He then proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites. Having performed the offerings up to the *sviṣṭakṛt*, they say that after waiting for three days or one day, he should study according to his lesson. With the two verses beginning "From section to section sprouting forth," he should plant *dūrvā* grass at the edge of the water.

Having made the ocean wavy, they run toward the eastern or northern direction as far as the boundary-mark. Having returned, they satisfy the Brahmins with cakes, parched grain flour, and boiled rice. Thus, at the conclusion of the *pārāyaṇa*, from the planting of the *kāṇḍa* grass until the planting of the *dūrvā* grass, excluding the running to the ocean, they constantly satisfy the gods, the seers, and the ancestors with water; they satisfy them, they satisfy them.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, having had his hair shaved, bathed, and eaten, he takes up the fire, four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, an unwashed garment, *darbha* grass, clarified butter, and a water-pot; then, having gone out from the village toward the north, and having established the fire in a place where the thatched roof is not visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water on the fire, and having performed the first propitiatory rite (*śānti*), he sprinkles water around the fire, anoints the fuel-sticks, and places them upon the fire.

[He performs the rite] with these four verses beginning with "The earth is the fuel. Then, having sprinkled [water] around, and having worshipped the deities with the formula, "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall observe the vow for the Śukriya rites," he wraps the head and face with an unwashed garment, [reciting]: "Ye are piled, ye are piled around; O lover of songs, may these songs encompass thee on every side. Increasing after the Increaser, may they be pleasing delights."

"Thou art the needle of Indra; thou art the firmness of Indra; thou belongest to Indra; for Indra thee! Having thus performed the subsequent pacification (*śānti*), he enters the village while restraining his speech. He remains awake, whether standing or sitting.

Then, when the next day has dawned, having gone out in that very direction and kindled the fire in a place where no roof-covering is visible, having strewn grass around it and placed the boiling water on the fire, and having performed the first *śānti* rite, he releases [the birds] with the verse, "The birds, the well-winged ones," and worships the sun with the verses, "Up from the darkness," "Up that [sun]," "The bright one," "That eye, established by the gods," and "He who has risen. They cause him to look at these: the fire, the sun, a stone, a water-pot, gold, a cow, and the earth.

Having performed the *uttarā śānti* (the subsequent pacification rite), he observes a vow for one year, twelve nights, or for a single day. On the eighth lunar day and on the full-moon and new-moon days, he performs the ritual bath at the prescribed time. Now, if he should see something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound and impoverished. And if it should rain upon him, he mutters: "O flowing waters, bestow strength! He sleeps on the ground and serves his teacher. He should study the *Śukriya* texts.

Having gone out in this very direction, having kindled the fire in a place where no roof-covering is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water on the fire, and having performed the first *śānti* rite, he offers fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood with these four verses beginning, "The sky is the fuel-stick. Then, having sprinkled water around the fire and worshipped the deities with these formulas, "O Āditya, lord of vows, I have performed the vow for the *Śukriya* texts," he gives a cow to his teacher. Having performed the subsequent *śānti* rite, the completion of the vow (*vratasamāpti*) takes place.
[This occurs] in the fortnight of Śravaṇā or in the fortnight of Taiṣī. Now, therefore, follows the intermediate initiation (*avāntaradīkṣā*); there are three [days].
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the third chapter.

Having studied the Veda and being about to perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), he prepares: a stalk of *erakā* grass and a pillow, a barber, a razor, a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood, pieces of wood for the under-layer, *vṛkala* twigs, a tooth-cleansing stick, cold and warm water, the powder of all fragrant substances, sandalwood paste, a new garment, an inner garment or a cloak, a jujube-stone set with gold, a thread, two ear-rings, clarified butter, a ladle, a garland, a mirror, collyrium, a staff, an umbrella, and sandals.

A bull’s hide that is entirely red—these are the materials prepared for him. Regarding the ritual bath, there is this deliberation: "One should bathe under the asterism Rohiṇī," so say some; for Rohiṇī belongs to Prajāpati, and thus his bath is performed under an asterism belonging to Prajāpati, and moreover, he rises above all prosperities (rohān). "One should bathe under the asterism Tiṣya," so say others.

This constellation belongs to Bṛhaspati; thus he bathes under the very constellation belonging to Bṛhaspati, thinking, "May I be impelled by Bṛhaspati. One [teacher] says he should bathe under the two Uttaraphalgunīs; this constellation belongs to Bhaga; thus he bathes under the very constellation belonging to Bhaga, thinking, "May I be fortunate. One [teacher] says he should bathe under Hasta.

This constellation belongs to Savitṛ; thus his bath takes place under the constellation of Savitṛ itself, and he thinks, "May I be impelled by Savitṛ. One [teacher] says he should bathe under Citrā; this constellation belongs to Indra; thus his bath takes place under the constellation of Indra itself, and he thinks, "May I be brilliant. One [teacher] says he should bathe under the two Viśākhās; this constellation belongs to Indra and Agni; thus his bath takes place under the constellation of Indra and Agni itself, and he thinks, "May I be distinguished (viśākha) in offspring and cattle. Under one of these constellations [he should bathe].

Before the rising of the sun, he should enter the cow-pen; thus the sun will not scorch him on that day. On that day, he shines with splendor and glory upon the faces of those who have bathed. They drive the cattle into the pen while covering it with a skin, hairy side inward. Having kindled the fire in the eastern part of the pen, he should then bring all these ritual materials at once—all together—just as it is stated in that Brāhmaṇa: "Whatever is human, all that [is brought] together."

Having strewn [the grass] around and placed a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood to the north, the barber stands to the south. He should give alms until midday. He may also cook a cow here, if it should be a barren cow; he should do so at this point. Having anointed the *pālāśa* fuel-stick with clarified butter, he places it on the fire at midday, [reciting]: "This hymn for the worthy Jātavedas, we fashion with our inspired thought like a chariot."

"For auspicious indeed is his guidance in the assembly; O Agni, in your friendship may we not suffer harm—Svāhā! Then, to the west of the fire, he spreads an *erakā* grass mat with its tips facing north. Upon it, he sits down with his head toward the north, reciting: "The triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Agastya, the triple life-span of Jamadagni, and that triple life-span which belongs to the gods—may that triple life-span be mine. As the [grass] is being lifted up, he consecrates it with the mantra: "Be auspicious to me, O bringer of welfare."

He consecrates the razor with the mantra: "Thou art named Razor; the axe is thy father; homage be to thee; do not harm me. He consecrates it as it is being applied with the mantra: "When thou cuttest with the razor, O shaver, thou shavest the hair and beard; make my face radiant; do not steal away my life. Having first shaved the beard, then the armpits, then the hair, and then the other limbs as they come up—this is because these [limbs] go forward for the sake of longevity through old age; by going forward for the sake of longevity, they become eaters of food.

Since those who know this shave their hair, therefore indeed a man who knows this may shave his hair at will. Or, having trimmed his nails at will, he may shave his hair. If he is about to have his hair shaved, he hands it to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) and says: "Having carried these eastward, deposit them in a cow-pen or in a clump of *darbha* grass. He then deposits them there. 2.

Then, having sat down to the east of the fire, he loosens his girdle with the mantra: "I loosen this bond of Varuṇa. To whomever may be a recipient there, he hands it over, saying: "Having carried this toward the east, deposit it in a *nyagrodha* or an *udumbara* tree. He then deposits it there, saying: "Here I conceal the evil of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, from those who hate him hereafter. Having run about with *vṛkala* twigs, he cleanses his teeth.

"For the sake of food, you arrange yourselves; Bhaga the King has come. May he enter my mouth for long life and for fortune. Then he pours together both kinds of water—hot into cold—with the thought, "For the distinction between the divine and the human. He sprinkles him three times with his joined palms using these [verses]: with the three beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," with the four beginning with "Golden-colored, pure, and purifying," and according to the Brāhmaṇa passage: "Man is indeed divided sixfold."

Having laid down this garment with the formula, "O self, enter my body," he puts on an inner garment. Then, having gathered all fragrant substances together, he sprinkles them three times around [the head] with his joined palms, saying: "Homage to Śāka and Jañjabha; homage to those deities who seize by force. He does the same for sandalwood. In the same manner from this point forward, having laid it down with the formula, "O self, enter my body," he puts on an unwashed garment. In the same way for the upper garment (āsaṅgya), in the same way for the turban (uṣṇīṣa); in the same manner from this point forward.
Then, having soaked this jujube-stone set with gold in urine, and having taken it up with a ladle and wound it around with the cord of the ladle-handle, he offers it as an oblation. 3.

"O herb, you are the protector, the overcoming, the powerful one. May she take hold of me by my name as [a father does] his son; may she make me possessed of the luster of Soma, may she make me possessed of the luster of the Sun, may she make me radiant with Vedic knowledge and an eater of food—*svāhā*! Then he causes him to float in a vessel of water with the verse, "And all things, through thee... Having said, "Thou art the releaser from bonds," he carries it around crosswise. For, according to this *Brāhmaṇa*, "they fasten the victim facing backward for the sake of distinction."

Then, having threaded these two ear-rings onto a cord, having placed them upon the handle of the ladle, and having wound the cord around the handle of the ladle, he offers [the first oblation] with: "May this gold—which bestows long life, splendor, increase of wealth, and is a source of prosperity—enter into this person for the sake of splendor and victory, svāhā! He offers the second [oblation] with: "Like a blessing, I have grasped the name of gold as that of a father; may it make me possessed of Soma-splendor, may it make me possessed of Sun-splendor, may it make me possessed of Veda-splendor, and may it make me an eater of food, svāhā!"

He offers the third oblation with: "O powerful one, conqueror of armies, victor in assemblies, winner of wealth—whatever prosperities and riches are contained within gold, svāhā! He offers the fourth oblation with: "The sovereign power and the self-ruling power, the glory that is in our house, and the glory that is at the head of the kingdom—with that, unite me, svāhā! He offers the fifth oblation with: "Make me glorious among the Brāhmaṇas, make me glorious among the Kṣatriyas; make me glorious among the Vaiśyas and the Śūdras; may I be a consumer of glory, svāhā!"

Then he causes the two of them to float in a vessel of water with the verse, "And by thee, we [cross] all... Having said, "Thou art a releaser from bonds," he washes one of the ear-rings and fastens it on the right ear.

He follows this with these five [verses] beginning with *āyuṣyaṃ varcasyam*, saying: "With the seasons, with the seasonal periods, with the nourishment of the year—with those I follow you. He does the same for the other [garland]. Having said, "You are a bond," he places the garland around [her head] diagonally, saying: "O auspicious one, ascend my head, beautifying my face; beautify my face indeed, and grant me abundant fortune—[the garland] which Jamadagni took from me for faith, passion, and another [purpose]."

"I release this thought for long life and for fortune," he says. He looks into a mirror: "My mind which has gone away, I behold it here in the mirror; I take it back again for long life and for fortune. Then, having applied collyrium made from *grai-kakud* grown on the heights of the Himalayas, he says: "By that which is collyrium, may there be for me long life and splendor. He takes up his staff, saying: "Be my protector."

He takes up the parasol with the formula: "Thou art the sky, the well-winged one; protect me from the intermediate space. Then he puts on the two sandals: the right one with "Thou art the sky," and the left one with "Thou art the earth. Having gone out toward the quarters, he worships the quarters with the verse: "O divine six wide ones, make us spacious; O all-gods, display your heroism here! "May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies; may we not fall into the power of the enemy, O King Soma! Having thus worshipped the moon, he goes toward whichever direction he desires. 5.

Having studied the Veda, before the rising of the sun, he should then sit down to the west of the fire facing east, [reciting] these five verses beginning with "This herb, the protecting one, bestowing long life and luster.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.

Now begins the fourth chapter: the other [ceremony], the Return Home (*samāvartana*). Now, as for the other [rite]: having bathed silently at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), he comes out. Then, they bring him a seat worthy of an Ārya and present him with water for washing his feet. He awaits that [water] with the mantra: "Come to me with splendor, with luster, with fame, and with milk. Having touched it, he says, "Sprinkle [it] toward the east. Therefore, he causes another [substance] to be brought. Having washed his feet with that, he then causes honey to be brought to him. He awaits that.

"Whatever of honey is honey-like, dear, and the supreme form of food—through that honey which is honey-like, dear, and the supreme form of food, may I be a consumer of food"—with these words he accepts it. "Dear to subjects, lord of cattle"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa; "Dear to cattle, lord of subjects"—thus for a Rājanya. He eats it with the formula: "May Brahman eat you; may Brahman eat you. Then he causes curd to be brought to him; he eats it with the formula: "May Brahman eat you; may Brahman eat you."

He causes rice-milk (odana) to be brought to him; he eats it, saying: "May Brahman eat you! May Brahman eat you! Then he causes him to be brought the stirred drink (mantha); he eats it, saying: "May Brahman eat you! May Brahman eat you! Then he dedicates a cow to him, releasing it with the words: "Go forth" or "Perform [the work]! Then on that day, either his son, or a brother, or a pupil should lead it forward for him, or she herself endures it.

If he obtains a chariot, he touches the right wheel with the words, "Thou art the Rathantara"; the left with, "Thou art the Bṛhat"; and the middle one with, "Thou art the Vāmadevya. Having mounted, he consecrates it as it moves forward with the formula: "O Aśvins, may this chariot of yours not suffer harm, neither in sorrow nor in joy.

If it should make a sound, he wakes up, puts on his sacrificial cord, sips water, and touches the ground with the formula: "In me be stability; in me be support; in me be self-sustenance; in me be delight; in me be enjoyment; in me be nourishment—may the Lord of Nourishment bestow it upon me. This is one [version]; the other is one.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the *Āgniveśya-gṛhyasūtra*. Now begins the fifth chapter. "May the paths be thornless and straight, by which our friends go to the desired goal. May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; O Gods, may our household be well-governed. This is the *kūrca* (seat-grass). "I first take Agni within me for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor. I place offspring and luster in me; may we be unharmed in body and possessed of heroic sons. O Fathers, that immortal Agni who has entered into the hearts of us mortals..."

We take him as our own; may he not abandon us and depart. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Prajāpati placed glory, seed, and the serpent in the woman. O Agni, grant me here a share of that fulfillment of desire and bliss. Joy, delight, bliss, and the serpent deposited in the two testicles—may I satisfy the longing for these, even as one runs, upon receiving sacrificial gifts. May we attain the thought of the mind, the intention, and the truth of speech.

"May the form of the cattle, the glory, and the prosperity of food rest upon me! Just as I have been satisfied by this woman, as a man is satisfied by a woman, and as a beloved woman is satisfied by her beloved man—so may I be satisfied by the fortune of the sacrifice, the desirable beloved of the rite. "I give," says Agni. "So be it," says Vāyu. "Amen," says the Moon, the truth. "The truth, Om! says the Sun. The Waters brought that truth—the glory of the sacrifice and the sacrificial fee. "May this desire of mine be fulfilled!"

With the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," with the four verses beginning "Golden-hued, pure, and purifying," and with this entire section beginning "Pavamāna, who dwells in the light"—and with the verse: "The goddesses who cut [the wool], who carded, who spun, and who placed the ends around—the goddesses, may they clothe you with old age; put on this long-lived garment!"—and with the verse: "Clothe her, dress her in the garment; make her live for a hundred years, grant her a long life."

Bṛhaspati gave this garment to King Soma that he might put it on: "You shall reach old age; put on the garment. Become a protector against the curses of the people. Live for a hundred autumns with radiant luster, and clothe yourself in the increase of wealth. Put on this garment for well-being; you have become a protector against the curses of kinsmen. Live for a hundred long autumns, and while living, distribute riches among the worthy. Together with me, these rites must be performed by you."

Offspring must be produced; for that purpose, I shall marry her. Homage to Indra! Homage to Agni! Homage to Yama! Homage to Nirṛti! Homage to Varuṇa! Homage to Vāyu! Homage to Soma! Homage to Īśāna! Homage to Brahmā! Homage to the Waters! Homage to Agni! Homage to the Self! O Aditi, give your consent! O Anumati, give your consent! O Sarasvatī, give your consent! O God Savitṛ, impel [me].

This fuel is your self, O Jātavedas; with it, kindle yourself and grow. As you grow, cause us to grow with progeny, cattle, Vedic splendor, and the enjoyment of food. Svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Indra, svāhā! To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā! You who lie across, saying, "I am the supporter."

Thee, O Vaiśvakarmanī, I offer with a stream of clarified butter; Svāhā! Thee, whom I lay down following [the fire], saying "I am the supporter," thee, O Saṃrādhinī goddess, I offer with a stream of clarified butter into the fire; Svāhā! To the Prasādhinī goddess, Svāhā! 1.

Be intent upon carrying [the oblation] forward, O Jātavedas; O Agni, know this rite as it is being performed. You are the physician, the maker of the remedy; through you, may we fully recover our cattle, horses, and men—Svāhā! Svāhā to Virūpākṣa! Svāhā to the conqueror of teeth! I worship Virūpākṣa, the one with long shanks and a speckled belly, who obstructs me from prosperity and nourishment—to him, Svāhā!

O oppressor, do not oppress me; do not oppress, you have oppressed [me]. They call you Nirṛti’s son; accomplish our rites, svāhā! I have caused the lord of the assembly, the wonderful one, the beloved and desirable friend of Indra, the winner of wealth, to be mindful; svāhā! O Jātavedas, however many Vedic knowledges are in you, and those women who destroy the ritual work of a man—for all these this portion is offered; may they, being satisfied, satisfy me with my desires, svāhā! For intention (ākūti) you, for desire (kāma) you, for prosperity (samṛdh) you!

I place [this] in front for immortality and for life, Svāhā! For his intention, for protection; for his desire, for its fulfillment. Indra’s people yoke their thoughts, Svāhā! I place the divine intention before my mind; may she, the mother of sacrifice, be easy for me to invoke. Whatever I desire with my mind, may that wish be attained; may I find this which has entered into my heart, Svāhā! To those sacrificed for, Svāhā! To those sacrificed over, Vaṣaṭ! To those not sacrificed for, Svāhā! A remedy for ill-sacrificing, Svāhā! For atonement, Svāhā! For misfortune, Svāhā!

Svāhā to the goddesses, to the bodies! Svāhā to prosperity! Svāhā to complete prosperity! Svāhā to thought! Svāhā to intention! Svāhā to purpose! Svāhā to resolve! Svāhā to what is known! Svāhā to consciousness! Svāhā to the mind! Svāhā to the Śakvarī verses! Svāhā to the new moon! Svāhā to the full moon! Svāhā to the Bṛhat! Svāhā to the Rathantara! Prajāpati bestowed the Jaya oblations upon Indra the Bull, he the fierce one, in the battles for booty.

To him all the people have bowed down; he is the fierce one, for he has become worthy of oblation—*svāhā*! Agni is the overlord of beings; may he protect me—*svāhā*! The fathers and grandfathers; Indra is the overlord of the eldest; may he protect me—*svāhā*! Yama is the overlord of the earth; may he protect me—*svāhā*! Vāyu is the overlord of the intermediate space; may he protect me—*svāhā*! Sūrya is the overlord of the sky; may he protect me—*svāhā*! Candramas is the overlord of the stars; may he protect me—*svāhā*!

Bṛhaspati is the lord of sacred knowledge; may he protect me, svāhā! Mitra is the lord of truths; may he protect me, svāhā! Varuṇa is the lord of the waters; may he protect me, svāhā! The ocean is the lord of rivers; may he protect me, svāhā! Food is the lord of sovereignties; may it protect me, svāhā! Soma is the lord of plants; may he protect me, svāhā! Savitṛ is the lord of instigations; may he protect me, svāhā! Rudra is the lord of animals; may he protect me, svāhā!

Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord of forms, may he protect me; svāhā! Viṣṇu, the lord of mountains, may he protect me; svāhā! The Maruts, the lords of the hosts, may they protect me; svāhā! Fathers, grandfathers, those beyond and those before, ancestors and great-ancestors, protect me here—on this sacred word (brahman), on this sovereignty (kṣatra), on this blessing (āśis), on this priestly office (purodhā), on this rite (karman), on this invocation of the gods (devahūti); svāhā!

Agni, the upholder of Truth, whose abode is Truth, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the plants, named Ūrjas. May he protect this spiritual power (brahman) and this ruling power (kṣatra); may they protect this spiritual power and this ruling power. To him, Svāhā! To them, Svāhā! Sūrya, the uniter, whose melody is the universe, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the rays, named Āyus. May he protect this spiritual power and this ruling power; may they protect this spiritual power and this ruling power. To him, Svāhā! To them, Svāhā!

Suṣumṇa Sūryaraśmi, the Moon, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are named Bekurayas. May he protect this priesthood and nobility; may they protect this priesthood and nobility. To him, Svāhā! To them, Svāhā! Bhujyu Suparṇa, the Sacrifice, is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are named Stavās. May he protect this priesthood and nobility; may they protect this priesthood and nobility. To him, Svāhā! To them, Svāhā!

Prajāpati Viśvakarman, with Mind as his Gandharva and the Ṛg- and Sāma-verses as his many Apsarases named Bahvī, may he protect this priesthood and nobility; may they protect this priesthood and nobility. To him, Svāhā! To them, Svāhā! Iṣira Viśvavyacas, with Vāta as his Gandharva and the Waters as his Apsarases named Mudā, may he protect this priesthood and nobility; may they protect this priesthood and nobility. To him, Svāhā! To them, Svāhā!

May Agni, the first among the gods, release her offspring from the noose of death. May King Varuṇa here grant his consent, so that this woman may not weep over the misfortune of losing a grandson. Svāhā! May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he lead her offspring to a long life. May she have an unfailing lap and be a living mother; may she fully experience the joy of a grandson. Svāhā! Let no cry of lamentation rise in your house at night; let those who weep settle elsewhere than with you.
Do not, O woman with disheveled hair, strike your breast! As a wife whose husband lives, shine in the world of your husband, beholding your offspring with a joyful mind—Svāhā!

May Savitṛ protect your suckling sons; may Bṛhaspati and the Viśvedevas protect them from behind until they have put on their garments—Svāhā! Childlessness, the death of a grandson, evil, or even affliction—I cast these off like a garland from my head and fasten the noose upon my enemies—Svāhā! With the Brahmanical power created by the gods and now being perfected, I strike down the Niṣādas and the Piśācas.

The flesh-eating death I cast down below; may your sons live a long life, Svāhā! May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan—with my hand I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—these gods have given you to me as my wife.

Be not fierce of eye, nor a slayer of thy husband; be auspicious to our cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster. O Pūṣan, send her forth who is most propitious, she in whom men sow the seed. She who, longing for us, shall spread her thighs wide, so that we, longing for her, may strike our phallus within her. Soma gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni. May Agni grant me cattle and sons; and so do I, [Name], take thee. Soma first obtained her; the Gandharva obtained her next.

Agni is your third husband; I am your fourth, born of man. O Sarasvatī, protect this [man], O blessed one, rich in strength! As such, we sing forth to you before all that exists. Ascend this stone; like a stone, be firm. Crush those who seek to harm us; overcome those who attack us in battle. And with you, may we cross over all enemies, as if crossing streams of water. 3.

I scatter these parched grains, which bring prosperity to me and to you; may Agni grant his approval for this act of unification. I unite you with fortune, as one mixes *surā* with honey. This woman speaks thus while scattering parched grains into the fire: "May my husband be long-lived; may my kinsmen prosper! Svāhā! "Hear this prayer of mine, O Varuṇa, and be gracious to me today. Seeking your protection, I call upon you. Svāhā! "I approach you with this sacred prayer, praising you; the sacrificer desires this through his oblations."

O Varuṇa, be mindful of us here without anger; O thou of wide renown, do not steal away our life—*svāhā*. Do thou, O Agni, knowing [the way], appease the wrath of the divine Varuṇa for us. Being the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and blazing brightly, release from us all those who hate us—*svāhā*. As such, O Agni, be our protector, our nearest helper at the dawning of this very light. Being gracious, turn Varuṇa away from us; grant us thy favor; be easy for us to invoke—*svāhā*. Thou, O Agni, art *ayās* (unwearied), established by a mind that is unwearied.

With this [oblation] you have carried the offering; with this, bestow a healing remedy—*svāhā*! O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings. Whatever desire we have as we offer to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches—*svāhā*! Whatever impairment has occurred in my self, Agni Jātavedas, the far-seeing, has restored that for me—*svāhā*! Agni has given sight back again; Indra and Bṛhaspati have given it back again. O Aśvins, you two have placed sight back in my eyes—*svāhā*!

Whatever honey of the sacrifice is performed that was not known as known—O Agni, make that right for him, for you indeed know it as it truly is; *svāhā*. The sacrifice is measured by the person, the sacrifice is measured by the person—O Agni, make that right for him, for you indeed know it as it truly is; *svāhā*. Whatever mortals, with simple minds and feeble resolve, conceive of the sacrifice—may Agni, the wise one who knows the will, being the best of sacrificers, worship the gods according to their respective rites; *svāhā*.

Protect us from sin, O Agni; Svāhā! Protect us, O All-Knowing One; Svāhā! Protect the sacrifice, O Radiant One; Svāhā! Protect everything, O Lord of a Hundred Powers; Svāhā! Bhūḥ! To Agni and to the Earth and to the Great One, Svāhā! Bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the Atmosphere and to the Great One, Svāhā! Suvaḥ! To Āditya and to the Sky and to the Great One, Svāhā! Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! To the Moon and to the Constellations and to the Quarters and to the Great One, Svāhā!

Homage to the gods! Svadhā to the ancestors! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ mahara oṃ svāhā! Oṃ svāhā! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā! Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever here I have done deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all of it well-sacrificed and well-offered for me.

To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the well-offerer, the offerer of the complete oblation, the fulfiller of all expiatory oblations and of desires—svāhā! Aditi, you have given your consent; Anumati, you have given your consent; Sarasvatī, you have given your consent; O God Savitṛ, you have impelled me. O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me.

O Āditya, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me. O Lord of Vows, among all vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it, may it be successful for me. I am she, you are he; you are she, I am he. I am the *ṛc*, you are she; I am the sky, you are the earth. Let your heart be in my heart; let your mind be in my mind. Listen with one-pointed attention to my word. Follow me alone in your vow; become my companion through me.

The charm that was brought forth from the rivers, the charm of the Cakravāka birds—by that charm known to the gods and Gandharvas, may we two be united. One for food, may Viṣṇu follow you; two for strength, may Viṣṇu follow you; three for sacred vows, may Viṣṇu follow you; four for well-being, may Viṣṇu follow you; five for cattle, may Viṣṇu follow you; six for the increase of wealth, may Viṣṇu follow you; seven for the seven priestly offices, may Viṣṇu follow you.

We two have become companions through the seven steps; may I attain friendship with you, may I not be separated from your friendship, and may you not be separated from my friendship. The Seven Sages led Arundhatī, the first of the Kṛttikās, to steadfastness. May this eighth one, shining among us, bear the primary conjunction with the six Kṛttikās. With a steady mind, I bow to the Steadfast One; may our friendship be firm and may there be long life for us.

May we both, free from enmity in this world and the next, surely enter into refuge when afflicted by suffering. Be a blessing to our bipeds and a blessing to our quadrupeds. May the cows settle here; may the horses and men settle here. May Pūṣan, who bestows a thousandfold sacrificial fees, settle here as our sovereign. 4.

O Agni, atonement! You are the atonement of the gods; I, a Brahmin seeking protection, approach you. That body of hers which is husband-slaying, we cause it to perish from here—*svāhā*! O Vāyu, atonement! You are the atonement of the gods; that body of hers which is son-slaying, we cause it to perish from here—*svāhā*! O Āditya, atonement! You are the atonement of the gods; I, a Brahmin seeking protection, approach you. That body of hers which is cattle-slaying, we cause it to perish from here—*svāhā*!

"O universal expiation, you are the expiation; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, approach you. That form of hers which is husband-slaying, son-slaying, cattle-slaying, and censurable—that we cause to perish from here. Svāhā! O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow," and so forth, ending with "O Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow. May your honors pronounce prosperity for us two, the husband and wife! Prosperity for you two, the husband and wife!

I touch you with my hand, which is free from enmity, so that we may never be at odds with one another, nor ever with those who are not our kin. With the bull, I cast out [the seed], having set aside its source; O husband, take up the seed. May a male child be conceived within the womb. May the embryo come to your womb; lay hold of a male embryo. Since you wear garments that are full of vigor, may a son be born to you, not a female; may a male be born after her. May that embryo grow, to be brought forth in the tenth month.
"May the paths be straight and free from thorns; may the fire-born one (Agni) convey them. I offer these five sons of yours who are still nursing into the fire at the beginning of the expiation.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter.

Then, having returned home, he should take a wife, according to the preceptor’s injunction: "Do not let the lineage of offspring be cut off. He should marry a girl who is complete in all her limbs, pleasing, younger than himself, a virgin, of a different *gotra* than his mother, not a *sapiṇḍa* relative of his mother, not previously betrothed, irreproachable, and not bearing the name of a lunar mansion, a river, or a tree. Then he sends messengers with the verse: "Straight and thornless... (RV 10.85.23).

He requests the bride-groom, saying: "To such-and-such a person of such-and-such a lineage, may you give this girl of such-and-such a lineage as a bride for the sake of dharma and progeny. When he has replied, "So be it," [the groom], having prepared auspicious dwellings during the waxing moon under an auspicious constellation, having tied the marriage-thread (*kautuka*) and performed the rites of auspiciousness and benediction (*svastyayana*), goes on foot to the bride's house. Having received the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and having performed the preparation of the hearth and other necessary materials, he gathers fried grain (*lāja*), a stone, and a new garment.

He performs the rites beginning with the entrance into the Brahma-chamber and ending with the putting on of the garment. At this time, the bride—who has had the marriage-thread tied around her wrist, who has performed the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, who wears the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), and who has sipped water—goes to the north and then beyond the fire. Standing to the south facing east, the groom goes from the north and then from the east of the fire; standing in front facing west, and holding a blade of *kuśa* grass in his hand, he [sprinkles] her with the *vyāhṛtis* and with the six verses beginning with "Prajāpati [created] women. Standing to the south facing north, he addresses her by name: "O so-and-so, of such-and-such a lineage..."

"I bestow this upon you, [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, for the sake of procreation and shared duties"—with these words, he accepts the water and the woman's property (*strīdhana*) given by the bridegroom.

Having sprinkled her with the three verses beginning *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, with the four verses beginning *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and with the entire section beginning *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, and having seated her behind the fire according to the way she entered, he then causes her to put on an unwashed garment, first setting aside that which was previously laid down, with the three verses beginning *yā akṛntan avayan*. He consecrates it with the verse *parīdaṃ vāsaḥ*.

Then, having seated her—who has sipped water—on his right side facing eastward, and while she maintains contact with him, he adorns the fire with perfumes and other offerings and sprinkles water around it: with "O Aditi, give your consent," he sprinkles from the south toward the east; with "O Anumati, give your consent," from the west toward the north; with "O Sarasvatī, give your consent," from the north toward the east; and with "O God Savitṛ, impel," he sprinkles all around in a clockwise direction. Finally, he places two upright fuel-sticks upon the fire for the sake of the after-offerings (anūyāja).

Having taken a portion from the fuel-wood (idhma) between the southern enclosing-stick (paridhi) and the fire, and between the northern enclosing-stick and the fire, he places it for the purpose of the *anūyāja* offerings during the leading forward of the *praṇītā* waters. Having anointed this fuel-wood, he places it upon the fire. Having touched water and having touched the root of the fuel-wood, he offers with the wooden spoon (*darvī*), saying "Svāhā to Prajāpati," while moving it toward the north; saying "Svāhā to Indra," while moving it toward the east; and having poured the two *āghāra* libations.

He offers the two portions of clarified butter: "To Agni, svāhā! on the north, and "To Soma, svāhā! on the south. Having offered the vyāhṛtis in the middle, he offers thirteen oblations with the verse, "Thou who liest across... (RV 10.124.8). 1.

Then he offers eight *samṛddhi* oblations with the formula, "To those who are desired, svāhā! Then he offers the *jaya* oblations with the formula, "Thought and thinking... and so forth; or he offers them in this manner with separate ladle-offerings: "To thought, svāhā! To thinking, svāhā! and so forth. Then he offers the *abhyātāna* oblations with the formula, "Agni is the overlord of beings; may he protect me, svāhā! Then, having arranged his sacred cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), he addresses the ancestors with the words, "O fathers, grandfathers... He then becomes one whose cord is over the left shoulder (*upavītī*) once again.

In this manner, he offers these seventeen *abhyātāna* oblations together with the *sādhivāda* formulas. Then he offers the six *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations consecrated with the word *svāhā*, beginning with "The one who conquers through truth, whose abode is truth... He offers the six principal oblations beginning with "May Agni come first. Both of them purify themselves with the verse "The divine waters for our aid... Then, with his right hand, he grasps the other's right hand, including the thumb, over the hair, saying "By the impulse of the god... Then he makes him stand up with these five verses beginning with "Bhaga, Aryaman..."

At this point, he should address her by name using the nominative case. Having placed a stone at the junction of the northern half-enclosing-stick (paridhi), he makes the bride step upon it with her right foot, saying: "Step upon this stone. They both circumambulate the fire three times to the right, saying: "May we, through thee, overcome all [enemies]. Then, having spread an under-layer of ghee in her joined palms, he pours fried grain (lāja) twice; for those who follow the five-fold division, he pours it thrice, saying: "I pour these fried grains. Having sprinkled them with ghee, he mixes them together with a ladle, saying: "I unite thee with fortune. Then he offers the oblation, saying: "This woman... (RV X.85.46).

Having established the second [fire] in this manner and having circumambulated it, he offers [the oblations]. Likewise the third. Having seated [the sacrificer] in his proper place, and having taken the *anūyāja* fuel-stick, he offers with the *darvī* ladle the two Vāruṇī offerings, the two Agnivāruṇī offerings, the medicinal one, the Vanaspati offering, the Prājāpatya offering, and the Sviṣṭakṛt offering; then, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt, he performs the expiatory offerings (*prāyaścitta*) with the five verses beginning "That which from my self... (*yan ma ātmanaḥ*). And this entire section begins with "Protect us, O Agni, from sin" (*pāhi no agne enasaḥ*).

Having offered oblations here with the Mahāvyāhṛtis—namely, "Bhūr agnaye ca pṛthivyai ca mahate ca svāhā"—one should offer the Praṇava at this very spot, both with the individual Vyāhṛtis and with them all together. Then, having anointed the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) and touched water in the southern half, and having taken half from each of the two northern halves of the strewn grass (*paristaraṇa*), one anoints the tip and the middle [of the middle enclosing-stick] with the wooden spoon (*darvī*); one anoints the base [of the middle enclosing-stick] in the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*). Again, one anoints the tip and the middle with the spoon, and the base in the vessel of clarified butter.

Again, [he should take] the root, the middle, and the tip from the vessel of clarified butter with the ladle. Then, having placed a single blade of grass [in the ladle] and touched water, he should cast the remainder into the fire. "He should not cast it with the very tip; for if he were to cast it with the very tip, so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having lifted the grass three times, he should also cast it after [the oblation]. Having raised his finger three times and touched the seats of the vital breaths, such as the eyes and so forth, and having taken up the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he should first cast the middle one, then the southern and the northern ones simultaneously.

He throws two fuel-sticks upward; he pushes the northern half [of the fire] among the embers. He should offer an oblation with the remnants of the ghee. Then he sprinkles water around [the fire]. He concludes the mantras as before with the words, "Thou hast assented" and "Thou hast granted permission. Taking the vessel for carrying the *praṇītā* waters, having carried it around the front of the fire, and having placed it to the south of the fire and to the west of the fire in the region of the stone, he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahman according to his ability. Then he silently sprinkles himself toward the east and the other directions.

Having sprinkled a little [water], he should wipe [his hands] with the three verses beginning *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, with the four verses beginning *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, with this entire section beginning *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, with the three verses beginning *kayā naś citra ābhuvat*, and with the two verses beginning *prājāpatyaṃ pavitram*. At this time, the Brahman priest should exit according to the manner in which he entered. From the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) until the Brahman’s exit, this is common to all *darvihoma* offerings.

Here he gives a boon to the teacher. Then he worships the deity with these [formulas]: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow," and so forth. With the words, "I am that one," he then mutters [this] into her right ear. Then, having touched her right shoulder repeatedly with his right hand, he touches the region of her heart with two [verses]: "May your heart be in my heart. Then, behind the fire, he strides the *Viṣṇukrama* steps, beginning with: "One step for strength; may Viṣṇu follow you."

He takes a small step forward with his right foot first; he follows with the left. At this very spot, he strides the seventh step. He does not step beyond the fire. At the seventh step, he mutters: "We two have become companions for seven steps. Then, standing behind the fire facing north, he pays homage to the Seven Seers (Sapta-ṛṣis) with the verse: "The Seven Seers were the first of the Kṛttikās. Then he pays homage to the Pole Star (Dhruva) with the words: "I pay homage to the Pole Star."

Having sat for a moment and having placed the *aupāsana* fire into a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like an *āhavanīya* fire, the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*) perform the rite of scattering grain (*āśīryāda*). Then he enters the dwelling. Then, taking her right hand with his right hand, he touches the southern doorpost, saying: "May you be auspicious for our two-footed ones, auspicious for our four-footed ones. He does the same for the northern doorpost. Having entered the house, he sits upon the hide of a bull with the hair side up, saying: "May the cows sit here. They remain there conversing with their kinsmen.

The two students, adorning themselves, shall observe the vow for three days, eating food that is not pungent or salty and not consisting of *śamī* grains, sleeping on the ground, and remaining apart from one another; they shall practice together. In the evening and in the morning, he offers oblations in the domestic fire with rice or barley.

In the evening, having first kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, having washed the cooking pot, heated it over the fire, and wiped it clean, having poured in a single handful of rice and carried fire around it, and having adorned the fire with perfumes and flowers, [he offers oblations] to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna, starting from the east and proceeding in each direction; thereafter, having adorned himself, touched water, and holding the *pavitra* grass in his hand, having sprinkled water around the fire with the mantra "O Aditi, give your consent," added a fuel-stick, and caused it to blaze, [he performs the rite] with his hand.

One should offer oblations of rice grains with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! in the evening; and "To Sūrya, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! in the morning. Having sprinkled water around the fire with the formula, "O Aditi, you have assented," one should first offer a smaller portion and then offer a larger portion afterward—so says the Brāhmaṇa. In this manner, one offers in the domestic fire (aupāsana). Then, furthermore, one should feed the wife. Therefore, the fire must be maintained perpetually; if it goes out, it should be produced by friction or fetched from the house of a learned Śrotriya.

He offers the expiation oblation with the verse: "O Agni, thou art the unerring one, free from imprecations; thou art truth itself, thou art the unerring one. Held by an unerring mind, with an unerring tongue thou carriest the offering; O unerring one, bestow healing upon us, Svāhā! When three days have passed, at night, he should perform the established rites beginning with the installation of the fire according to the *Dārvihomika* manual, up to the *Rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings. He should follow the model of the marriage ceremony, excluding the collection of materials such as parched grains (*lāja*), the sprinkling of water (*pratitadda*), the cleansing (*mārjana*), and the wearing of the *vāma* garment. In this way, this constitutes the model for the marriage of all [classes].

He offers the *prāyaścitta* oblations at the improper time with the four verses beginning, "O Agni, [you are] the expiation" (*agne prāyaścitta*). The ritual from the *Vāruṇī* offering onwards is the same. There is the release of the vow (*vratavisarga*). Then he releases the vow with these formulas: "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow," and so forth. Then, having caused [the officiant] to pronounce an auspicious day, he says: "May you all say 'Prosperity' for us two, the husband and wife. The response is: "Prosperity for you two, the husband and wife. Then he touches her lap with the formula: "I touch you with what is auspicious."

He enters [the womb] with the verse, "I ascend upon the bull.
