Having performed the ritual up to the point of satisfaction (*ratyantam*), he should mutter the three verses beginning with, "May the embryo enter thy womb. In this very manner, month by month, at the time of the *ṛtu*, the taking of a wife (*bhāryopayamana*) is completed.

Now, when he has returned from his teacher's house, he should take a wife; then he offers the eight *samṛddhi* oblations. Having established [the fire] for the second time in this same way, [he performs] three [oblations].
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the *Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Now, therefore, we shall describe the embellishment of the sacrificial post (*sthāgara*). A mirror, collyrium, unwashed cloth, all kinds of fragrant substances, rice grains, and a lower and upper grinding stone—these are the materials prepared for it.

After the taking of the hand, on the following day, the mother-in-law, the father-in-law, or the brother-in-law, having smeared with cow-dung a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide, having sprinkled it, having scratched the ritual marks upon it, and having sprinkled it with water, covers it with pure, white, and dry cloth. Then, having thoroughly washed their hands and feet and sipped water, the couple, with *pavitra* blades in their hands, sit down on the western half of the mound. On the eastern half, having scattered rice grains and established the lower and upper grinding stones, he wraps them with an unwashed garment.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, barley, unbroken grains, and rice, he recites the *Daśahotṛ* formula together with its *Gṛha* (house) formula in the east; the *Caturhotṛ* formula beginning with "Consciousness is the ladle" (*cittiḥ sruc*) in the south; the *Pañcahotṛ* formula beginning with "The earth" (*pṛthivī*) in the west; the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula beginning with "Agni is the hotṛ" (*agnirhotā*) in the north; the *Saptahotṛ* formula beginning with "The sun is your eye" (*sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ*) above; and the *Mahāhavirhotṛ* formula in the zenith.

At this time, the bridegroom’s sister sits down facing east on two grinding stones, grinds all fragrant substances, offers them to the deities, and anoints [the bride] with the ointment. Having had her look into a mirror, she adorns her daughter with what remains, and [anoints] the face of the son-in-law with the verses, "Agni with the Yajus-formulas" and "The army of Indra. Whatever women say in this matter, they do that; she becomes beloved. "He indeed becomes beloved," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 1.

Then, one should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblation of food either in the domestic fire (aupāsana) or in the household fire (gṛhya). At evening, [one offers] with "To Agni, svāhā! At morning, [one offers] with "To Sūrya, svāhā! [And then: "To Soma, to Dhanvantari, to Anupati, to Prajāpati, to the Viśvedevas, to all the deities, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"

Then he should offer the *bali* oblation according to the directions: to Brahmā and the attendants of Brahmā; to Indra and the attendants of Indra; to Agni, to Yama and the attendants of Yama; to Nirṛti, to Varuṇa and the attendants of Varuṇa; to Vāyu, to Soma and the attendants of Soma; and to Īśāna. Then he offers the *bali* to the household deities.

With the formula "To the mortar and pestle," he offers on the mortar and pestle; with "To the lower and upper millstones," on the lower and upper millstones; with "To the water-jar," in the water-jar; with "To the herbs and trees," at the door; with "To those who roam by day," during the day; with "To those who roam by night," at night. To the south, wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he says: "Svadhā! To the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers; to the fathers! He should pour the remainder toward the south. 2.

Now, therefore, having performed the morning oblation on the fifteenth day and having gathered the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he binds the fuel-sticks and the wood-cutter’s axe with a cord according to the prescribed characteristics; he places them where he intends to eat and kindles the fire. To the west of the fire, he lays four fuel-sticks with their tips pointing eastward. Taking both [the axe and the fuel], he places them into the fire. Having silently approached [the fire], he lays two more fuel-sticks into it.

"May [the waters] rest for the sacrifice tomorrow for the sake of the deities; I take you for the sacrifice, for the worship of the gods. Having thus addressed them and offered the *apakāra-homa*, he strews grass around the fire and, fasting that night, lies down behind the fire with his head toward the north. On the following day, having performed the bath as prescribed and the morning *homa*, he strews *darbha* grass around the fire in each direction starting from the east, with the tips pointing east and north. He places the southern blades to the north and the northern blades to the south.

From that time forward, having performed the gathering of the ritual materials, having procured rice, a vessel for the *caru* offering, a *juhū* ladle, and a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), having performed the rites beginning with the entry of the Brahman up to the consecration of the *praṇītā* waters, and having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling water, he pours out the rice across the strainer into the *juhū* ladle to the west of the fire.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour out what is pleasing to Agni"—thus at the full moon sacrifice; "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni and Soma"—thus at the new moon sacrifice. He pours out three handfuls with the *yajus* formula and a fourth silently. The wife husks [the grain]. Having triple-dehusked [the grain] and washed it three times, he pours it into the pot across the strainer.

Having cooked [the oblation] in that fire, at the time of heating the *darvī* ladle, he heats the *juhū* and sets it down. Having prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*) and poured it over [the oblation], he takes down the *caru* and pours the butter over it. Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the *vyāhṛti* offerings, he offers the sacrificial food (*havis*). At the full moon sacrifice, [the offerings are]: for Agni, for Agni-Soma, and for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; at the new moon sacrifice, [they are]: for Agni, for Indra-Agni, and for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* with the *ājya*, he cuts off two portions [of the oblation] and pours butter over them once.

For those who offer five-fold portions, he spreads the base [of clarified butter] once for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and cuts off the portion once; for those who offer five-fold portions, he does so twice. He pours clarified butter over it twice. When the *sviṣṭakṛt* has been cut off, he offers the two *pārvaṇa-homas*: "We sacrifice to the full moon, the bull, the vigorous one; may it yield us excellent heroism and thousandfold abundance of wealth. To Prāṇa, the bounteous, to the Full Moon, Svāhā! Full behind and full before. Thus at the full moon.

The new moon is fortunate and very gracious, swelling again like a cow; may she milk for us heroic vigor and thousandfold abundance of wealth for our out-breath and for the bountiful one—svāhā to the new moon! "That portion which the gods assigned to thee," thus [he says] regarding the new moon. He offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the northern half, not touching the other two oblations.

Having thrown the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) after [the offerings] and touched water, having filled the *juhū* ladle with water, wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*), and with his palm turned downwards, he pours out the wash-water from the inner enclosing-sticks once, ending toward the south, saying: "In Vaiśvānara I offer this oblation; this is a thousandfold spring with a hundred streams. In it, he has sustained the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather in the heavenly world, swelling [with milk]. Svāhā!"

Having washed the *sruva* spoon and heated it, he offers a *sruk* ladle filled with water outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), ending toward the north, with the mantra: "This ocean, a hundred-streamed fountain, spreading in the midst of the world; milking ghee for Aditi for the sake of mankind—O Agni, do not harm her in the highest heaven, *svāhā*. Having touched water, he should offer the cord used for binding the fuel-wood (*idhma*). From the oblation to Varuṇa onwards, beginning with the *jaya* offering, the ritual is established until the granting of the boon of the cow. Prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he should throw the chip from the cutting of the fuel-wood into the fire.
The New and Full Moon sacrifices are completed; the New and Full Moon sacrifices are completed.

(3) One who intends to perform the *vrīhy-āgrayaṇa* sacrifice does so on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, Kārttika, or Śatabhiṣaj. At the time of the *anvādhāna*, having performed the ritual attendance with the formula, "May the deities delight in the sacrifice! For the sake of the sacrifice, I take you for the worship of the gods," at the time of gathering the sacrificial materials, he gathers fresh grain moistened with water from a well. At the time of the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), [he says]: "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra and Agni; I pour out what is pleasing to the Viśvedevas and to Heaven and Earth."

At the time of the *homa*, [offerings are made] to Indra-Agni, to the Viśvedevas, to Heaven and Earth, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. At the time of granting the boon, he gives the first-born calf as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The remainder is well-known, following the procedure for the *sthālīpāka*. He consumes the food remaining from the oblation with the mantra: "O gods, you have led us from good to better. In this very manner, during each season of the year, one should offer oblations with food mixed with the fruits characteristic of that particular season.

At the time of the principal offerings, one should sacrifice the pairs of six seasons: Madhu and Mādhava, Śukra and Śuci, Nabhas and Nabhasya, Iṣa and Ūrja, Sahas and Sahasya, and Tapas and Tapasya. The remainder [of the ritual] is to be performed as in the case of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering and so forth. Now follows the decoration with *sthāgara* paste; now follows the Vaiśvadeva; now follows the four [offerings] by means of the first-fruits of rice on the fifteenth day.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhya-sūtra.
The first question is completed;
now begins the second question,
the first chapter.

Now, therefore, follows the *puṃsavana* (the rite for securing a male child). In the third month, during the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the fire and strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers four oblations to Dhātṛ with the verses: "May Dhātṛ give us wealth," and so forth. He also offers with the verses: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "I stretch out to thee," "Do thou, O Agni, [grant] us," "So do thou, O Agni, [grant] us," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess," and "Whatever I have done too much. At this point, some offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as subsidiary offerings.

As before, having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", he seats his wife—who has bathed, put on clean garments, is adorned, and has conversed with Brahmins—facing east behind the fire within a circular enclosure. He places a barley grain in her right hand with the words, "Thou art a bull. On both sides [of the barley], he places a barley grain and a mustard seed, or a grain of rice and a bean, with the words, "Ye two are testicles. With the words, "The dog has run away," he gives her a drop of curd to eat.

When she has sipped water, he touches her belly with these [verses]: "With ten [fingers] I touch you, so that you may give birth after ten months. Or he should insert into her right nostril a banyan shoot moistened with ghee, or a silkworm cocoon with *praiyaṅgu* porridge, or a splinter from a sacrificial post, or having churned fire from the northern-eastern corner of the hearth, [he inserts it] for the sake of laying the foundation of the fetus. If the fetus should be discharged, he wipes upwards three times above the navel with her hand while it is still moist.
"May Tvaṣṭṛ bind you, who face away, not towards us, in this bond; may he lie down for the seasons and ten months, not slaying our heroes. (1)

Now, therefore, follows the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). In the fourth month of her first pregnancy, during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, she offers four oblations to Dhātṛ with the verse, "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth," and also with the verses, "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "I stretch out to thee," "Do thou, O Agni," "So do thou, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess," and "Whatever I have overdone in this rite. At this point, some offer additional oblations known as the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*.

As before, having served food to the Brahmins and having had them pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", he seats his wife—having bathed, wearing clean garments, adorned, and having conversed with Brahmins—to the west of the fire in a circular space, facing the east. Standing to the east facing westward, taking a drop of *śalālu* with a three-pronged porcupine quill, he parts her hair upward with the *vyāhṛtis* and the two verses, "I invoke Rākā" and "Those which are thine, O Rākā," and then consecrates it, saying: "Soma alone is our..."
"O Gaṅgā, the Brahmin subjects call you 'King'; seated upon your bank, your wheel has turned. And with you, may we all cross over our enemies, as one crosses flowing streams of water. (2)

At the time of birth, she gives birth quickly. Having placed a water-pot at her head and a *tūryantī* plant at her feet, he then touches her belly with the mantra: "Just as the wind blows, just as the ocean stirs, so let your embryo stir; let it move away together with the afterbirth. With these words, he wipes her with water. When the child is born, having placed an axe on a stone and gold upon it, he holds the boy over them with the mantra: "Be a stone, be an axe, be uncrushable gold."

"Thou art indeed the Veda, named 'son'; live thou for a hundred autumns! From limb by limb thou art produced, from the heart thou art born; thou art indeed the self, named 'son'; live thou for a hundred autumns! If she does not fall [in labor], then, having taken water in his joined palms, he should sprinkle her head with it, saying: "Fall upon the sesame, do not fall upon the flesh; do not fall upon the husk; [may it be] well with thee. They carry out the *aupāsana* fire and they carry away the *sūtaka* fire. This [latter] is indeed the *uttapanīya* fire.

No ritual action whatsoever is performed upon this [image], except for the fumigation. Then he fumigates it with grains mixed with mustard seeds: "Śaṇḍa, Marka, Upavīra, Śāṇḍikera, Ulūkhala—let Cyavana perish from here, Svāhā! Ālikhat, Vilikhant, Animiṣa, Kimvadanta, Upaśruti—Svāhā! Aryaman’s Kumbhiśatru, Pātrapāṇi, Nipuṇi—Svāhā! Āntramukha, Sarṣapāṇi, Uruṇa—let them perish from here, Svāhā!"

Keśinī, Svalominī, Khajā, Apojā, and Upakāśinī—depart from here, perish! Svāhā! The Kauverikās, clothed in all manner of garments, sent by the King of the Rākṣasas, go toward the village with their kin, seeking those who have not performed the *pariṣeka* rite. Svāhā! "Kill them! Bind them! Thus speaks this messenger of Brahmā. Agni has surrounded them; Indra has surrounded them; Bṛhaspati has surrounded them. I know those Brāhmaṇas—the ones with false teeth, the disheveled-haired, and the pendulous-breasted. Svāhā!

To the night-walkers, breast-adorned, spear-handed, skull-drinking—*svāhā*! Among them, the father goes first, the one with the piercing ear; the mother follows behind, moving through the village seeking a mate—*svāhā*! The night-walking sister gazes upon the household through the twilight; she who wakes while others sleep—to her, when she has given birth, [I offer] the mind—*svāhā*! O Fire of the Black Trail, for them you [consume] the lungs, the heart, and the liver.

"O Agni, burn out their eyes, svāhā!"—with each mantra he throws [the grain] onto the embers. Then, having washed his hands, he touches the earth with the two mantras: "O thou of beautiful boundaries, that heart of thine which wanders and rests in the sky—bestow upon us a portion of that immortality; may I not weep for the misfortune of a grandson. O Earth, that heart of thine which is in the sky, in the moon—bestow upon us a portion of that immortality; may I not weep for the misfortune of a grandson. (3)

Now, therefore, follows the rite for generating intelligence (*medhājanana*). Then, having tied a piece of gold with a blade of *darbha* grass and placed it [in the child's mouth], he makes him eat clarified butter while holding it facing eastward, saying: "Bhūḥ! I offer the *ṛc*s into you, svāhā! Bhuvaḥ! I offer the *yajus* formulas into you, svāhā! Svaḥ! I offer the *sāmans* into you, svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ! I offer the *Atharvāṅgirases* into you, svāhā! Then he bathes him with lukewarm water, saying: "From the *kṣetriyā*, from *nirṛti*, from malice, I release you from the noose of Varuṇa."

"I make you blameless for the sake of Brahman; may both these, Heaven and Earth, be auspicious to you. May Agni together with the waters be well-disposed toward you; may Heaven and Earth together with the plants be well-disposed toward you. May the intermediate space together with the wind be well-disposed toward you; may the four quarters of space be well-disposed toward you. Just as the gods released the Sun from darkness and from the grasp of the Seizer, and freed him from sin, even so do I free this man from *kṣetriya*, from reproach, and from the curse, and release him from the noose of Varuṇa."

Then he places him in his mother’s lap with the verse: “The four goddesses who are the quarters, whose husband is Vāta—over whom the Sun looks on—you, O child, I place you within their reach of old age; let consumption go away and Nirṛti far off. Having placed him there, he addresses him with the mantra: “May no *rakṣas* harm your son, nor a cow that is too heavy to carry; may you be dear to wealth, flourishing under your own control. Having washed the right breast, he makes him suckle it with the words: “This boy sucks at old age; he attains a full lifespan.”

"O breast, swell for him [the child]—long life, fame, luster, glory, and strength. In this same way, he [the father] addresses the left breast. "He does not cry nor does he weep where we speak; and where we touch him," with these words the mother and father touch the boy. "May the waters be watchful in our houses; as they are watchful among the gods, so be watchful for this woman who has a good son. Having thus completed [the rite], he places a water-pot, its mouth covered, in the place of the mother's head. Every day, fumigation with grain-husks (kaṇa) should be performed. 4.1.16–20.

On the twelfth day, after the mother and son have bathed, he decorates the house. Having extinguished the *sūtakāgni* (the birth-impurity fire) and having established the *aupāsana* fire, the parents make a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), saying: "We shall give a name to the newborn boy. Thereafter, having kindled the *aupāsana* fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, they offer four oblations with the mantra "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth," just as in the *sīmanta* rite, and [recite]: "May Anumati today approve our sacrifice among the gods."

And may Agni, the bearer of oblations, bring milk to you who offer it; *svāhā*. This is for Anumati. O Anumati, do thou grant us thy approval and bestow welfare upon us; impel us toward wisdom and skill, and prolong our lives; *svāhā*. This is for Anumati. May she grant her approval, she who is ever approving, granting us undecaying wealth accompanied by progeny; may we never incur her displeasure. May that goddess, who is easily invoked, grant us protection; *svāhā*. This is for Anumati.

In whatever direction this world shines, whom the Āyus honor with their worship—she whose lap is the wide mid-air, may that goddess, easy to invoke, grant us protection. *Svāhā!* To Anumati, this [offering]. I call upon Rākā, who is easy to invoke, with a beautiful hymn; may the fortunate one hear us and take note of us herself. May she sew together our works with a needle that does not break, and may she grant us a hero-son who bestows a hundredfold and is worthy of praise. *Svāhā!* To Rākā, this [offering].

O Rākā, those benevolent thoughts of yours which are well-formed, by which you bestow riches upon the donor—with those, come to us today with a gracious mind, O fortunate one, granting thousandfold prosperity. *Svāhā!* This is for Rākā. O Sinīvālī, broad-tressed one, you who are the sister of the gods—enjoy the offered oblation; O goddess, grant us progeny. *Svāhā!* This is for Sinīvālī. She who has beautiful hands, beautiful fingers, who is prolific and possesses many offspring—to her, the mistress of the people, to Sinīvālī, offer the oblation. *Svāhā!*

"Sinīvālī, this [is for you]. I invoke Kuhū, the fortunate one, skilled in action, who is easily invoked at this sacrifice. May she grant us the renown of the ancestors; O Goddess, we shall worship you with this oblation, Svāhā! This is for Kuhū. Having thus offered twelve or thirteen oblations, [he recites]: "O Varuṇa, this [is for you]... I go to you for that truth... O Agni, do thou [protect us]... Do thou, O Agni, [be our friend]... O Agni, thou art the leader... [and] whatever in this rite I have done in excess."

At this point, some offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*. As previously described, having served food to the Brahmins and having caused them to pronounce "an auspicious day," "well-being," and "prosperity," he should give a name to the son. It should consist of two or four syllables, begin with a sonant consonant, have a semivowel in the middle, and end with a long vowel or a visarga (*abhiniṣṭāna*). For it is known that a name in which the prefix *su-* occurs is firmly established. The father and mother should both utter the words "Father" and "Mother" [in the presence of the child].

And it is known that my first name is "Jātavedas. One should give two names; for it is known that "therefore a Brāhmaṇa who has two names prospers. The second name should be derived from a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). One of the two should be secret; they should address him by one or the other. It is known that "one who performs the Soma sacrifice should take a third name. Having returned from a journey, he touches his son who has arrived, saying: "I touch you with the splendor of Soma, with the brilliance of Agni, and with the luster of Sūrya."

"I smell you with the *hiṅkāra* of cattle, O [Name], for the sake of long life and splendor—thus offered. Having smelled him on the head, he then takes his right hand, including the thumb, with his own right hand, using the five sections beginning with "Agni is long-lived. He mutters "Bestowing long life upon you from all sides" into his right ear, as performed previously.

Now follows the *puṃsavana* (rite for securing a male child); now follows the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) at the time of childbirth; now follows the *medhājanana* (production of intelligence) on the twelfth day. These are the five [rites]. Thus ends the first chapter of the second book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the second chapter.

This [rite] should be performed every year, or every six months, or every four months, or monthly, on the birth-star (janmanakṣatra). Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses beginning, "Agni is the head of the world" (*agnirmūrdhā bhuvaḥ*). Then he offers oblations with two *ṛc*-verses addressed to the deities of the respective stars according to their characteristics, namely, "May Anumati favor us today" (*anu no'dyānumatiḥ*) and "O Anumati, follow after" (*anvidanumate*). When the portion has been cut off for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he then offers additional oblations of clarified butter.

Having offered oblations to the deities of the constellations, he says: "Svāhā to the Moon! Svāhā to her who is visible! Svāhā to Day and Night! Svāhā to the Half-months! Svāhā to the Months! Thus month by month; or, "Svāhā to the Seasons! thus season by season; or, "Svāhā to the Year! thus once a year. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established up to the gift of the cow as a boon. Before the first feeding of solid food, he causes [the child] to eat the remainder of the clarified butter with the mantra: "Thou art life."

He sips water and touches his belly with two verses: "O Indra, from whatever we fear, from that grant us security; the giver of well-being, the lord of the people. This [rite] bestows long life, it bestows long life.

Thereafter, year by year, this should be performed on the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*). Then, having performed the rites from the smearing of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations of cooked food with the two verses beginning, "Agni is the head of the world" (*agnirmūrdhā bhuvaḥ*). Then he offers with the two *ṛc*-verses dedicated to the deities of the asterism, using the entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning, "He becomes ever new as he is born" (*navo navo bhavati jāyamānaḥ*), according to the respective characteristics of each. Having removed the verse addressed to Agni, he offers to Anumati, reciting two verses for each *ṛc*.

When the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been performed, he subsequently offers oblations of clarified butter: having offered to the deities of the lunar mansions, he offers with the *anuvāka* beginning "Candramā vai akāmayata" accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā*. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* onwards, the rite is established until the gift of the cow and the granting of the boon. With the verse "Āyur asi," he causes [the sacrificer] to eat the remainder of the food that was offered. He sips water and touches his belly with the two verses, "Yata indra bhayāmahe" and "Svastidā viśaspatiḥ. This is the rite for long life; this is the rite for long life.

Thereafter, in the fourth month—or in the sixth or eighth—the rite of taking the child out of the house (*upaniṣkrāmaṇa*) is performed. Under one of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) of Hasta, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Āśleṣā, or Revatī, having had the auspicious rites (*svastyayana*) performed, they lead the infant, carried on foot by his mother and provided with an umbrella, to a crossroads. Whatever women say on this occasion, that they do.

Now, in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place. During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers the following: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "To that I go for refuge," "Do thou, O Agni, release us from sin," "So do thou, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess. At this point, some offer additional oblations known as the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*.

As before, having served food to the Brahmins and having caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", he then makes him eat the threefold mixture of curd, honey, and ghee with the words: "Bhūḥ, I give to you; Bhuvaḥ, I give to you; Svaḥ, I give to you; Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, I give to you. Then he makes him eat food with the words: "I make you eat the essence of the waters and the plants. May the waters and the plants be auspicious for you. May the waters and the plants be free from disease for you. 4

In the third year, the *caulakarma* (tonsure ceremony) takes place. During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers the following: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "For that I entreat thee," "Do thou release us from sin, O Agni," "So do thou, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess. At this point, some offer additional oblations known as the *jayas*, *abhyātānas*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛts*.

As before, having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", the boy sits down to the west of the fire facing east. To the north, his mother or a student holds a lump of bull-dung with which she catches his hair. Then he mixes hot water with cold water. Having poured the hot water into the cold, he anoints the right side of the head where the hair is parted, saying: "May the waters moisten you for life, for long life, and for luster."

"O herb, protect him!"—with these words he places the herbs upright. "O axe, do not harm him!"—with these words he applies the razor. "O you who hear the gods, I shave these"—with these words he shaves. He proceeds in the same manner for the others, moving clockwise. "With that razor with which Savitṛ, the wise one, shaved King Soma and Varuṇa..."

With the words, "O Brahmans, shave this [hair] for him; unite him with wealth and splendor," he shaves from the west. With the words, "That with which Pūṣan shaved the hair of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra for the sake of nourishment—that very thing do I shave here, O [Name]," he shaves from the north. With the words, "So that he may long be well-disposed, and so that he may long behold the sun," he shaves from the east. Having shaved according to the prescribed manner, he performs the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) as previously described, or according to the *ṛṣis*. Having deposited the hair where Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, Soma, and Agni [are present]...

They searched for that treasure in many ways between heaven and earth, the waters, and the sky. He buries it in a cow-pen, in an *udumbara* tree, or in a clump of *darbha* grass, for one who is his friend. He gives [the remainder] to a Brahmin according to his faith. He presents rice-milk with clarified butter to the barber. Thus is the *godāna* ceremony prescribed for the sixteenth year; he has his hair shaved, leaving the top-knot (*śikhā*) intact. According to some, he leaves only the top-knot. Or he becomes one whose hair is burnt by fire (*agnigodāna*). He gives a cow to the teacher. This is repeated every year thereafter.
In the fourth month, the ceremony of going out [of the house]; then in the sixth month, the first feeding with solid food; in the third year, the five [ceremonies].
Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the third chapter.

Then, on a pure and level spot, having thrice cleared the site for the fire-altar with a wooden splinter and cast away the splinter, and having touched water and sprinkled it with water containing fire-particles, he digs. "Whatever in this [site] is impure, that he thereby removes; he sprinkles it with water for the sake of pacification," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Having selected five *prasthas* of pure, white, dry sand that is not damp, he prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) that is square, measuring one *aratni* on each side, sloping toward the north and east, and one *prādeśa* deep. With rice grains, he draws a line from south to north on the right side; likewise in the middle; likewise on the left side. With rice grains, he draws a line from west to east at the back; likewise in the middle; likewise in front.

Having set aside the rice grains, touched water, and sprinkled the ground with water, he should establish the fire with the mantra: *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ pratiṣṭha*. Then, having prepared sacrificial grass (*barhis*) one cubit long (thirty-six finger-breadths), three wooden sticks as enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*)—the middle one being the thickest, the southern one thinner than the middle, and the northern one the thinnest and shortest—and twelve pieces of fuel-wood each a thumb’s length, as well as eighteen pieces of wood suitable for sacrifice, a vessel for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇī*), a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), and a vessel for Prajāpati;

The pouring of the *praṇītā* water is one-fourth of a *prastha*; the vessel for the *caru* offering is two parts of a full *prastha*. The measure of the portions (*vadāna*) is stated to be the size of a thumb-joint; the measure of the oblation (*āhuti*) is four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*). The measure of the *darvī* ladle is twenty-one thumb-joints: its front part is fourteen thumb-joints, its raised portion is two thumb-joints, and the cavity is five thumb-joints. Such is the *sruk* ladle. The *pavitra* strainer is a span (*prādeśa*) long. Such also is the *upaveṣaṇa* fire-stirring stick. Thus is explained the instruction on the measures for the *homa* sacrifice. 1.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the Nāndīmukha ancestors on the preceding day. During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having prepared food either saying, "I shall perform it tomorrow," or on the very next day, he invites pure Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas.

Having put on a clean, white, and dry garment, wearing the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder, and having sipped water, he offers four oblations of white balls made of curd, rice, and fragrant white flowers, saying: "To Agni, to Soma, to Prajāpati, to the Viśvedevas, to the Ṛṣis, to the Bhūtas, to the Pitṛs, and to all deities, obeisance! Having spread Darbha grass with the tips pointing eastward upon the fire-altar, he places eight oblations upon them, saying: "To Agni, to Soma, to Prajāpati, to the Viśvedevas, to the Ṛṣis, to the Bhūtas, to the Pitṛs, and to all deities, obeisance! He causes sacrificial food to be given to the Brāhmaṇas.

Eating beans, fish, meat, and other foods with curd is another [alternative]. Then, having taken four items—rice (*vrīhi*), barley (*yava*), *puṣya* grains, and mustard seeds—and having taken a water-pot together with those very items, he says: "Oṃ, may your minds be composed; may you be gracious. To this, the others should reply according to the purpose: "May the ancestors, together with the *praṇava*, be pleased at the *nāndīmukha* ceremony. "We shall declare the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) for this rite. Having performed the preliminary rites from the preparation of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) up to the *upanāndī*, he performs the rites beginning with the water-offering and ending with the *śikhā*.

Having again performed the salutation beginning with the mental visualization (*kalpanā*), he performs the *anvāhārya* offering and so forth, starting with the *praṇava*. In other cases—excluding the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and the naming-rite (*nāmakaraṇa*)—the *nāndīśrāddha* is completed on the preceding day; the *nāndīśrāddha* is completed.
In each of those instances, the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) and so forth is specifically prescribed.
I shall now explain in detail the subsidiary part of the ritual for the sake of purification:
intending to have the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) proclaimed, one who is pure, wearing white garments,
with hands purified by sacred grass (*pavitra*) and having sipped water (*ācānta*), should then commence the rite.

One should cause the pure and excellent twice-born, who are learned in the Vedas, whose feet have been washed, and who have sipped water (ācamana), to enter and sit in pairs upon seats prepared with *darbha* grass;
having seated them, one should wash a new pitcher with water and fill it.
Then, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with unbroken grains (akṣata) accompanied by fruits— the auspicious, stainless vessel filled with āḍhaka—
having placed it upon darbha grass with a tuft of hair and its mouth covered.
Then, having properly honored the best of the twice-born who are seated,
he should offer water and the other items, saying: "Water, fragrance,
and flowers," and "May the waters be auspicious," and "May the fragrances protect."
They should say, "May there be joy"; the other twice-born ones should say, "May it be so," and "May the rite be auspicious. Having spoken thus, he gave water to the Brahmins;
[they said], "The waters, well-being, may the rite be auspicious," and the other twice-born ones should say, "May it be so."
Then the twice-born [host] should give them food to eat, saying, "This is the *anvāhārya*";
the others should accept it, saying, "May our *anvāhārya* be well-prepared," whether it be boiled rice or raw rice grains.
The twice-born should also give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), saying, "This is the *dakṣiṇā*."

"May the *svasti* and other blessings protect; may there be much to give"—thus [the host says], and the others should accept with "May it be so. Regarding unbroken rice (*akṣata*), one should say "May it be unbroken, may it be uninjured," ending with "May it be so," once they have been honored.
One should have [the officiants] recite while their hands rest on the names [of the ancestors] who have partaken;
thereafter they should rise, saying, "May our minds be concentrated," and [the others respond], "Our minds are concentrated; may you be gracious."

They should say, "We are pleased," and what is called *śānti* (pacification) and *puṣṭi* (nourishment) is also expressed as *tuṣṭi* (contentment), *ṛddhi* (prosperity), "may there be no obstacle," and "may there be long life. May there be health, auspiciousness, and success in one's undertakings.

Thus the Brahmins should say at nightfall. They should respond, "May it be so, accompanied by the *praṇava*. "May Prajāpati be pleased; may the blessed Lord Prajāpati be pleased. In this manner, whatever is prescribed for each respective rite should be recited. "May you declare it an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). "Om, an auspicious day! "May you declare prosperity (*svasti*) for the one named [so-and-so]. "Om, prosperity! "May you declare success (*ṛddhi*). "Om, may there be success! "Om, three times. "May there be the success of the auspicious day; may the rite be auspicious."

The response is as follows: "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. The response is: "O venerable Nāndīmukha ancestors. One should sprinkle oneself with the mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, just like the sprinkling of the *praṇītā* water. The auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) is concluded. 4.

Now we shall explain the *kautuka* ceremony. Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), "I shall perform the binding of the *kautuka* for the boy Paramasvāmiśarman," one should take rice, a water-pot, a boar’s tusk, a thorny branch, a conch shell, a mirror, collyrium, and the *kautuka* thread; placing these together in one spot, at night, having decorated the house with a canopy for the assembly hall and other ornaments, having smeared it with cow dung, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains, and having placed the water-pot to the north of the mound, [one proceeds] to the south of the pot.

Having set out the ritual materials and seated four Brahmins with well-washed hands and feet, one for each direction, he himself sits upon *darbha* grass and begins the rite. Having seated the boy to be consecrated to his right, he sprinkles his own heart with water while reciting the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, and then mutters these sections together with the Brahmins: *kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīm*, *indraṃ vo viśvataspari*, and *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*.

"O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations; I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise. With the bones of Dadhyañc, O missile of the eye, O missile of the mind, we cause the rival to fall"—thus [he recites] to the end. Having muttered these sections, the maternal uncle sits down near the boy, takes three items beginning with a porcupine quill and ending with a conch shell, and, having passed them along the boy's right arm, he rotates them three times clockwise. Then, taking collyrium, he applies it to the right eye.

Taking up a mirror, he shows his face. Taking up a thread, [he recites]: "I anoint the demon-slaying, vigorous steed; I approach the most beloved friend for protection. Agni, sharpening himself with our rites, kindled, may he protect us from harm by day and by night. All those deeds of yours, O Maghavan Indra, which you have performed at the libations for the one who presses the Soma, are to be proclaimed.

"Whatever wealth of the pigeon was gathered for the man, you disclosed it to Śarabha, the kinsman of the seers"—having tied this as a thread, he performs the protection with the words: "The Bṛhat-sāman, which sustains the kṣatra and possesses increased virility; the Triṣṭubh, adorned with vigor and fierce heroes; with the fifteen-fold stoma of Indra, protect this center with the wind and the ocean. Thus he provides protection.

Then, taking rice grains, he performs the protection rite with these Ṛg and Yajus verses beginning with: "May the Vasus protect you from the east with the Rudras; may the wife of Pīvarī, whose neck is glistening with clarified butter, grant this very blessing"; "Full vessel after full vessel becomes new as he is born"; "We worship Tryambaka"; "O Viṣṇu, you are our closest relative"; and "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu. In this manner, having turned along the left arm of the woman, he causes her to turn clockwise.
"Where there is the *nāndī-śrāddha*, there is the *kautuka* (marriage thread)," so says the venerable Āgniveśya. 5
Now, in a pure and unblemished place; now, therefore, for the sake of the Nāndīmukha ancestors; here and there; or indeed, according to one's faith; now, the five auspicious rites (kautuka).
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

One intending to build a hall should bathe during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Tiṣya (Puṣya), the two Uttaraphalgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, or the two Viśākhās. Having gone to where there is water, having established the fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers these: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "For that I entreat thee," "Do thou release us from this sin, O Agni," "Thou indeed, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess. And [he recites]: "Whatever in this rite I have overdone."

In this regard, some offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*. As before, having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity!", having put on a new garment, and having touched water, he takes up the fire with the formula, "By the impulse of the god... Having traced a circle three times clockwise with the formula, "It has been traced around," he digs the pits as required and places the earth inside. [With the verse: "Right here I fix the firm house; may it stand in security, dripping with ghee."

"O house (śālā), may we follow thee, having all heroes, possessing good heroes, and with unharmed heroes," with these words he raises the southern door-post. "Be thou firmly established, O house, rich in horses, rich in cattle, rich in pleasantness; swelling with vigor and milk, rise up for great good fortune," with these words he raises the northern one. "May a young boy come to thee, may a calf [come] along with the moving world; may a golden jar, the pitchers of curd, come to thee," with these words he touches the house when it has been measured out.

In this very manner he erects the pillar; in this manner he touches it: "By Truth, ascend the pillar, O fierce beam, shining brightly; drive away our enemies. Then grant us wealth together with heroic sons"—with these words he places the backbone (the ridge-pole). "May she not be a rival wife; may she be a refuge, a pleasant one; O Goddess, thou art measured out by the gods in the beginning. Clothed in grass, well-disposed, be auspicious to us—be a blessing to our bipeds and a blessing to our quadrupeds"—with these words he touches the thatched roof.

Then, on the Rurākā day, having established the fire for the pacification of the site (vāstuśamana) in the inner chamber during the night and having performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers two [oblations] with the verses "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*) and "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*).

O Vāstoṣpati, be our furtherer; O Indu, increase our household with cattle and horses. May we remain unaging in your friendship; as a father his sons, favor us. Svāhā! Let death depart; let immortality come to us. May Vaivasvata grant us fearlessness. Like the leaf of a tree, may wealth fall upon us; may the Lord of Might attend to us. Svāhā! Go away, O Death, along your own path, which is other than the way of the gods.

"To you who have eyes, to you who have ears, I speak: do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes. Svāhā! To me, O Varuṇa; for that I entreat you; from us, O Agni; may he [protect] us, O Agni; you, O Agni, are the path; O Prajāpati, whatever of this ritual I have done in excess. And here some offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*—so says the venerable Āgniveśya.

Now we shall explain the ritual for the pond (*taṭāka-kalpa*). Without having performed worship, he approaches the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the verse: "The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky. Then, having turned clockwise, having placed [the fire] toward the west, having prepared a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*) behind the sacrificial post, and having established the fire and strewn grass around it, he performs the *agnimukha* rite and offers oblations with the two verses: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa" and "For this I entreat thee."

He offers cooked oblations from the *oṣadhi* and *vanaspati* [vessels] with two verses beginning, "The herbs that have been born. Then he offers cooked oblations from the *prāsāda* [vessel] with two verses beginning, "O Vāstoṣpati, O Vāstoṣpati. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter: "To Brahman, svāhā! To Rudra, svāhā! To Yama, svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To Śrī, svāhā! To Yaśaskara, svāhā! To Day, svāhā! To Night, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! To Candramas, svāhā!"

He offers twelve oblations with the formula, "To the constellations, svāhā! He recites this entire section beginning with, "To the well-springs, svāhā! To the waters, svāhā! The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the granting of the boon of a cow. Having prepared a full sacrificial offering (*bali*) consisting of milk-rice and sesame powder mixed with milk, marked with the proper signs, and having scattered the offerings, he causes [the officiant] to recite either the *Yamasūkta* or the *Puruṣasūkta*. Then, having made his way to the surging ocean, bathed, sipped water, and put on a new garment, he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

"He gives gold and grain to the Brahmins; having caused dancing, singing, instrumental music, and so forth to be proclaimed, and having adorned the entire world, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu—so said the Blessed Āgniveśya. (3)

Now, one who considers himself as if unpurified—just like a thief or a killer of an embryo—is he who emits semen in a non-vaginal place, whether it falls during sleep or due to a desire for women. On either the new moon or the full moon day, having shaved his hair, beard, body hair, and nails, bathed, and dressed in clean garments, he undertakes the vow according to the rule of a student (*brahmacārin*) for a year, a month, twenty-four days and nights, twelve nights, six nights, or three nights.

He shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, and he shall not sit upon a high seat; he should loathe falsehood. Subsisting on milk is the primary rule. Alternatively, consuming barley-gruel, he should perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance, or he may beg for alms—a rice gruel if he is a Kṣatriya, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) if he is a Vaiśya.

In the forenoon, having established the sacred fire according to the ritual of the *pākayajña* and having kindled it, he should offer oblations of clarified butter verse by verse with these three sections: "Whatever debt I have incurred to the gods through divine play, or whatever debt I have incurred while not gambling," and "Bestowing long life upon you from every side. Then, having offered four oblations with the verses beginning "In the lion, in the tiger, and in the viper," and four oblations with the verses beginning "O Agni who returns, O Agni Aṅgiras, return with vigor and wealth," the sacrificer, with fuel-sticks in hand, stands in his place for Vaiśvānara.

Having worshipped with the hymn of twelve verses beginning with "We declare," he offers a fuel-stick with the mantra: "Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech—from all that, O Agni, deliver me; for you know the truth as it truly is, svāhā! Having offered the fuel-stick, he gives a boon. The ritual from the *jaya* offerings onwards is established up to the giving of the boon consisting of a cow.

Having performed the service in a single fire, then at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), having offered a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verses, "O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, whatever debt I incurred while not gambling," and "Bestowing long life upon you from all sides," one who is about to begin the *agnihotra* should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula; one about to begin the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) should offer the *caturhotṛ*; one about to begin the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*) should offer the *pañcahotṛ*; for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*; and for the Soma sacrifice the *saptahotṛ*.

Now, therefore, one who desires purification, or one who is about to establish the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), or one who is about to undertake some other great rite, should fast during the first half of the month under an auspicious constellation. At dawn, having departed from the village toward the east or the north, having performed the purificatory rites and sipped water, and having bathed as prescribed, he should return home—whether from rivers or from a pure reservoir—and being pure, having put on two clean, unwashed garments, he should kindle the fire and perform the rites as at the *darśa* sacrifice, up to the time of the offering, [reciting] "devasya tvā... and so forth.

Having recited thus, he should offer three handfuls with the *yajus* formula, "I offer what is pleasing to Gaṇa," and the fourth silently. He cooks it with clarified butter. Having performed the rites up to the offering to Agni, he should make oblations of the food mixed with ghee. He should offer verse by verse the following: the *kṣmāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the two groups of hymns beginning with *mṛgāra* and *aṃhomuc*, the *pāvamānya*, the *kūśmāṇḍya*, and the verses addressed to Vaiśvānara.

He should offer oblations with the verses: "This I implore of you, O Varuṇa, according to truth," "Do thou [protect] us, O Agni," "So do thou [protect] us, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess," and so forth. From the *jayā* offerings onwards, the procedure is established up to the granting of the boon of a cow. Having given himself to the Guru here, and having performed auspicious rites together with his wives, he goes to a crossroads. There, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one *gocarya* with cow-dung, having placed a vessel upon it, and having strewn grass around it, he fills it with water while reciting the section of the text beginning with "May the sins depart" and ending with "In the lion is my wrath."

Then, taking the vessel and standing facing the east, he should recite: "Go away, O Evil One! Become a destroyer again for us, O Evil One, in the world of the well-done. O Evil One, place [us] unharmed; whoever among us, O Evil One, does not abandon you—that one do thou slay. Let him not enter into this [world], the thousand-eyed immortal. He who hates us may perish; him whom we hate, do thou slay. Having thus placed it behind him and touched water, he should turn to the right. In this very manner he should perform the three daily libations for seven days, remaining silent, eating sacrificial food, and restraining the activities of his senses.
One is liberated from all sins, even from great transgressions;
one is freed even from the accumulation of evil committed in old age, youth, or childhood, or that which was produced in previous births.
At the conclusion of the meal for the twice-born, one should cause cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold to be given to those who have eaten, along with milk-rice and clarified butter.
Having performed this, one conquers all worlds; so said the venerable Āgniveśya. 5

Now we shall explain the Śatābhiṣeka (the hundredfold consecration). If one thousand months have elapsed—that is, a hundred years—during the northern course of the sun, under an auspicious constellation, having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!", then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground up to the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters, he should rise and, in front of the fire, prepare a square altar (*sthaṇḍila*) in each direction with rice grains and fruits in all directions.

Having scattered flowers, rice, unbroken grains, barley, and sesame seeds, and having prepared two bundles of grass (*kūrca*) one span long with their tips pointing eastward, he places them upon the leveled ground with their tips facing east. Then, having placed twenty-five jars made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, and having wrapped them with thread, he sets them down upon the sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*). Having strewn [grass] all around and placed the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*) therein, he pours water into the water-strainer which is joined with all types of perfumes, fruits, flowers, and sesame seeds.

Having placed a *kūrca* [seat-grass] and having adorned the jars with unbroken rice, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth, he invokes [the deities] into the jars of all the directions. Then, in the center, he invokes: "I invoke Brahmā; I invoke Prajāpati; I invoke Parameṣṭhin; I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha; I invoke Svayaṃbhū.

Having thus invoked them, and having invoked Indra and the others in the jars in sequence starting from the east, saying "I invoke," and having performed the rites beginning with the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), and having worshipped the deity, and having honored him with the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, he bathes him according to the rule.

Having performed the purification with the three verses beginning *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, with the four verses beginning *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and with this entire section beginning *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, he gratifies them with these very names, saying, "Salutation to so-and-so! Salutation to so-and-so! He should offer perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and incense, and cover [the vessel] with a new, unwashed cloth.

He performs the consecration with twelve jars using the Varuṇa-hymn, the remainder of the *Śeṣatādanta* hymn, the water for the removal of curses (*śāpavetrika*), or else with the four verses beginning with "He who has gone beyond" (*pare paretya*) according to their meters, and with the five sections beginning with "Agni is long-lived" (*agnirāyuṣmān*). Then he performs the sprinkling with these. Then, having washed his hands and feet and sipped water, he puts on a new, unwashed garment. In the same manner, he subsequently anoints himself all over with all kinds of perfumes mixed with sandalwood and aloe-wood; then he causes him to gaze at the sun with the verse, "By truth... (*ā satyena*).

Then he worships him with the verses: "Upward from the darkness," "Upward that [splendor]," "The bright eye, beneficial to the gods," and "He who has risen. Having spread out *erakā* grass and sat upon it facing east, he then offers oblations of clarified butter with the six verses beginning with "Brahma, being born. The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established as complete, ending with the gift of the cow as a boon.

Then, having placed the remnants of the oblation upon a clump of *darbha* grass in front of the fire with the two verses, "Bestowing life upon you from every side" and "This Agni is most excellent, the giver of life," and then, having placed gold in the remnant of the clarified butter with the four verses beginning with "For Indra, thee, the radiant one, [I place] the radiant one," he shows his reflection in the remnant of the clarified butter while reciting the half-verses according to their meters. With the verse, "O Agni, grant me life and splendor," he gives [the gold] to a Brāhmaṇa. [He says: "Thou art life; thou art all-encompassing life."

"Thou art all life; thou art the full span of life. With these four verses in their respective meters, which conclude with "Whence the garment, swift as thought," he pronounces the benediction. Having fed the Brahmins with three-fold food and having caused them to pronounce blessings, [he says], "May the Brahmin be pleased. Then, with his face turned toward the north, he circumambulates the village. Then he proceeds, accompanied by various coverings, secondary offerings, chowries, and palm-leaf fans.

Then, having mounted the child upon a swift vehicle accompanied by the sounding of conchs and songs, one should mutter the *Svastisūkta*, beginning with "May he measure out well-being for us" (*svasti no 'bhimīta*), and so forth, up to "May there be well-being in narrow straits; may there be fearlessness for us"—this is the same [as before]. Then, one offers the door-oblation (*dvārabali*). Then, having gone inside the house, having honored the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, they say to the children:

"A thousand-year life, a thousand months! Having shown the young moon, the Brahmin attains union and residence in the same world as [the deity] through his sons and grandsons—thus said the blessed Āgniveśya. 6.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa has committed acts such as the great sins (mahāpātaka) that cause him to fall from his caste, what should his sapinda relatives do?
On an inauspicious day, in the evening, the sapinda relatives should assemble together at a crossroads;
likewise, the ground should be smeared with cow dung.
Having placed the censured water-jar for cold and hot water,
his female slave should thereafter fill the jar with water;
as they were rising, the sapinda relatives spoke these words to him.
From this point forward, one should not engage in conversation, travel together, share a seat or bed, or eat with him;
having uttered these words, one should perform the circumambulation of the jar.
Or they should strike him with the heel of the left foot while remaining near him; then, all of them, without looking back, should go away as previously stated,
and thereafter perform the various penances according to the scriptures as prescribed.
Having been purified in this manner, he should thereafter bathe in a clean reservoir of water; then,
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, he should enter the crossroads, smear it with cow dung, and install a new water-pot (*kumbha*).

Then, having filled [the jar] with the water of a slave-girl, one should cause the sapindas to wait around it; then, having performed the recitation of the *svasti* formula, one should circumambulate the jar from left to right,
drink the water contained in the jar, and enter one's own home.
Then, having fed the Brahmins, he should eat together with his sapinda relatives.

For in this way his ancestors—his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—as well as the elders of his lineage, will pronounce blessings upon him who is thus purified in soul. From that point forward, he shall indeed fulfill all his desires; so he should do, so he should do. 7.

Now we shall explain the ritual procedure for the offering (*bali*) to the crows that portend auspicious and inauspicious signs. Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, one should smear a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, sprinkle it with water, scratch the ritual marks upon it, and sprinkle it again with water; then, moving clockwise, one prepares a seat for the crows, saying: "I prepare a seat for the Aṅkatas; I prepare a seat for the Kaṅkatas; I prepare a seat for the sons of Kadrū; I prepare a seat for the Vāsas."

I assign them to the sons of Brahmā. Then he invokes them: "Neither the Kapilas, nor the Kokilas, nor the Ariṣṭas, nor the Mahāriṣṭas, nor those who are mere crows—let the birds, the crows that eat offerings, come quickly! I invoke the Kaṅkatas; I invoke the Kaṅkatas; I invoke the sons of Kadrū; I invoke the crows."

Having invoked them with "I invoke the sons of Brahmā," he should purify [the area] with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," the four verses beginning "The golden-colored, pure, purifying ones," and this entire section beginning "Pavamāna, the one who dwells in the light. Then, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, saying "Salutation to such-and-such! Salutation to such-and-such!", he should offer a ball of rice-milk (*pāyasodana*) in a clockwise direction, saying "To such-and-such, Svāhā! To such-and-such, Svāhā!". Finally, having performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) with "Salutation to such-and-such! Salutation to such-and-such!", he should say: "You are truth; speak the truth; delight in truth, O crows!"
"One should speak the truth here and not eat the offering of falsehood," he said;
then [he addressed him] again regarding the killing of a mother or the killing of a father.
He who would eat an improper sacrificial offering (mithyābali) would incur that evil deed;
he who would eat an improper sacrificial offering would incur the same evil as one who has offered oblations into a hundred tawny cows, especially to Brahmins.
He who would eat an improper sacrificial offering would incur that evil deed.
Thus one should speak:
for existence one should take the left [hand], but for non-existence the right;
furthermore, "it does not exist" is one response, and "it will exist" is another.
"In the middle, for the sake of attaining all goals," he said. Having understood this, one should undertake all activities; one should undertake all activities—thus [it is taught]. 8.

Now we shall explain the ritual procedure for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). During the waxing moon, under an auspicious lunar mansion, a Brahmin maiden or a Brahmin widow, having thoroughly washed her hands and feet and being pure, dressed in clean, unwashed white garments, should go to where cotton grows. Having gathered ripe fruit and having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, she should install the ritual diagram (*yantra*) in its center. Sitting there facing either east or north, she should spin the thread over and over again.

He never treats anyone with contempt; he gives to a Brāhmaṇa. Then the Brāhmaṇa, having hired [the reciter] with gold, grain, or wealth, and having washed his hands and feet thoroughly, sipped water, and holding the *pavitra* grass in his hand, sits down facing either the east or the north. With the fingers of his right hand joined together, he counts ninety-six times, triples that number, and then purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ" and the two verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ."

With the anuvāka beginning "The purifying one, the dweller in heaven," he calls the Brāhmaṇas. Standing to the east, one [of them] and two to the west, having made the thread threefold with his right hand by reciting "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he fastens it upon a sacrificial tree. He strikes it with a blade of grass. Taking the thread from hand to hand, he winds it around his knees with the words: "Bhūḥ! Agni, the earth, and me; and the three worlds and the year."

"May Prajāpati settle you! By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! Then the second: "Bhuvaḥ! Vāyu and the intermediate space and me, and the three worlds and the year—may Prajāpati settle you! By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! Then the third: "Svaḥ! Āditya and the sky and me, and the three worlds and the year—may Prajāpati settle you!"

With the words, "By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras," he then makes a knot, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May Prajāpati establish you—the moon, the quarters, myself, the three worlds, and the year. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras."

Then he becomes one who wears the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītī*). [He recites: "I invest myself with the sacrificial thread for the sake of long life, for good progeny, for heroic vigor, for sovereignty over all the Vedas, for prosperity, for glory, for sacred knowledge (*brahman*), and for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Having sipped water, he becomes fit for all rites; he becomes fit for all rites.

Now we shall explain the propitiation of the deities. Having put on clean, white, and dry garments, with the *pavitra* grass in hand and having sipped water, he should perform the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*). Then, having performed his fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), he should invoke the deity in a mandala, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), in water, in the heart, or in a blazing fire.
In the same way, having invoked Hari into an image, one should worship him;
the wise person should mentally contemplate a lotus within the heart, and in the center of that lotus's pericarp, he should perceive the light established there.
In the midst of the light is Mahāviṣṇu, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;

having thus invoked him with these twelve names, one should worship him with sandalwood paste and other offerings up to the lamp, beginning with the mantra "O Keśava. Thereafter, [one should proceed].
One should likewise worship Hari after having invoked him in a mandala, and likewise on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and likewise in a blazing fire.
Furthermore, when making an image, one may do so with gold, or with metal, or, if unable, with stone.

Having fashioned [an image] with four arms holding a conch, a discus, and a mace, and having installed it either in a house or in a celestial chariot (vimāna), he performs the consecration with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," with the four verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," and with the entire section beginning "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ."

Then, saying "I invoke the deity," he invokes [the deity] by the names beginning with Keśava; then, having offered a garment with the mantra "yuvam vastrāṇi"; then, having offered perfume with "gandhadvārām"; then, having offered a flower with "yo'pāṃ puṣpaṃ veda"; then, having offered incense with "dhūrasi"; then, having offered a lamp with "uddīpyasva," he performs the anointing with the remains of that [lamp-oil].

Saying, "Water for honoring," he should offer the *arghya*; saying, "Water for the feet," he should offer the *pādya*; and saying, "Water for sipping," he should offer the *ācamanīya*. Then he cooks the *caru* (oblation of rice). He cooks it in milk with either an *āḍhaka*, half an *āḍhaka*, a *prastha*, or an *ājya* (measure) of water. Then there is the food. Having offered it, he performs the sprinkling, saying, "I sprinkle you, the Real, with the Right" (*satyaṃ tvarttena pariṣiñcāmi*), or "I sprinkle you, the Right, with the Real" (*ṛtaṃ tvā satyena pariṣiñcāmi*).

Then, having touched the food, he makes an under-layer with the ten-verse hymn beginning, "I am the first-born of the Cosmic Order," and with the formula, "Thou art the under-layer of immortality. Then follows the offering to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*). "To the *prāṇa* [breath], seated within, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspicious, for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the *prāṇa*!"—thus for the *prāṇa*. "To the *apāna* [down-breath], seated within, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspicious, for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the *apāna*!"—thus for the *apāna*. "To the *vyāna* [pervading breath], seated within, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspicious, for the sake of non-burning."—thus for the *vyāna*.

"To Vyāna, Svāhā!"—thus, established in Vyāna, I offer the nectar (amṛta) into Udāna; may the Auspicious One enter me for the sake of non-burning. "To Udāna, Svāhā!"—thus, established in Udāna, I offer the nectar into Samāna; may the Auspicious One enter me for the sake of non-burning. "To Samāna, Svāhā!"—thus, [established] in Samāna. In this manner, he performs the fivefold oblation of breath. Then, having approached the Deity, he mutters the twelve names beginning with Keśava and the verse: "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu."

Then he performs the covering with the mantra, "Thou art the lid of immortality" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), bringing water and covering [the vessel]. With the words, "He who knows the abode of the waters becomes possessed of an abode," he prepares the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). Then, having offered betel, he dismisses the deity. Having dismissed Keśava either to the Ocean of Milk, to Mount Meru, or to the solar orb, and having placed the food offering (*naivedya*) in the water, he gives a fourth part to a Brāhmaṇa; thus said the venerable Āgniveśya. 10.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Sun (Ravikalpa). It is intended for one who desires long life, or brilliance, or fame, or prosperity, or sons, or beauty. He should not eat at night, nor sleep on the ground, and he must abstain from sexual intercourse. Having dressed in clean, white, and dry garments, being self-restrained and pure, he becomes ritually fit. Then, when the next day has dawned on a Sunday, as soon as the sun has risen, one should smear a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung in the center, and place upon it a lotus made of gold or silver; or else, [one may do so] upon the bare ground.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
one should place Sūrya on the eastern petal and Divākara in the south-eastern [petal];
having placed Vivasvat in the southern [petal], one should place Bhaga in the south-western [petal].
One should place Varuṇa on the western petal, Indra in the north-western, Savitṛ in the north-eastern, and Āditya on the northern petal;
then one should place Arka, together with Vājina, on the eastern petal along with the pericarp.
One should place Sahasrāṃśu in the south, Mārtāṇḍa in the western direction, and the god Ravi in the north; in the center of that, one should place Bhāskara.

Having thus placed the twelve Ādityas in their proper order, and having placed the form of all the Ādityas in the center, one then purifies [the deity] with water using the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ," the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," and this entire section (anuvāka) beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ."

Then, the red-colored preceptor, having worshipped with red sandalwood paste, red flowers, perfumes, incense, and lamps, saying "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such!", and having offered water from a lotus-shaped vessel while performing prostrations, saying "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such!", he then dismisses the deities. The dismissal is performed with the twelve names in the same manner as the previous invocation. He should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor according to his ability.

Thus, having performed worship on the Sundays throughout the year and having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one who desires long life shall obtain a long life; one who desires splendor becomes splendid; one who desires fame becomes famous; one who desires prosperity becomes prosperous; one who desires a son obtains a son; and one who desires all things obtains everything. Thus spoke the Blessed Āgniveśya. [11] And the *praṇava* has Agni as its deity and is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.
The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the seer is proclaimed to be Brahman.

Listen as I pay homage to the *praṇava*, which embodies all the deities. Regarding what was said to Viṣṇu concerning the *praṇava* with its three syllables—the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*: *a* is Agni, *u* is Sūrya, and *m* is Candra; *a* is Brahmā, *u* is Viṣṇu, and *m* is Īśvara; *a* is neuter, *u* is masculine, and *m* is feminine; *a* is the mixed color (*miśravarṇa*), *u* is red (*raktavarṇa*), and *m* is white (*śvetavarṇa*).

They are beyond comparison, consisting of the syllable *oṃ*, comprising the three times, comprising the three worlds, consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, and comprising the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. By the utterance of the *praṇava*, they bestow great sovereignty; situated in the *mūlādhāra*, the *anāhata*, and the middle of the eyebrows, they are the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, and are acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*). "I shall declare the supreme secret. One should recite the *praṇava* thrice in the *Ṛgveda*, the *praṇava* in the *Yajurveda*, and the *praṇava* in the *Sāmaveda*. The subsequent verse is for the sake of further explanation. 12.

Now, [the section] on building a hall; now we shall explain the ritual for a pond; now one should offer oblations with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras; now, therefore, [the ritual] for one desiring purification; now, the rite of the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣeka*); now, regarding the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth of a Brāhmaṇa; now, regarding auspicious and inauspicious omens; now, the rule for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); now, the propitiation of the deities; now, therefore, we shall explain the *Ravi-kalpa*. The syllable *Oṃ* (Praṇava) has Agni as its deity; [there are] twelve [verses].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the *Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra*. Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the offerings for the planets, the guest-reception, the bali-oblations, and the ritual gifts.
The planets clearly lead a man to the abode of Yama who lacks faith, has not offered oblations, does not recite prayers, and has abandoned auspicious rites.

I shall declare the offerings for the planets of fierce activity that move along the path of the constellations, for the sake of pacification, according to the rule: month by month, season by season, at the solstices, during a lunar eclipse, a solar eclipse, at one's birth constellation, at the equinoxes, or on auspicious or inauspicious days;
by offering hospitality to those planets even once a year, one attains all desires. Having performed the procedure for the single fire as previously stated:
The Sun and Mars are red; Venus and the Moon are white;
both Mercury and Jupiter are known to be yellow;
one should know Saturn to be black, as are Rāhu and Ketu.

A wise person should provide flowers of the colors corresponding to the planets there, as well as an offering (bali), a gift (upahāra), and likewise perfumes and garlands; he should present these to all of them in due order and succession. Thus it is said.
One should offer fuel-sticks of *arka* for Āditya, of *pālāśa* for Soma, of *svādira* for Aṅgāraka, and of *apāmārga* for Budha.

For Bṛhaspati, an *aśvattha* [wood]; for Śukra, an *audumbara*; for Śanaiścara, a *śamī*; for Rāhu, *dūrvā* grass; and for Ketu, *kuśa* grass. In the center, a circle for Āditya; in the southeast, a square for Soma; in the south, a triangle for Aṅgāraka; in the northeast, a bow-shaped figure for Budha; in the north, a long rectangle for Bṛhaspati; in the east, a pentagon for Śukra; in the west, a bow-shaped figure for Śanaiścara; in the southwest, a winnowing-basket-shaped figure for Rāhu; and in the northwest, a banner-shaped figure for the Ketus.

Having performed the rites from the putting on of the garments up to the end of the *agnimukha* (the invocation of the fire), he offers oblations of cooked food: with the verses "We choose Agni as the messenger by truth" (*ā satyena*) and "He rules over these" (*eṣām īśe*), he offers to Āditya; with "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*), "In the waters Soma spoke to me" (*apsu me somo abravīt*), and "The cow has lowed" (*gaurī mimāya*), he offers to Soma; with "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*), "O gracious Earth" (*syonā pṛthivi*), and "By the Lord of the Field" (*kṣetrasya patinā*), he offers to Aṅgāraka (Mars); with "Awake! (*udbudhyasva*), "This Viṣṇu" (*idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*), and "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇo rarāṭam asi*), he offers to Budha (Mercury); and with "O Bṛhaspati" (*bṛhaspate*), "Beyond [the heavens]" (*ati*), "O Indra accompanied by the Maruts" (*indra marutvaḥ*), and "The Brahman was born" (*brahma jajñānam*), he offers to Bṛhaspati (Jupiter).

"Forward to your bright [Soma]! "Indrāṇī! "Indra for you from every side!"—these for Śukra. "May the goddesses be auspicious to us! "O Prajāpati, none other than you! "Come here, O Yama, sit upon this sacrificial grass (prastara)"—these for Śanaiścara. "With what [splendor] will he come to us, the wonderful one? "Whom the cow... "What thou, O Goddess Nirṛti, hast bound upon me"—these for Rāhu. "Making a banner, the Brahman of the gods... "The wonderful, the illuminating, for him"—these for Ketu.

One should offer into the fire oblations of clarified butter with eight thousand, eight hundred, or twenty-eight fuel-sticks soaked in ghee, reciting one verse for each offering; or one may offer clarified butter verse by verse. The sacrificial food offerings (*upahāra*) are as follows: rice cooked with clarified butter for Āditya, milk-porridge for Soma, molasses-rice for Aṅgāraka (Mars), milk-rice for Budha (Mercury), curd-rice for Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), ghee-rice for Śukra (Venus), rice mixed with sesame and ground beans for Śanaiścara (Saturn), meat-rice for Rāhu, and variegated rice for Ketu. In the absence of all these, sacrificial food fit for oblation (*haviṣya*) may be used.
