He offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the mantra, "To Aryaman, to King Soma. The ritual from the *jaya* offerings onwards is established up to the gift of the cow as a boon. He worships the cups in front of the fire.

Having purified himself with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ*, with the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and with this entire Anuvāka beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*; having worshipped [the deities] with their respective mantras using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) and paid homage; and having dismissed them, he sits down behind the fire facing east and purifies himself with water using the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ*. Then he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

One should give a tawny cow to the Sun, a conch to the Moon, a red ox to Mars, gold to Mercury, a garment to Jupiter, silver to Venus, a black cow to Saturn, a goat to Rāhu, and an elephant to Ketu. If none of these are available, one may give gold, or whatever else pleases the preceptor;
just as a machine that has become stuck is set in motion again by means of another machine.
One should always quickly bring to peace such terrible calamities as they arise;
just as armor serves as a defense against the blows of weapons,
so does pacification serve as a defense against the afflictions caused by fate.
For one who is non-violent, self-controlled, who has acquired wealth through righteous means,
and who is constantly established in his observances, the planets are always gracious;
for the planets, the cows, the lords of men, and especially the Brahmins, are likewise so disposed.
When honored, these deities honor [the worshipper] in return; when treated with contempt, they consume [him].
In the form of planetary spirits (grahas), they manifest auspicious and inauspicious results;
they manifest auspicious and inauspicious results. 1.

Now, if at an improper time a pillar should sprout, or a dove should alight in the middle of the house, or a cow should suckle another cow, or a cow should suckle herself, or a bull should scratch himself, or smoke should arise without fire, or a flame should blaze without fire, or honey should be produced, or resin should be produced, or a mushroom should grow, or a frog should appear on the ground, or a dog should give birth, or the master of the house or his wife should suffer from a burning sensation, or in other such miraculous portents—

Then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers two oblations with the verses: "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*) and "Be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ naḥ*). [He offers] "Indra and Agni" (*indrāgnī*), "With what [splendor] toward us? (*kayā naścitra*), "Who yokes [the horses] today? (*ko adya yuṅkte*), and "May you two be of one mind toward us" (*bhavataṃ naḥ samanasau*). From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established until the granting of the boon of a milch-cow. To the west of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon *śamī* leaves with the verse: "May the divine waters be auspicious to us for our protection" (*śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaye*).

Having poured together the rinsings of the cooking pot, the remnants of the clarified butter, and the remnants of the water into a vessel, he should pour them out during these portents; or he should sprinkle [the house] with the mantra: "We choose that auspiciousness of Śamyoḥ. Having prepared the food and honored the Brahmins, he causes them to pronounce blessings, saying: "Auspicious! Auspicious! The *adbhuta* (portent) has been explained. 2.

The *āyuṣya-homa-caru* (the sacrificial porridge for long life), which imitates the *āhuti* oblation, should be performed every year, or every six months, or every four months, or month by month, under the birth constellation (*janmanakṣatra*). Then, having performed the rites from the drawing of the lines for the *devayajana* up to the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water, he pours out the rice with the formula: "I pour out what is agreeable to Agni Āyuṣmat," or silently. Then he pours out the grain with the formula: "I pour out what is agreeable to Prāṇa," or silently.

Having sprinkled them with water, brought them down, husked them three times, and washed them three times, he sets them aside. Then, having poured water or milk into the pot across the strainers and placed it on the fire, he pours the rice grains into it across the strainers. Then, having placed the clarified butter on the fire and carried fire around both of them, he cleans the stirring-spoon and the dipping-spoon. Then, having cooked this sacrificial porridge (*caru*), having basted it [with butter], and having removed it from the fire toward the north, he bastes it once more when it has been set down. This indeed is the procedure for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for all *sthālīpāka* offerings.

Having performed the rites from the putting on of the garments up to the opening of the fire (*agnimukha*), he offers oblations of the cooked food. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "Bestowing life upon thee from every side," he offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation. He then offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, between the fire and the vessel of clarified butter, he places the vessel for the cooked rice (*caru*). He performs the *sahasrasampāta* oblation. [He recites: "He who is the Brahman, who extracted the Brahman, the Lord of Breath, clothed in skin, the wielder of the Pināka bow."

May the Lord God grant us life; to him I offer oblation with clarified butter, Svāhā! He who comes shining from the midst of the ocean, radiant and glowing with the brilliance of heat—may that God, casting us off from the terrible noose of death, partake of our clarified butter here for the sake of long life, Svāhā! The light of Brahman, whom the Consort of Brahman bore as a multiform, victorious embryo—the Sun, the seizer of golden light, the object of worship—him we magnify with clarified butter for the sake of long life, Svāhā!

They call her Śrī, Lakṣmī, Aupalā, Ambikā, Gā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Jayā, and Indrasenā. We satisfy with clarified butter for the sake of long life that Vidyā, whose source is Brahman, who is of like form here—svāhā! The daughters of Dakṣa, belonging to all wombs, sharing the same womb, thousands in number, universal in form and diverse in form; together with their sons, their husbands, and their companions, may they enjoy this clarified butter for the sake of long life—svāhā! May the divine hosts, multiform and ancient, not destroy our lifespan or our heroes—pramathantu vīrān.

To them I offer in many ways with clarified butter; do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes—*svāhā*! The One who was here in the beginning, from whom the guardian of the world arose—he to whom the world returns at the final transition, may that God consume our oblation of clarified butter here for the sake of long life—*svāhā*! To the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, Ṛbhus, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and all the Pitṛs...

"Having offered ghee to all the Bhṛgus, Sarpas, and Aṅgirases, we perpetually honor our own life-span; Svāhā! Having performed this one hundred and twenty-six times, it results in eight thousand oblations. From the other cooked portion, he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice. Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, "Havyavāham abhimātiṣāham," he offers with the *yājyā*, "Sviṣṭam agne. The rite is completed from the *jaya* offerings onwards up to the granting of the boon of a cow.

Then, in front of the fire, he places the remains of the oblation upon a clump of *dūrvā* grass with two verses: "Mā no mahāntam" and "Mā nas tokam. Sitting to the west of the fire, facing east, remaining silent and accompanied by his attendants, he eats the *sthālīpāka* with the formula: "Thou art life; thou art all-life; thou art whole-life; thou art complete-life; may all life be mine; may I attain all life. Having eaten and sipped water, he touches his belly with two verses: "yata indra bhayāmahe" and "svastidā viśaspatiḥ."

One should recite the *Āyuṣya* and the *Ghṛtasūkta* daily for the sake of securing well-being for boys seized by malevolent spirits (*graha*). With these very mantras, one should offer oblations; with these very mantras, one should present the sacrificial food (*bali*). One indeed becomes free from [the affliction]. This is the "Prosperous Course" (*ṛddhamayana*) for those possessed by spirits: the *Rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings, the five *Śoḍāya* offerings, the *Sarpāhuti*, and the *Gandharvāhuti*. One indeed becomes free from [the affliction]. This is the "Prosperous Course": other oblations are imitations of what has been offered, and the *Saṃśrayas* are imitations of the stages of life (*āśrama*). 3.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for conquering untimely death (*apamṛtyuñjaya*). On an auspicious lunar mansion, on one’s birth star, or on the day of one’s birth, or on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having smeared with cow dung either a temple, a riverbank, a cow-pen, a most sacred spot, or one’s own home, and having caused [the officiants] to recite "Auspicious Day," "Welfare," and "Prosperity," then, having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), and having offered the expiation oblation (*prāyaścitta*) with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," [one should offer] white *dūrvā* grass...

Having offered eight thousand, eight hundred, or twenty-eight fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood—having first mixed together curd, honey, clarified butter, and milk—and having sacrificed with the mantra "We sacrifice to Tryambaka," he then sacrifices with the mantras "May death depart," "O Death, go beyond," "Do not harm us in our elders," "Do not harm us in our children," "Tryambaka," and "Those thousand [forms] of yours. Then, having taken a portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he further offers oblations of clarified butter with the mantra: "May death perish for Śarman, born under this asterism and in this zodiac sign; may his life increase! Bhūḥ Svāhā! As before, [he repeats it] for Śarman.

"May death perish, may life increase; *bhuvaḥ* svāhā!"—as before, [he offers] for Śarman: "May death perish, may life increase; *svaḥ* svāhā!"—as before, [he offers] for Śarman: "May death perish, may life increase; *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* svāhā! Then, having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) "Sviṣṭakṛt, the bearer of oblations, the overcomer of hostility," he makes the offering with the offering verse (*yājyā*) "O Agni, well-sacrificed."

Having offered the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, and having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantra*), he places the remnants of the oblation upon a clump of *darbha* grass with the verse, "That we choose for the sake of peace and well-being. Then he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He should give it in such a way that the teacher becomes satisfied and pleased in heart. Having given to the others also according to his ability, he should feed the Brahmins. 4

Now, the oblation is indeed with the *jayā* formulas; however, he prepares the *bādhaka* [vessel], the *sruc*, and the *sruva*. Having anointed the fuel-stick of *vaibhītaka* wood with the *bādhaka* [substance] and having poured it out with the *bādhaka* *sruva*, he offers it with a fourfold-drawn portion into the *bādhaka* *sruc*. Cattle are four-footed; verily, he wins cattle.

"Mind and thought, intention and purpose, consciousness and the known, the mind and the *śakvarī* verses, the new moon and the full moon, the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*—Prajāpati gave these victories to Indra the Bull; the fierce one prevailed in the battles for the hosts. To him all the people bowed down; he became fierce and worthy of sacrifice, Svāhā! Then [he offers] the fuel-stick of *vaibhītaka* wood.

The gods and the Asuras were arrayed for battle. Indra went to Prajāpati; he gave these Jaya oblations to him, and he offered them. Then indeed the gods conquered the Asuras. Because they conquered (*ajayan*), that is the "conquering" (*jayatva*) of the Jayas. These should be offered by one who is contending; he surely conquers that host. A Brāhmaṇa says: "They should be offered at whatever rite one desires to prosper. Whatever rite he may desire, [thinking] "May this be successful for me," [he should offer them]. 5

We shall now explain the *prajārthihoma* (the sacrifice for the sake of progeny). On the bank of a river or in the shade of an *aśvattha* tree, one should smear a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung. Having established Brahmā in the eastern direction, and Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ on the two sides—with Dhātṛ to the south and Vidhātṛ to the north—one should worship them; Dhātṛ being black in color and Vidhātṛ white, while [Brahmā] has four faces and is variegated in color. Then one should worship them, first invoking Brahmā.

One should invoke Parameṣṭhin; one should invoke Hiraṇyagarbha—having thus invoked, one should perform the purification (mārjana) with the Praṇava, with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," with the four verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," and with this entire section (anuvāka) beginning "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ. Then, [one should offer] pure rice to Brahmā, mung-bean rice to Dhātṛ, and yellow rice to Vidhātṛ.

Then, having summoned that woman for the sake of the sacrificer, [he addresses her with] "Thou art reality, thou art light, thou hast gone to the Lord of All, O giver of names. On the new moon day, on the full moon day, during the two solstices, at the *vyatīpāta* conjunction, at the equinoxes, under the asterisms of Tiṣya, Rohiṇī, or Śravaṇā, or on her birthday, or when she has bathed after her menses—having caused her to put on a new garment, having given gold to the teacher, having herself put on unwashed clothes, having sipped water, and having adorned herself with perfumes and white flowers; then, from the tracing of the lines for the divine sacrifice onwards, he establishes the fire.

Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] around with the mantra, "Seven are thy fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues, seven the Ṛṣis, seven thy beloved abodes," he should sit down to the south of the women. Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the *agnimukha* offering, he should offer oblations from the cooked food with the *Puruṣasūkta*. He offers two verses each as the *yājyā* and the *puronuvākyā*. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) verse by verse. He should offer one thousand and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī* mantra.

Having touched water, he offers eight thousand oblations with the *sudarśana* mantra and eight thousand with the fire-seed (*agnibīja*) mantra, accompanied by the *praṇava*. [He may offer] eight thousand with the *praṇava*, or one hundred and eight, or twenty-eight. It is taught that the middle offering consists of one hundred and eight. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation onwards, the rite is established until the granting of the boon of the cow. Then he offers the residue (*sampāta*) upon his head. He should perform the consecration of the sacrificial site (*yajñavāstu*) with the *praṇava* ending in a salutation. That becomes pregnant for him.

"Thus, those who have produced a son are never deprived [of one]; they are never deprived. Then, having worshipped the Lord Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) and having recited the Sudarśana mantra eight thousand times, he said: "A son is necessarily born; a son is born. He said: "A son is born."

At times prescribed by Śiva, or at rivers, or at a pure reservoir of water, having performed an ablution with eight thousand, or eight hundred, or twenty-eight middle-sized *palāśa* leaves while reciting the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," and this entire section beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," he performs an ablution with eight thousand repetitions of the *gāyatrī*. He also performs an ablution with the *Puruṣasūkta*, that is, with the section beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ. "He becomes a son," so said the venerable Āgniveśya. 6.

Now follows the Viṣṇubali. In the eighth month, during the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion—on the twelfth, the seventh, or under Rohiṇī or Śravaṇā—one should serve food to the Brāhmaṇas and cause them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Prosperity! Success! Then, having performed the rites from the drawing of the lines for the sacrificial ground up to the carrying forward of the Praṇītā water, one should rise and, standing before the fire, invoke the deity: "Om Bhūḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Om Bhuvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Om Svaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Om Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ..."

Having invoked with the words, "I invoke the Person (Puruṣa)," and having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), and having worshipped the deity, he should sprinkle himself with water using the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*, and this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*. Then he satiates [the deities] with water: Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara.

"I satisfy [them]," he says. With these very names, using scents, flowers, incense, and lamps, he says, "Salutation to such-and-such; salutation to such-and-such. Then he offers oblations to Viṣṇu with the verses: *viṣṇornukaṃ*, *tadasya priyaṃ*, *pra tadviṣṇuḥ*, *paro mātrayā*, and *trirdevaḥ*. The rite is completed from the *jaya* offerings up to the granting of the boon by the cow. Then he presents an offering of rice-pudding mixed with ghee and food, saying "Svāhā to such-and-such; Svāhā to such-and-such," twelve times according to the respective deities.

They praise with Vaiṣṇava hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas. With the *vyāhṛtis*, he causes the Puruṣa to rise, saying, "I cause the Puruṣa to rise. He causes the wife to eat the remainder of the food; it is known [from scripture] that she thereby gives birth to a male child. 7

Now, the Śūlagava sacrifice is to be performed every year on the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa; or alternatively, having established the fire in the forest and strewn it around, and having performed the rites up to the *praṇītā* waters, he takes sacrificial grass and dedicates the cow with the formula: "I dedicate you, acceptable to Īśāna. According to some, [the dedication] is silent. He then causes it to be slaughtered right there, with its head turned westward and its feet turned northward. For that animal once slaughtered, there is a sprinkling with water.

Having invigorated the vital breaths and silently extracted the omentum, he draws out the heart and the well-known portions. Having placed these upon those very spits, they cook them on this same fire. Then, having removed these from the spits, they cook them again in the pot. Then, having taken them off after they have been sprinkled with clarified butter, he sprinkles the established offering with clarified butter.

Having performed the rites from the putting on of the garments up to the invocation of the fire (*agnimukha*), he invokes the deity with the mantra: "May the conscious bay horses bring you here, together with white horses that possess banners, swift as the wind, victorious, bountiful, and fleet as thought; come quickly for my oblation, O Śarva! Then, with the *sruva* ladle, he offers the oblation that has been spread with *barhis* grass and sprinkled with clarified butter. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "Thousands upon thousands," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "Thee, the Lord of beings, the glory of the world. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter.

Then, having cut off these portions from the *iḍāsūna*, and having mixed together the rice, the meat, and the broth with clarified butter, he offers them by dipping with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) into the eastern half [of the fire], saying: "To the god Bhava, svāhā! To the god Śarva, svāhā! To the god Īśāna, svāhā! To the god Paśupati, svāhā! To the god Rudra, svāhā! To the god Ugra, svāhā! To the god Bhīma, svāhā! To the great god, svāhā!"

Then, in the middle, he offers oblations, saying: "Svāhā to the wife of the god Bhava; svāhā to the wife of the god Śarva; svāhā to the wife of the god Īśāna; svāhā to the wife of the god Paśupati; svāhā to the wife of the god Rudra; svāhā to the wife of the god Ugra; svāhā to the wife of the god Bhīma; svāhā to the wife of the great god. Then he offers in the latter half.

"Oblation to the son of the god Bhava! Oblation to the son of the god Śarva! Oblation to the son of the god Īśāna! Oblation to the son of the god Paśupati! Oblation to the son of the god Rudra! Oblation to the son of the god Ugra! Oblation to the son of the god Bhīma! Oblation to the son of the great god! Thus [he says]. Then he offers oblations of clarified butter, reciting from "Homage to you, O Rudra, to your wrath" until the end of the section.

The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the granting of the boon of the cows. Then, to the west of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon *arka* leaves with the mantra: "To that Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants, and who has entered all beings—to that Rudra let there be homage. Having poured the rinsings of the cooking pot, the remainder of the clarified butter, and the remainder of the water into a vessel, and having sprinkled them with a branch of cane, he circumambulates the cows three times clockwise while reciting the hymn beginning: "The cows have come; they have brought auspiciousness."

They declare this to be a great means of securing well-being. Now, if he does not obtain a cow, he should sacrifice a ram or a goat; or he cooks a *sthālīpāka* for Īśāna when that which is to be done with a cow is required. That is explained as the *śūlagava* (the spit-ox sacrifice). In this very same way, it may be performed on the eighth day at nightfall; only this much is different: there is no formal dedication (*upākaraṇa*) of the animal here.

Now, therefore, one who desires the prosperity of his house should begin the House-Purification (gṛhaśānti) every month, every season, or every year, during the bright fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion. Having bound together Apāmārga, Pālāśa, Śirīṣa, Udumbara, Sadābhadrā, Amṛtatṛṇa, and Indravallī plants, he sweeps around the house with them.

Having swept around [the site], sprinkled it with water, and consecrated it by sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using a handful of *darbha* grass, and having scattered mustard seeds, he should perform the preliminary rites for the fire (*agnimukha*). Then, having offered two oblations in the center with the verses "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*) and "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*), he should offer a thousand oblations with the *Sāvitrī* verse. Then, [he should offer] in the southeast, then in the southwest, then in the northwest, or in the center. From the *jaya* oblations onwards, the rite is established until the granting of the boon of the *dhenu*.

He gives a cow, clothing, or gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), serves the Brahmins with food, and causes them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity! By practicing in this way until the end of his life, he thrives with great nourishment. He has many sons; nor do children die young. Fire does not burn him. Fanged beasts do not devour him. Neither thieves, rivals, Rākṣasas, nor Piśācas cause him harm.

If cattle should suffer from heat, one should offer a thousand oblations in the midst of the cattle. By this very same procedure, the case of horses, camels, donkeys, goats, sheep, buffaloes, and elephants, as well as any other group of bipeds or quadrupeds, is explained. 9

The materials for one desiring rain are as follows: a black garment, a black horse with a black tail-hair fringe, a black ram, a black antelope skin, black *vrīhi* rice, black honey, an unbaked cooking-pot, dates and flour, and *karīra* fruit and flour; a garland of *varṣābhū* mushrooms, three lotus leaves, and ten thousand fuel-sticks of reeds—these are the materials prepared for this rite.

Having kindled the fire, at the time when the wind blows from behind, he puts on a black garment with a black fringe, [saying]: "Thou art of the Maruts; thou art the vigor of the Maruts; pierce the stream of the waters! Restrain the Maruts—the falcon, the guileful, the mind-swift, the bull, the well-rolling one—by whom the fierce host is let loose as it comes; O Aśvins, provide that with well-being."

Leading the fire, they hold a black horse and a black cloud in front, facing westward; to the south, they pour out raw grains into a pot; behind, they place garlands of *varṣābhū* plants. Having strewn grass all around and prepared the portions for offering, he takes three handfuls with the sacrificial formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer what is pleasing to Varuṇa," and a fourth silently. The wife husks the grain.

Having husked [the grains] three times and washed them three times, he pours water into the pot across the strainers, places it over the fire, carries fire around it, sprinkles clarified butter over it, and having removed the *caru* from the fire, he sprinkles clarified butter over it. Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), he mixes the flour of date-palms (*kharjūra-saktu*) and the flour of *karīra* fruit with black honey in that vessel, reciting: "The refreshing, the longing, the pure, the swift, the luminous, the dispelling darkness, the all-encompassing, the well-foaming."

Having formed three lumps [of food] and placed them upon these lotus leaves, he applies black ointment to a ram. Having repeated one hundred times each of these ten mantras—"For whatever of thine," "Whatever here the gamblers," "This my prayer, O Varuṇa," "To thee I go," "So for us, O Agni," "Be thou for us, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "Avert thy wrath," "The highest [knot]," and "We worship Tryambaka"—he should offer fuel-sticks with each mantra. Having thus repeated with these mantras, he should offer the oblation.

In the same manner, having practiced [the ritual], he should offer oblations of clarified butter. The rites beginning with the *jayas* and ending with the gift of the cow as a boon are established. He gives a cow to the teacher. He sprinkles a black horse with water, [reciting]: "By Parjanya, the bearer of waters, they create darkness even by day; when they moisten the earth with rain, the men of liberal gifts have caused the treasury of heaven to flow for the donor. The clouds release rain through the two worlds, and the showers go forth across the desert."

Saying "Say," Kṛṣṇa sprinkles [the earth] with water from the hollows of his hands and says: "O Maruts, you who have risen from the ocean, cause the rain to pour forth; O possessors of the soil, you cause the rain to fall. O wonder-workers, your milch-cows do not fail; as you go toward splendor, the chariots have followed after. Saying "Say," Kṛṣṇa sprinkles the two black stones with water and shakes them. If it makes dung, it rains; if it runs away, or sits down, it does not rain. He fills a raw earthen pot with water.

"Send down rain from heaven; fill the ocean with waters! You are born of the waters, you are the first-born; you are the strength of the ocean. Moisture the earth; cleave the celestial firmament! Give us of the celestial water; O Lord, release the leather bag! If that jar, filled with water, is broken, it rains; if it remains intact, it does not rain. He offers a ladle full of water with the verse addressed to Parjanya: "Moisture the earth..."

Now, if it should not rain, one should cook a *sthālīpāka* of these very black rice grains (*kṛṣṇavrīhi*) and perform the oblation for the three pressings for seven days. Thus concludes the rite for one desiring rain; thus concludes the rite for one desiring rain. 10.

Now we shall explain the *bhūtabali* (offering to beings). One who desires rain is the qualified performer (*adhikārī*). A black garment, a black cow, two black stones, black rice, black honey, an unbaked jar, dates, parched grain flour, clarified butter, and three lotus leaves—these are the materials prepared for this rite. "In that one offers the *bali* to the beings, that constitutes the completion of the *bhūtayajña*," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Every year, every six months, when it is the new moon and the water has dried up, or when he finds the cessation of rain, he should offer the *bhūtabali*. Having gone to the pond, having scooped up earth from a pure spot with the verse "Being dug up," having sprinkled it with water with the verse "May the goddesses [grant] us peace," and having demarcated the sacrificial ground, he draws a line around it with the formula "It is circumscribed."

At the time when the wind blows from behind, at that time the Brāhmaṇa, having put on a black garment with the mantra "Thou art the Marut; the vigor of the Maruts," having touched water, having donned the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), having sipped water, and having taken a vessel of water and placed it to the west, he worships. Having performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he offers eight oblations with the names of the winds, beginning with: "The east wind raining, refreshing, and turning back, svāhā!"

Then he offers oblations of cooked rice from black *kṛṣṇavrīhi* grains, saying: "Svāhā to Mitra and Varuṇa; Svāhā to Agni, the illuminator of the abodes; Svāhā to the Maruts; Svāhā to Sūrya; Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having offered from the oblation to Varuṇa up to the Sviṣṭakṛt, he then takes a portion of the remaining food and dates-powder into a bronze vessel or a shallow bowl, and mixes it with clarified butter or honey while reciting the two verses beginning with "Māndā vāśā. To the west of the fire, he should pour it out upon three lotus leaves, saying: "O gods who possess wealth..."

With three [verses], he offers half of the remainder of the food to the deity with the mantra "devasya tvā. Then, having gone to the water, he offers three balls (*piṇḍas*) of the residue into the water with the three mantras beginning "udno dattodadhim bhinta," ending with the utterance of *svāhā*. Then, having taken up water with his joined palms (*añjali*), he should sprinkle it upward with the two verses beginning "udīrayatha marutaḥ. Then, having gone to the deities of the site (*vāstudeva*): "To those who are the deities of the site, and to the hosts of cruel *rakṣas*s and spirits, I offer this oblation (*bali*) desiring rain; may they be peaceful and grant peace."

"Obeisance to all, obeisance to the beings, obeisance!"—having thus [spoken], he fills the water-pot with water; "Make the earth swell!"—with this [verse] he [addresses] the black cow; "Those gods who have their portion in heaven"—with this he worships the deities; "May the rivers flow, may the rain-clouds rain"—with this he worships the rain-clouds. Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce an auspicious day and having fed the Brahmins, if it should rain [during that time], he should sacrifice only then; if it does not rain, he should offer the oblation on the following day—so says the Brāhmaṇa. 11.

Now we shall explain the sowing of seeds. Under Rohiṇī, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Mūla, Viśākhā, Maghā, Śravaṇā, Revatī, the two stars of Mitra and Varuṇa (Anurādhā), or the Uttarās of the Maruts (Uttara-phalgunī)—under one of these constellations, having taken the seeds and performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), he goes to the field under one of these same constellations. Having worshipped the eastern direction with perfumes and other offerings, having scattered *śirīṣa* leaves, and having smeared himself with the remains of the perfumes, he gives perfumes and other gifts to the plowman and sows the seeds while reciting the section beginning with "The plants that have been born" (*yā jātā oṣadhayaḥ*).

Then, prior to the invitation, having cooked the *caru* of rice, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and having sprinkled with water using the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*) and the four verses beginning with "Golden-colored, pure, purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), and with this section (*anuvāka*) beginning with "The purifying one, belonging to the world of light" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*), he then offers the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) with the verse: "O Lord of the Field, pour upon us a honeyed wave, as a cow yields her milk."

"May the lords of nectar, dripping with sweetness like well-purified clarified butter, be gracious to us. Then, [he performs the sowing] to the south-east, then to the south-west, then to the east, north, and west, and then in the middle, performing the sowing as prescribed. With that grain, he subsequently performs the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice. Now, therefore, [follow] the offerings for guests (*atithya*) and the ritual gifts (*balikarma*). Now, if a pillar of the house should crack, there is a rite imitating an oblation. Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for conquering untimely death (*apamṛtyuñjaya*). Now, the *Homa* for one desiring offspring using the *Jaya* mantras. Now, the offering to Viṣṇu (*viṣṇubali*). Now, the *Śūlagava* (the spit-ox sacrifice). Now, regarding the domestic rites (*gṛhakarma*).
For one desiring rain, there is the offering to the Atharvans and the sowing of seeds; [these constitute] twelve [rites].
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for sipping water (ācamana). Facing either east or north, having washed both hands, with his topknot tied and wearing the sacred thread, whether in water or on land, with the knees apart, and holding the hands in the shape of a cow’s ear with the nine fingers [except the thumbs] joined together, he should drink water—standing, not bowing, not laughing, not talking, not walking, not using hot water, not discolored water, not water with bubbles, and without moving—so that the water reaches the depth of a bean.

In the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa there are five *tīrthas* and five deities. The *daiva-tīrtha* is in the middle of the fingers; the *ārṣa-tīrtha* is at the tips of the fingers; the *paitṛka-tīrtha* is between the thumb and the forefinger; the *brāhma-tīrtha* is on the lines above the root of the thumb; and the *agnitīrtha* is in the center [of the palm]. Fire resides in the thumb, Vāyu in the forefinger, Prajāpati in the middle finger, Brahmā in the ring finger, and Indra in the little finger. Then, one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) three times with the *praṇava*.

When he drinks for the first time, by that he gratifies the Ṛgveda; when he drinks for the second time, by that he gratifies the Yajurveda; when he drinks for the third time, by that he gratifies the Sāmaveda. When he wipes [the cup] for the first time, by that he gratifies the Atharvaveda; when he wipes for the second time, by that he gratifies the Itihāsa.

By that which he touches, he gratifies Agni; by that with which he sprinkles his feet, Viṣṇu; by that [which he touches] the *sahya* [mountain], the Pitṛs, and the ancient seers (*ṛṣis*); by that [which he touches] the moon and the sun; by that which [he touches] the nostrils, the out-breath and the in-breath (*prāṇa-apāna*); by that which is the ear, the quarters; by that which are the arms, Indra; by that which is the navel, the earth; by that which is the heart, Rudra; and by that which is the head, he gratifies the Seven Seers (*saptarṣis*).

One should touch the eyes with the thumb and the ring finger; the nostrils with the forefinger and the thumb; the ears with the thumb and the little finger; the arms with the middle finger and the thumb; the navel with the thumb; the heart with the tips of the fingers; and the head with the palms of all the fingers, saying, "May they fulfill all my desires. Now, I shall explain the procedure for bathing thereafter. For the purpose of bathing, one digs up earth, saying:
"O Earth, destroy the sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me."
"By the slaying of this sinful one, may I live for a hundred autumns. O Earth, grant me nourishment; everything is established in you.
Thus he pours water.
"Gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣāṃ nityapuṣṭāṃ karīṣiṇīm | īśvarīm̐ sarvabhūtānāṃ tām ihopahvaye śriyam" — with these words, he forms it into a ball.

Then, having washed his hands and feet and taken up his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a lump of earth, he goes to the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and washes his feet three times and himself three times. Now, some say that one must not enter a cremation ground, water, a temple, a cow-pen, or a place where Brāhmaṇas are, without having first washed one's feet. Then he approaches the water, saying: "I seek refuge in Varuṇa whose horns are of gold; grant me a way [into the water] as I entreat you. Whatever I have eaten of the unrighteous, and whatever acceptance of gifts from the wicked [I have made]," [so may it be purified].
"Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through mind, speech, or action, may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify that for me again and again. Thus.

Then, with his hands cupped in añjali, he offers water, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. He sprinkles that water toward the direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water, he turns three times clockwise through the water, saying: "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, and whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart. Having submerged himself in the water and emerged, there is no further straining required for one who has been in the water.

If [the waters] have been enclosed, there is neither the beating of the garment nor the touching; rather, he worships with the respective [mantras]: "Homage to Agni accompanied by water, homage to Indra, homage to Varuṇa, homage to Vāruṇī, homage to the Waters. Having emerged and sipped water, once he has sipped, he should sip again: "May the Waters purify the Earth; may the purified Earth purify me. May Brahmaṇaspati purify; may the purified Veda purify me. Whatever is impure from food, or whatever evil deed I have committed..."

"May the waters purify everything for me, and [purify] the acceptance of gifts from the wicked, svāhā. Having thus made two strainers (*pavitra*), he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of happiness," the four verses beginning with "The golden-colored, pure, and purifying ones," and this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with "Pavamāna, who dwells in the light. Having purified himself, he goes into the water, performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and then emerges. He wrings out his garment, puts on other unwashed clothes that have been washed and aired, and sips water.

Sitting on *darbha* grass and holding *darbha* blades, he should recite the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times, or one hundred times, or at least ten times. Then he worships the sun with the verses: "Up from the darkness," "Up that [sun] which," "The bright," "That eye, established by the gods," and "Those who [come] from the water. Furthermore, they cite this: "The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *Sāvitrī*—these five are the *brahmayajñas*; day after day they purify the Brāhmaṇa from sin. Purified by these five *brahmayajñas*, he then offers libations to the deities."

I satiate Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Sarpas—these deities of the eastern gate, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. I satiate the Vasus. I satiate the Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni—these deities of the southern gate, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. I satiate the Rudras.

I satiate Mitra, Indra, the Great Ancestors, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these deities of the western doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. I satiate the Ādityas. I satiate the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama—these deities of the northern doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. I satiate the Viśvedevas.

I satisfy the Sādhyas. I satisfy Brahmā. I satisfy Prajāpati. I satisfy Parameṣṭhin. Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa. Oṃ bhūḥ, I satisfy. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I satisfy. Oṃ svaḥ, I satisfy. Oṃ mahaḥ, I satisfy. Oṃ janaḥ, I satisfy. Oṃ tapaḥ, I satisfy. Oṃ satyam, I satisfy. Oṃ, I satisfy the god Bhava. I satisfy the god Śarva. I satisfy the god Īśāna.

I satiate the god Paśupati; I satiate the god Rudra; I satiate the god Ugra; I satiate the god Bhīma; I satiate the god Mahān; I satiate the consort of the god Bhava; I satiate the consort of the god Śarva; I satiate the consort of the god Īśāna; I satiate the consort of the god Paśupati; I satiate the consort of the god Rudra; I satiate the consort of the god Ugra.

I satiate the wife of the god Bhīma. I satiate the wife of the great god. I satiate the son of the god Bhava. I satiate the son of the god Śarva. I satiate the son of the god Īśāna. I satiate the son of the god Paśupati. I satiate the son of the god Rudra. I satiate the son of the god Ugra. I satiate the son of the god Bhīma. I satiate the son of the great god.

I satiate the Rudras; I satiate the attendants of Rudra; I satiate the female attendants of Rudra. I satiate Sanatkumāra; I satiate Skanda; I satiate Indra; I satiate Ṣaṣṭhī; I satiate Viśākha; I satiate the attendants of Skanda; I satiate the female attendants of Skanda. I satiate Vighna; I satiate Vināyaka; I satiate Vīra; I satiate Śūra; I satiate Gaṇapati.

I propitiate Varada; I propitiate Hastimukha; I propitiate the male attendants of Vighna; I propitiate the female attendants of Vighna; I propitiate Vaivasvata; I propitiate Yama; I propitiate Mṛtyu; I propitiate the male attendants of Vaivasvata; I propitiate the female attendants of Vaivasvata; I propitiate Viṣṇu; I propitiate the goddess Śrī; I propitiate Puṣṭi; I propitiate Sarasvatī; I propitiate the male attendants of Viṣṇu.

I satiate the attendants of Viṣṇu. I satiate Vidyā. I satiate Mitra. I satiate Dhanvantari. I satiate the attendants of Dhanvantari. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (nivītī): I satiate the Ṛṣis. I satiate the Parama-Ṛṣis. I satiate the Brahmarṣis. I satiate the Rājarṣis. I satiate the Deva-Ṛṣis. I satiate the Śruta-Ṛṣis. I satiate the Tapas-Ṛṣis. I satiate the Saptarṣis. I satiate the Kāṇḍa-Ṛṣis. I satiate the Ṛṣikās.

I satisfy the daughters of the seers. I satisfy the sons of the seers. I satisfy Bodhāyana. I satisfy Āpastamba. I satisfy the author of the Sūtras. I satisfy Satyāṣāḍha. I satisfy Hiraṇyakeśin. I satisfy Vyāsa. I satisfy the Praṇava. I satisfy the Vyāhṛtis. I satisfy the Sāvitrī. I satisfy the meters. I satisfy the Ṛgveda. I satisfy the Yajurveda. I satisfy the Sāmaveda.

I satiate the Atharvaveda. I satiate the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. I satiate all the divine beings. I satiate all living beings. I satiate the Atharvans. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), I satiate the ancestors with the cry of *svadhā* and obeisance (*namas*). I satiate the grandfathers with *svadhā* and *namas*. I satiate the great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and *namas*. I satiate the mothers with *svadhā* and *namas*. I satiate the grandmothers with *svadhā* and *namas*. I satiate the great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and *namas*.

I satiate the maternal grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the maternal great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the maternal great-great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the maternal grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the maternal great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the maternal great-great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the wives of the teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satiate the gurus with *svadhā* and obeisance.

I satiate the wives of my teachers with *svadhā* and salutations. I satiate my friends with *svadhā* and salutations. I satiate the wives of my friends with *svadhā* and salutations. I satiate my kinsmen with *svadhā* and salutations. I satiate the wives of my kinsmen with *svadhā* and salutations. I satiate my ministers with *svadhā* and salutations. I satiate the wives of my ministers with *svadhā* and salutations. I satiate all [of them] with *svadhā* and salutations.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the private recitation (*svādhyāya*). Having gone out from the village facing either the east or the north, having bathed in water, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), having sipped water (*ācānta*), and wearing unwashed clothes, he should spread a large quantity of *darbha* grass with its points directed toward the east. Sitting upon them facing the east and performing the ritual prostration (*upasthāna*), he should join his right and left hands together so that they hold the *darbha* strainers (*pavitras*). It is known: "The *darbhas* are indeed the essence of waters and plants; thus he makes the *brahman* itself possessed of essence. Gazing at the junction of heaven and earth, he should proceed.

Either with eyes closed or in whatever manner he considers himself fit, thus composed, he should study his own Veda (*svādhyāya*). [He recites] the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ*. He recites the *sāvitrī* verse: first quarter by quarter, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole—this is the third [recitation]. Then he should study his own Veda: the *ṛcs*, the *yajus* formulas, the *sāmans*, the *Atharva-aṅgirases*, the *brāhmaṇas*, the *kalpas*, the *gāthās*, the *nārāśaṃsīs*, and the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*.

When he studies the Ṛg-verses, streams of milk flow for his ancestors as a *svadhā* offering; when the Yajus-formulas, streams of clarified butter; when the Sāmans, streams of honey; when the Atharvans and Aṅgirases, streams of Soma; and when the Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpas, the Gāthās, the Nārāśaṃsīs, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas, streams of ambrosia flow for them.

Having studied as much as he deems necessary, he concludes with this [verse]: "Homage to Brahman, homage to Agni, homage to the Earth, homage to the Plants, homage to Speech, homage to the Lord of Speech, homage to the Great Viṣṇu, I perform. From this point onward, the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña) is taught for all.

There, without contradicting his own means, he should offer as a gift in the morning to his wife—or cook for himself—the grains of *kodrava*, *cīnara*, *rājamāṣa*, *mamūra*, *kulattha*, *varaka*, and *varu* excluded, along with the husked rice of various specific medicinal herbs and barley. Having thoroughly swept the house and smeared its doors, he should perform his fixed duties morning and evening, doing other necessary tasks at other times. He should offer oblations silently into the fire with the mantra "To Agni Jātavedas, Svāhā! and a second time silently. He worships the sun with the verse, "Upwards that Jātavedas... and so forth.

One should offer an oblation at the Brahma-spot with the words, "Salutation to Brahman. With "To Soma," [one offers] at the water-jar; with "To Vāyu," at the dwelling-house; with "To the House-lord," at the door of the house; with "To Prajāpati," at the Garga-house; with "To the All-gods," at the temple; with "May the goddesses be auspicious to us," toward the directions beginning with the north-east; with "To those belonging to the quarters," in each direction; with "To the houses," in the intermediate space on all sides; with "Salutation to the Lord of Beasts, to the gods," in the north-east or at the Brahma-spot; and with "Svadhā to the ancestors," in the south.

He places [the offering]. Having offered the Vaiśvadeva oblation—either with this [formula], or with the previously mentioned one, or by means of the *vāsabali* offering—he waits for guests for the duration of time it takes to milk a cow. [The guests may be] a *śrotriya*, one who observes Vedic vows, an ascetic (*yati*), one devoted to dharma, or one of the same livelihood.
The *manasvatī* oblation is prescribed as his expiation when [the fire] has been interrupted for two or three days, or when [the rites] have not been performed due to negligence;
having offered three *tantumatī* oblations, he should then sacrifice four *vāruṇī* oblations.
If the offerings are interrupted in every respect for ten or twelve days,
one should offer the four *abhyāvartinī* oblations and then perform the *tāntumant* caru-offering; this applies to one whose wife or unmarried son offers the fire-oblation in the house.
The Kūṣmāṇḍī verses should be offered there; having offered them for the prosperity of the sacrifice,
he who departs on a journey and has no performer of rites in his house goes forth together with the sacrifices of these five great ones.
While traveling abroad, he should offer them whatever food is available;
if no food is produced, he should enter into them with water alone.
He should perform his vow with water itself, following the practice according to what is obtained.

Through the sacrifice to the gods, the twice-born attains equality with the gods; through the sacrifice to the ancestors, with the ancestors; through the sacrifices that bring prosperity to beings, with those beings;
through the sacrifice to humans, with Manu; and through the sacrifice to Brahman, with Brahman.
Having attained equanimity toward these deities for a hundred years, they go to the bliss of Brahman—certain, eternal, and imperishable. Thus it is said.
Now, his guest may be one who follows the same conduct as his teacher, or a Vaikhānasa, or a Snātaka, or a king.

He is endowed with righteousness (*dharmayukta*). Rising up for them, he offers a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), hospitality (*arhaṇa*), and the guest-offering (*arghya*). Whatever medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) are available there should be given; or else, he may perform another form of hospitality. However, the distribution of medicinal herbs should be performed by one who possesses wealth. In their absence, land, water, grass, or kind words—these indeed never fail in the house of a virtuous man. These very things they call the Supreme Brahman.

Upon seizing them, he shall observe a vow for twelve nights, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, sleeping on the ground, and practicing celibacy. Having fasted for three nights, he may seize the two others who were previously cast out. The offering of the *bali* has been explained.

Now we shall explain the *madhuparka*. Having placed four vessels made of bronze, curds, honey, and clarified butter, along with three bunches of grass (*kūrca*), two garments, and a pair of earrings upon *darbha* grass, he covers them with *darbha* blades.

Having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters by pouring them across the strainer and having sprinkled these [materials], he should pour water into a vessel placed over the strainers, purify it, and place therein the materials for the guest-offering (*argha*). In the same manner, he should prepare the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). Into a bronze bowl (*kaṃsa*), having poured across the strainers curds, honey, and ghee, and having purified it three times by bringing it back [to the source], he should place therein the materials for the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). He should present these to the teacher, the father-in-law, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, a *snātaka*, a guest, and a king; or, at a wedding, to the bridegroom. Then, during the ritual, he should offer water and say, "This is the *kūrca*," presenting a seat of grass.

While he sits there facing the east, [the host says]: "This is the teacher's seat; may it not fail you. Then, having grasped two *kūrca* grass mats, he should offer the guest water worthy of honor (*arhaṇīya*), saying, "Water worthy of honor. He consecrates that water with the mantra: "Come to me with splendor, with luster, with glory, and with milk. Having taken it in his joined palms and said, "It should be poured forward," he pours it out toward the east. In exactly the same way, he should offer water for washing the feet (*pādya*), saying, "Water for the feet."

He consecrates it with the mantra: "Thou art glory; bestow glory upon me. Thou art sovereignty; bestow sovereignty upon me. Another person washes his feet with that water. He touches the hand of the one who has washed them with the mantra: "In me be greatness, in me be splendor, in me be glory. Having touched water, he touches himself with the mantra: "In me be sensory power and vigor. [The water] for sipping is as follows: he sips it with the mantra: "Thou art the under-layer of immortality."

Having sipped water, he should then offer him the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), saying: "This is the honey-mixture. He consecrates it with the mantra: "May he protect me; may he guard me; may he be pleased with me. He should give two garments and two earrings. Having put on the unwashed garment with the words, "Enter my own body," and having likewise fastened the upper garment and taken the earrings, and having performed the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) rite and sipped water, he takes the honey-mixture with the words: "Thou art prosperity; come, rest in me."

Then, having grasped [the water] with his thumb and ring finger, he smells it with his nose, saying: "I offer this oblation to you; lead me to preeminence and lordship. Having touched water and drawn it up with his fingers, he sips it, saying: "You are named 'Most Beloved,' the one who leads to the gods; I take you for my prosperity and glory. He does this a second time, saying: "You are Soma; make me a drinker of Soma. He does it a third time, saying: "You are food; make me an eater of food."

Having set aside the remnants of what he has drunk, and having sipped water for rinsing with the formula, "Thou art the covering of immortality," he consecrates his sacrificial cord and the cow with the formula, "Slay my evil and that of the one who receives me. He should say to her, "Release her," or "Drive her away," or "Prepare her. If he releases her, he consecrates her with the two verses beginning, "The cow is to be a milch-cow. When she has been released, he sacrifices a ram or a goat, or else with the meat of a wild animal; however, the guest-offering must never be without meat. Or, in case of inability, he should offer rice mixed with barley-meal, according to what is available.
Then, having performed the five sacrifices in their proper sequence beginning with the Brahma-sacrifice,
and having performed the sacrifice to the gods (deva-yajña), followed by the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛ-yajña),
and having performed the sacrifice to all beings (bhūta-yajña) as well as the human sacrifice (mānuṣya-yajña);

Having thus performed the fivefold sacrifices according to the injunctions of the scriptures, one should prepare a circular mound of cow dung at the entrance of the house and properly offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) there for outcasts, dogs, and other such beings.

Having performed the worship ordained by the gods, he smears a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung; for a Kṣatriya, he smears a triangle, for a Vaiśya, he smears a circle, and then takes his meal.
[He honors] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śrī, and Agni.
They subsist upon the *maṇḍala*; therefore, one should prepare the *maṇḍala*.
For *yātudhānas*, *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and *kinnaras* surely destroy the strength of food that is devoid of the *maṇḍala*. Thus it is said.

Having prepared the *maṇḍala* with care according to the instruction, one should sit on the ground with wet feet, facing east. Having placed the left foot down and remaining silent with the face turned downward, one should touch with the left hand a vessel made of leaves or of bell-metal. Food consisting of oily substances, salt, condiments, and so forth, along with clarified butter (*ājya*) and unhusked grain (*akṛta*), should be offered. Then one should eat; so they say. Food shown by a woman in her courses or others [is forbidden]. At the mere sight [of such food], one should lift the right hand from the head or from the heart. One sprinkles it with clarified butter. Then one sprinkles it with water, moving clockwise around it.

"I sprinkle you with *ṛta* by means of *satya*"—thus in the evening; "I sprinkle you with *satya* by means of *ṛta*"—thus in the morning. Having washed his hands, he touches the food with the *Annasūkta*, the ten-verse hymn beginning, "I am the first-born of *ṛta*. Then he causes [the guest] to sip water with the formula, "Thou art the under-layer for immortality. Then he offers the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*), starting with the breath: "Seated in the breath, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspicious, not burning; *svāhā* to the breath! Thus for the breath.

"Seated in the *apāna*, I offer the nectar; may Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning—*svāhā* to the *apāna*! thus for the *apāna*. "Seated in the *vyāna*, I offer the nectar; may Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning—*svāhā* to the *vyāna*! thus for the *vyāna*. "Seated in the *udāna*, I offer the nectar; may Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning—*svāhā* to the *udāna*! thus for the *udāna*. "Seated in the *samāna*, I offer the nectar; may Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning—*svāhā* to the *samāna*! thus for the *samāna*.

Or [he may offer] with the words: "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Apāna, svāhā! To Vyāna, svāhā! To Udāna, svāhā! To Samāna, svāhā! Having offered these oblations, he eats as he pleases. He should not chew roots, fruits, or other condiments with his teeth; all oily substances and condiments should be removed from the ground [before eating]. There is no fault in drinking repeatedly.

Having offered oblations according to the ritual with curd mixed with the sacrificial food and the three-fold grain, and having sipped water while reciting "Thou art the covering of immortality," he sips again; then, reciting "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen me," he touches the region of the navel. By performing this at every meal, one obtains the fruit of fasting for a day and night.

If he desires to lie down, he should not do so with his head toward the north, nor along the length of a bamboo pole, nor toward a door, nor toward his feet, nor toward a joint, nor during festivals, nor on ashes, nor toward a house for the planets, a sanctuary, or a fire-altar; nor naked, nor impure, nor during the two twilights, nor on a broken bedstead, nor in the shade of a cremation ground or a great tree; nor should he think that there is no other occasion for negligence. He should lie down with his head toward the east or toward the south. (7)

Then, in the afternoon, having taken a water-pot made either of copper or clay, and having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, he goes to a bathing place (tīrtha) and takes water. Having taken earth for the purpose of purification in a clean spot—earth that is not saline, not containing feces, not alkaline, not from an anthill, not mixed with gravel, and not mixed with grass—he places the sacred thread over his ear, scatters grass with the words, "Thou art a purifier," and voids urine and feces upon them.

One should not perform purification on a funeral pyre, nor by a river, nor in the divine shade of grassy groves, nor on a path, nor in ashes, nor in the middle of a field, nor on black earth, nor on cow dung, nor in the shade of a cremation ground, a large tree, or an anthill. During the day and at the twilights, one should face north; if at night, one should face south. Having held the penis and stood up, one should diligently perform purification until the odor and the residue are removed.

Having touched the water-pot with one [hand], having washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water (ācamana), he should become pure by meditating on the syllable *Oṃ* in his mind. Then, when the sun has set, he purifies himself with water using the verse: "O Dadhikrāvan, O Viṣṇu, I have performed [the rite]... He then drinks water using this section (*anuvāka*): "May Agni and Manyu... Having sipped water, he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning: "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss... He should then silently cause the water to flow around [himself] from left to right.

Then, taking water in his joined palms, standing up and facing the sun, he should consecrate it with the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī* mantra, and throw it upwards three times. Thereafter, he should perform a circumambulation. Then, sitting down, he satiates [the deities] with water: "I satiate Dhātṛ; I satiate Aryaman; I satiate Mitra; I satiate Varuṇa; I satiate Aṃśumat; I satiate Bhaga; I satiate Indra; I satiate Vivasvat."

"I satisfy Pūṣan; I satisfy Parjanya; I satisfy Tvaṣṭṛ; I satisfy Viṣṇu. Then, having scattered *darbha* grass near water and sat down with the *pavitra* in hand, facing west, he should mentally invoke the Gāyatrī: "May the boon-granting Goddess come, she who is the imperishable, equal to Brahman. O Gāyatrī, mother of the meters, may you take pleasure in this our sacred knowledge (*brahman*)."

You are vigor, you are endurance, you are strength, you are splendor; you are the abode of the gods by name; you are the universe, you are the life of the universe; you are all, you are the life of all; you are the conqueror—*Oṃ*, I invoke Gāyatrī; I invoke Sāvitrī; I invoke Sarasvatī.

Having thus invoked [the deity], and having repeated three times this Anuvāka—*oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ suvaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam, oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*—and having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should repeat the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, or a hundred times, or at least ten times, with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, prior to the rising of the stars.

Then he should dismiss the Goddess with the verse, "On the highest peak... Having risen, he worships the western direction (the quarter of Varuṇa) with the three verses beginning, "Whatever indeed of yours [is due] as among the people... and with the two verses beginning, "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa... Turning around toward his right arm, he worships the southern direction with the following: "To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka; to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, and to the Destroyer of all beings; to Audumbara, to Dadhna, to Nīla, and to Parameṣṭhin."

"Salutation indeed to Vṛkodara, to Citra, and to Citragupta. Thus he worships the northern direction. "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person who is dark and tawny, whose seed is drawn up, the three-eyed one—salutation indeed to the one of universal form. Having turned around in this very manner and standing facing west, he touches his mouth with the mantra: "O Sarasvatī, whatever sweetness is in your waters, in your cows, and in your horses—with that, O Sarasvatī, rich in steeds, anoint my mouth."

"O Indra, envelop the Piśāca with sharp, tawny-tipped [missiles]; strike down every Rākṣasa!"—with these words he touches his shoulder. Having performed three circumambulations from left to right, he performs the salutation. Thus, having performed the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*), at the time of the *āpośana* rite, he consecrates the water with this section beginning "Sūryaś ca mā manyuś ca," and then drinks it. Standing facing the east, he should mutter the *Sāvitrī*. He worships the eastern direction with the three verses beginning "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people."

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for sipping water (ācamana). Now, having washed the hands and feet; "Agni is Prajāpati. Now, therefore, the rule for Vedic study (svādhyāya); having offered the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; now we shall explain the Madhuparka; the five sacrifices; "now in the afternoon," "eight"—thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhya Sūtra. Now begins the seventh chapter.

We shall now explain the re-initiation (punarupanayana). [The student] becomes one who eats the leavings of one who is not his guru, and one who eats honey and meat. He neglects the twilight rituals, the water-pot offering, and the fire-ritual for a long time. He may follow or cremate the corpse of one who is not his guru. In both cases, for ten days, there is a lapse of celibacy regarding the families and the food and drink.

If these and other such omens occur during the bright fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion, one should prepare a sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide smeared with cow-dung; having performed the expiation through self-restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and controls (*yantra*), as well as vows and fasts, and having established the fire and strewn it around, one performs the initiation (*upanayana*) as before up to the handing over of the staff, and then causes [the student] to recite the *Sāvitrī*.
He does not beg for alms, he does not eat, and he does not shave his beard.
He should not shave his head, nor put on [new] garments,
nor apply ornaments; furthermore, he should not wear the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), nor the girdle (*mekhalā*), nor even [new] clothing.
There is no recitation of mantras, nor the wearing of an antelope skin,
nor the handing over of a staff, nor likewise the practice of begging for alms;
there is no taking of a garment, and likewise no initiation into the vow.
For by performing it thus according to the rule, a man becomes purified;
having performed the re-consecration (punar-saṃskāra), he becomes purified again. "Having performed the Sāvitrī-vow on that very day, one should release it on that very day," so it is said.

The fire that begins with the taking of the hand [in marriage] is called the *aupāsana*. In that fire, the domestic rites (*gṛhya-karmāṇi*) are performed. Through this *aupāsana* fire, one attains the status of an *agnihotrin*, just as one attains the status of a performer of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices through the *pārvaṇa* offerings of cooked rice (*caru*). Therefore, it must be maintained perpetually; if it goes out, it should be kindled by friction or fetched from the house of a learned *śrotriya*. And in the event of its going out, there shall be a fast for either the wife or the husband.

And he should offer these oblations: "Svāhā to Mitra! Svāhā to Varuṇa! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Sūrya! Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Agni, the ascetic, the lord of people, the purifier! Svāhā to Agni, the pure! Svāhā to Agni, the luminous! Svāhā to Agni, the lord of vows!"—thus with the *vyāhṛtis* both separately and combined. Now, if [the ritual] is interrupted for two or three days in the evening or morning, one should offer to Agni Tantumant.

If the *sthālīpāka* is spilled, one should offer oblations to Agni Pathikṛt or to Agni Vaiśvānara. The *Āgrayaṇa* and *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* for this [rite] have also been explained. If [the fire] has been interrupted for twelve days, it must be re-established; or, having calculated [the lapse], one may perform the oblations again. We shall explain the re-establishment of the fire (*punarādheya*) later.

In an enclosed space, having dug up the ground and sprinkled it with water, having strewn it with sand and covered it with branches of the *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, or *pālāśa* trees, one should produce fire by churning sacrificial wood or bring it from the house of a learned *śrotriya*. Having placed it in a vessel and kindled it, one should remove the branches, and having established it with the formula, "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar oṃ pratiṣṭha," one adds fuel to it.

Having performed [the rites] up to the *vyāhṛti*s, he offers three *tantumatī* oblations with the verses: "Stretching the thread," "Awake, O Agni," and "The thirty-three threads. Then he offers four *abhyāvartanī* oblations with the verses: "O Agni, who turns back," "O Agni Aṅgiras," and "Return with vigor and with wealth. Having offered this *prājāpatyā*, the *manasvatī*, and the *sāptapatī*, he offers two *mindā* oblations with the verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self" and "Agni has given sight back again."

He offers the *prāyaścittīyā* oblation with the verse: "O Agni, thou art *ayās* (unwearied) and free from reproach; thou art truly *ayās*. Anointed by an *ayās* mind, thou shalt carry the offering with an *ayās* [mind]. O *ayās*, bestow healing upon us, *svāhā*! Having mentally recited the *daśahotṛ* formula and offered it together with the *sagraha* [libation], he offers with the verses: "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa"; "For that I entreat thee"; "Do thou, O Agni, release us from sin"; "So do thou, O Agni"; "Thou, O Agni, art *ayās*"; "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess," and so on. At this point, some offer the *jayā*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as supplementary offerings.

As previously described, having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Prosperity! Success!", the *sthālīpāka* offering to Agni is performed in the established manner. Here, he gives a gift to the teacher: two garments, a cow, or a bull. If he intends to travel, he should perform the ritual worship with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and then depart. If he must set out on a journey, the procedure for the internal consignment (*samāropaṇa*) of the fires into himself or the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), as well as the descent (*upāvarohaṇa*), has already been explained. Alternatively, the consignment and descent may be performed upon a fuel-stick (*samidh*).

Or he should consign the fire into the kindling woods (*araṇī*) according to the prescribed rule. Or, having brought fire from the house of a *śrotriya* where he is staying, and having placed it down with the two verses beginning "Being invoked" (*ājuhvānaḥ*) and "Awake! (*udbudhyasva*), and having strewn grass around it, he performs the oblation on that wood in which the fire was consigned. The ritual procedure for the oblation has been explained. 2.

Now, for a householder who has two wives: having established the fire, strewn it around, melted the clarified butter (ājya), purified it, heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, wiped them clean, and taken four portions of the butter into the *sruk*, the sacrificer, while his wife holds on to him, offers the oblation with the mantra: "Homage to thee, O Fever! For non-separation, for thee; for the ancestral offering (*svadhā*), for thee! May we, unharmed by thee, O Indra, not be struck down from any side! Thus, O Brahman, let this be thine; Svāhā! Then he consigns this fire into himself with the verse: "This is thy seasonal womb."

Having placed [the fire] upon the eastern fire and added fuel, while offering oblations with the two verses beginning "ājuhvāna" and "udbudhyasva," having strewn grass all around, melted the clarified butter, purified it, heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, wiped them, and taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, the sacrificer, while his two wives hold on to him, offers the oblation with this hymn, "yo brahmā brahmaṇa ujjahāra," taking four portions each time.

Having performed the rites up to the *praṇītā* waters, having cooked four *śarāva*-measurements of rice, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having removed it from the fire toward the north, he sprinkles it with butter once it has been set down. Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the *agnimukha*, he offers oblations from the cooked rice. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "May you two be united; be of one mind," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "O Agni Purīṣya, be our protector; do thou [protect] us. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the formulas beginning with "Thou art Agni Purīṣya" until the end of the section.
From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is established up to the gift of the cow as a boon; the domestic ritual (*aupāsana-tantra*) is concluded, the domestic ritual is concluded. 3.

Then one performs the domestic expiations (*gṛhyaprāyaścitta*): when the fire has gone out; when there is a lapse of time regarding the two daily oblations (*homa*) or the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); when the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice has not been performed; when eating new grain; when a wife has given birth before her first pregnancy ceremony (*sīmanta*) was performed; when twins are born among women or cattle; upon approaching another woman; upon approaching a woman during her menses; upon sexual intercourse by day; when the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) for a son have not yet been performed; upon an inversion of mantras; upon an inversion of ritual acts; upon an inversion of the vows of a student (*brahmacārin*); upon the breaking of his girdle (*mekhalā*); upon the breaking of his staff; and upon the failure to wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).

In the event of the omission of the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), the omission of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), or the omission of the water-pitcher (*udakumbha*), as well as other such omissions prescribed by the ritual manuals (*kalpa*), one should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, take four portions of clarified butter, and offer it with the mantra: "Protect us, O Agni, from sin; Svāhā! Having offered oblations both before and after with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, this indeed becomes his expiation (*prāyaścitta*), which ensures that the performance remains uninterrupted and continuous.

The fire from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the marriage fire (*vivāha-agni*), the fire of birth-impurity (*sūtaka-agni*), and the cremation fire (*śmaśāna-agni*) should be extinguished by scattering [the ashes] either within four days, ten days, or until the collection of the bones (*sañcayana*). Having sprinkled water with the mantra: "Struck down are the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the Piśācas who dwell upon the earth; let them go elsewhere, wherever their minds have gone," one should quickly deposit the ashes.

Having brought fire from the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) with the verse, "This is your seasonal womb," and having placed it down with the two verses beginning with "Being invoked" and "Awake," he strews grass around it, sprinkles water around it, and performs the expiation offering (*prāyaścitta*). He offers the *ayās* oblation for Agni, the five *hotṛ*s, the single *hotṛ* for the Brāhmaṇa, the *manasvatī*, the two *indāhuti*s, and the *vyāhṛti*s. Alternatively, even if he interrupts his four-day vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) at the time of the immediate rite, he should offer the *sārasvata* oblation, the *manasvatī*, the two *indāhuti*s, and the *mahāvyāhṛti*s together with the *praṇava*. 4.

Now, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) becomes one who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*) by discharging semen outside the womb, or by neglecting the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), or by neglecting the water-pot, or by neglecting the fire-ritual. If other causes for impurity occur, he shall cover himself with a fresh white garment, observe a fast, and, having performed the prescribed restraints and observances, kindle the fire on the night of the new moon. Having performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers two portions of clarified butter, saying: "I am overcome by lust; I am overcome! To Lust, the seeker of desire, svāhā!"

"Afflicted by desire, I am afflicted; svāhā to the one who desires desire!"—with these words, he should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, reciting the section beginning with "May my sensory power return to me. He should also offer oblations of clarified butter verse by verse, reciting the section beginning with "O gods, whatever offense we have committed against the gods. The rites from the *vāruṇī* offering through the *jaya* offerings are established as usual, ending with the gift of the boon of a cow. He gives a cow to his teacher. Now, if semen should be discharged in a dream, he should discard his clothes and put on others. At dawn, having gone out from the village toward the east or north, he should bathe in rivers.
One obtains the fruit of a three-night fast by bathing in a river that flows into the ocean;
and by bathing in a river flowing into the ocean on the new moon day at the winter solstice, one gains infinite merit.

Thus he performs the bath according to the prescribed rule. Having recited the *anuvāka* beginning with "May the sense-organ return to me," he becomes purified; so said the venerable Āgniveśya. Now, after the post-menstrual bath, she should not look at her husband's face, but should instead carefully show her own face to him. She should not engage in sexual intercourse on that day. If she should do so—
A son born on that day (the first) will have a short life and be destitute of wealth;
on the fifth, however, she who undergoes sexual union will give birth to a barren woman;
but on the sixth, she who undergoes union shall be a virtuous wife, possessed of sons and grandsons.
On the seventh day, however, a woman is born; on the eighth, one resembling the six-faced [Kārttikeya];
on the ninth, a beloved wife; on the tenth, an excellent son;
on the eleventh, a wicked-souled person; and on the twelfth, a lord of wealth.
On the thirteenth day, however, one obtains misfortune; on the fourteenth, a sinful son; likewise, on the fifteenth, a woman obtains a devoted wife;
and on the sixteenth, one obtains a son of such Brahmanic fame as there is none like him.
Beyond that, there is no further union; it is merely for the enjoyment of desire.
Therefore, with every effort, one should strive until the sixteenth day.
Through the excellence of the semen, one obtains a son; through the excellence of the blood, one obtains a daughter.
One should not intentionally go to sleep on a day that is censured;
however, if one should do so through negligence, one should recite that Vaiṣṇava ṛc and various names beginning with Keśava.
Then, having gone to the fire-sanctuary and offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
one should likewise not sleep during the three nights following [the initiation],
