nor on the two festival days (*parvan*); and having performed the *śrāddha*, one should not eat on that day.
On Mondays, Sundays, Tuesdays, and Saturdays; during the equinoxes, the solstices, the vyatīpāta yoga, and at the transit of the sun—
on these and other such censured days, one should not engage in sexual intercourse.
On the *viṣṭi* day, on the eighth, and likewise on the other *pakṣacchidra* days;
on the sixteenth, the twelfth, and likewise on the fifteenth,
the fourteenth, the ninth, the sixth, and the eighth.
Having observed any one of these [auspicious signs], he should perform purification as prescribed;
having gazed upon a favorable constellation and the rising of auspicious planets,
and having washed both his hands and feet and sipped water, he should meditate on Hari with his mind.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace,
one should display the *bhaga* with her right hand and,
saying "I touch you with auspiciousness," insert the penis into the womb.

With the verse beginning "ekayā ṛṣabheṇa," one who gazes properly, having performed purification to the utmost degree of satisfaction, should thereafter recite the verses correctly, starting with "ā te yonim. The wise man who, knowing this, performs the touching [of the womb] obtains a virtuous son. In this very manner, performing [this rite] month after month at the time of the fertile period (*ṛtuvelā*), he obtains a son who is handsome, intelligent, and most powerful; indeed, he obtains one who is most powerful—so it is said.
The Blessed One Āgniveśya said:
"I shall now describe the Brahmakūrca, the supreme purifier of the body,
as well as the Veda-ādi-jaya-homa, even when performed without mantras or consecrated rites."
In the case of eating the food of a Śūdra, selling the Vedas,

being licked by a crow or a dog, the *utkaṇṭhaka* [impurity] of deer and birds, and contact with the fifth type of barbarian (*mleccha*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are the means of purification.
One should take cow's urine from a blue-colored cow, collect black cow dung, [milk] from a copper-colored cow, curd from a white cow,
and ghee from a tawny cow; this destroys even the greatest of sins.
If none of the [prescribed] castes are available, one should take it from a Kapila cow alone:
one pala of cow urine, half the size of a thumb of cow dung,
seven palas of milk, and three palas of curd.

One should offer one pala of ghee and likewise water with *kuśa* grass; one should take cow’s urine with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, cow dung with "Gandhadvārām," milk with "Āpyāyasva," and curd with "Dadhikrāvṇo."

Having stirred the clarified butter with the mantra "ājyaṃ śukramasi," the water from the *kuśa* grass with "devasya tvā," and the water for mixing with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," and having consecrated it with "mā naḥ toke," he should lift it up with the *praṇava*, churn it with the *praṇava*, and drink it with the *praṇava* alone, [dedicating it] to Agni and Soma.
Having offered oblations with the verses "irāvatī," "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame," and "mā nas toke," and with the *prajāpati* verse,
using a middle-sized leaf of the *palāśa* tree or a lotus petal, he should drink that [water] which removes whatever sin resides in his body, having reached the skin and the bones.
"Like fire consumes fuel, [the recitation of] the *brahmakūrca* water burns away all [sins]. Thus [ends section 6].
Now, therefore, we shall explain the occasional expiations (*naimittika-prāyaścitta*). In all cases, one should mutter the *vaiṣṇava-ṛc*.

"Viṣṇoḥ nu kaṃ vīryāṇi pravocaṃ... (I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu...). Now, during an interval in the ritual, if he should feel hunger or spit, he mutters: "Sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ... (The Puruṣa has a thousand heads...). Having touched water with his thumb and ring finger, he should touch his right ear. If he should urinate, he should wash his feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), meditate on the syllable *Oṃ* in his mind, become pure, and then mutter two verses beginning with: "Puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam... (The Puruṣa indeed is all this...).

If he should urinate, having performed purification as before, he should mutter the three verses beginning with "The Puruṣa rose up three-footed. If he touches something impure, he should bathe in a reservoir of pure water, sip water for purification, and mutter the four verses beginning with "From that sacrifice, which was entirely offered... If he sees a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, or the like, he should sip water, gaze at the sun, and mutter: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms; that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born."

One should mutter the three verses beginning with "The moon was born from the mind; from the eye the sun was born. If the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be interrupted midway, one should mutter the three verses beginning with "I know this great Puruṣa. Having offered two *mindā* oblations, one should complete the remainder of the rite again. If the vessels have been licked by a dog or other such animal, those made of wood should be thrown into the fire, those made of clay should be thrown into water, and those made of metal are purified by ashes.

Having taken up other new vessels, one should mutter the two verses beginning with "O Viṣṇu, you are our closest" (*viṣṇo tvanno antamaḥ*) and "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇornukaṃ vīryāṇi pravocam*). One should then offer six oblations with the mantras: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self," "Agni has given back my sight," "This prayer of mine, O Varuṇa," "For that I entreat thee," and "Do thou, O Agni, drive away from us."

If the fire has been licked by a woman in her courses or the like, one should extinguish the fire, perform purification as before, churn out a new fire or bring a common (laukika) fire, heat and wipe the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, take four portions of clarified butter into the *sruk*, offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and then perform the consecration as before. If the fire-wood (*araṇi*) should become impure, one should fetch other wood, take four portions of clarified butter, mentally recite the *Puruṣasūkta*, and offer it as an oblation.

If a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or a death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) should occur during that period, one does not perform the *homa* nor the *sthālīpāka* for those days. One gives that material to a Brāhmaṇa during a *vyatīpāta*; thus says the venerable Āgniveśya.

Now, therefore, the domestic expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are recorded; we shall explain them. The remaining [expiations] pertain to the *vaitānika* (Vedic) rites. Whatever is the rule for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), that is the rule for one who has established the fires, as well as for one who maintains the domestic fire (*aupāsanika*). Such is the *Śāṭyāyanīya* Brāhmaṇa. In that [context], whatever are the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), here they are the cooked rice offerings (*caru*).

The preparation of milk, curds, and ghee-mixtures (pṛṣadājya) is like that of clarified butter (*ājya*). One should not place curds on the fire, nor pour it out, nor stir it. Having performed the rites for Agni, the Rudras, the Rākṣasas, the Pitṛs, and the Nairṛtas, as well as cutting, splitting, throwing away, and touching oneself, one should touch water. In all cases—whether [the offering] has been spilled, broken, dried up, burnt, inverted, or interrupted—one should offer two *mindā* oblations with the verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self" and "Agni has given back my sight."

Having consecrated what has spilled with the mantra, "I sprinkle [the earth] for the sake of healing," he should remove it, pour water over it, worship it with "Bhūḥ," and offer two oblations with the mantras, "The sky has not fallen" and "The earth. If it is clarified butter, he should also consecrate it with "O gods, [protect] the people and the trees from distress," and give away some of it. Then, if [the vessel] is broken, he should consecrate the broken piece with "The earth by its abundance," remove it, pour water over it, and offer an oblation with the verse, "Thirty-three are the threads. Wooden items should be thrown into the fire.

Then, over the scorched portion, he should recite the mantra: "For Nirṛti, thee! Having cast it away toward the south-west or the north-west direction with the words: "Go away a little; go downward; go to the demons!", he should offer three oblations of clarified butter with the mantra: "Agni drives away the demons. If a portion of the sacrificial offerings has been touched by impurity, having removed that part and performed the aforementioned rite, he should offer the oblation with this [mantra]. By this, the cases of undercooked and overcooked offerings are explained. He should throw the [remnants] into water.

Having consecrated the well-cooked [oblation] with "To Rudra thee," and the poorly cooked with "To Yama thee," then, upon the burning of the surrounding grass-strew, he should consecrate it with "Homage to Agni Kṣāmavat; homage! O Kṣāmavat, do not harm me; [do not harm] my house, my wealth, or my cattle," and then offer it with "Svāhā to Agni Kṣāmavat! Then, having strewn [grass] around again with "Indraṃ vo viśvataspari," he should offer with "Svāhā to Indra! Then, upon the burning of the enclosing sticks, [he should say]: "Homage to the forest-fire Agni; homage to the forest-fire!"

From this point upward, the procedure is the same: he should offer two oblations with the verses, "Thou art the kindling-stick of Agni" for the western half, "Thou art the kindling-stick of Yama" for the southern half, and "Thou art the kindling-stick of Soma" for the northern half. He should offer two oblations with the verses, "Kindling thee, for a hundred winters," and "For me. He should entrust the other [the sacrificer] to [Agni] with the verse, "Thou art the Gandharva," reciting each mantra separately. Now, in case of a transposition, he should offer four oblations with the verses, "O Agni, do thou protect us," "So do thou, O Agni, protect us," "Thou, O Agni, art Ayās," and "O Prajāpati."

One should perform these very *mano jyotiḥ* offerings as the fifth [offering] for the omitted [rite], and one should also perform the omitted rite itself. If something is offered after the [sacrifice] has already concluded, and the oblation of the subsequent time has arrived while the previous one has not yet been completed, this constitutes a lapse of time (*kālātipatti*). For that lapse, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is that one should offer the *mano jyotiḥ* for the previous [rite], and likewise offer it for the subsequent one. In this manner, for each omitted oblation up to ten nights, there shall be a breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Fasting is prescribed for up to twenty nights starting from the eleventh day; beyond thirty nights, a *prājāpatya* penance is ordained. Alternatively, it is stated that starting from the eleventh day, one should offer three *tantumatī* oblations for twelve days; if [the fire] has been interrupted, it must be re-established. Or likewise: if a *parvan* has passed, having offered four oblations with the mantras "mano jyotiḥ," "ayāścāgne," "yad asmin," and "svasti na indra," one should prepare a *sthālīpāka* for Agni Pathikṛt before the eighth [day].

From this point forward, one should observe a fast; when two [Pārvaṇas] have passed among three, or three [have passed], the expiation is a fire-oblation as in the Pārvaṇa rite, and when the Pitṛyajña has been omitted for two fortnights, a fast must be observed—this is established.

Now, regarding the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*): on a single day, one should offer the *mano jyotiḥ* oblation; on two, three, four, five, or six days and so forth, having offered three *tantumatī* oblations, one should mutter the four *vāruṇī* verses—namely, *imaṃ me varuṇa*, *tattvā yāmi*, *yatkiñca*, and *ava te heḍaḥ*—until the ninth night. From then until the tenth night, one should offer four *abhyāvartinī* oblations. At the end of all [these rites], [the offering is performed] with the *vyāhṛtis*; thus it is established. 9

Henceforth, we shall explain the rules for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Having practiced the blameless duties of a householder, having performed sacrifices, having procreated a son, having performed his sacraments, having taught him the Veda, having provided for his livelihood, and having entrusted the burden of the family to a virtuous son, he—clad in *kuśa* grass, bark, skin, or rags; wearing matted hair (*jaṭā*); with a black antelope skin as an upper garment; having assumed the outward signs of departure; and having performed the internal transference of the sacred fires (*agnisamāropaṇa*)—sets out either accompanied by his wife or without her during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion.

He should take refuge in the forest. Having established the *śramaṇa*-fire, he should tend the fire morning and evening with wild roots, fruits, herbs, bamboo, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and other such forest products. Having daily performed the sacrifices to the gods, Brahmins, ancestors, spirits, and men using unploughed grains, or else at the proper time, he should dry up his body according to his capacity through restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), mantras, fasting, and so forth. Subsisting on withered leaves, using his teeth as a mortar, or crushing food with stones, he should give even to those who might arrive at that time.

Sleeping on the bare ground, with vital energy drawn upward (celibate), fond of guests, free from envy, always pure, and avoiding quarreling, backbiting, lying, and violence; not looking at the roof of a village, dwelling in the forest, devoted to the sacred fire, granting fearlessness to all beings, and not consuming food touched by others or belonging to another stage of life; dedicated to the single fire, vigilant, and not treading upon cultivated land where seeds have been sown or where crops are growing; he should offer water and fruit to one superior in austerity, superior in sacrifice, or superior in age.

Having thus lived among the deer, dwelling in motionlessness, he will pass his time and go to the heavenly world; or else, having observed the vow of the forest-dweller for a third part of his life, he may wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having fasted during the preliminary period, one should prepare the necessary materials. One prepares the two saffron-colored garments, a *plakṣa*-leaf purifier, sandals, a seat, a bamboo staff, a sling, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a razor, a vessel of *alābu* gourd, a bundle of *kuśa* grass, and other such materials. Having consigned the sacred fire and entered the village from the forest, one should have the hair and beard shaved and bathe in rivers or in a pure reservoir of water.

Having sipped water on the bank of a river or in a temple, and having approached Brahmins, one who is free from anger and hatred should renounce all ritual actions. One should not renounce the Veda; by renouncing the Veda, one becomes a Śūdra. Therefore, one should not renounce the Veda. In the presence of Brahmins, having uttered the mantra, he should drink water, saying: "I have renounced. Having taken up the requisites—beginning with the staff of bamboo and ending with the [other items]—which were brought by his householder son, and gazing at the orb of the sun, he should proclaim three times aloud: "I have renounced."

Then, having approached a Brāhmaṇa who wears the *nivīta* cord and has performed many sacrifices, and having said, "I must give staffs," and having taken up the staffs, being one whose name has been established and who is permitted, he should properly attend to the duties of an ascetic (*yati*). He should always wear the topknot (*śikhā*), always wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), always perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*), always bathe in the morning, always subsist on alms (*bhikṣā*), always observe restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), self-control (*yantra*), vows (*vrata*), and fasting (*upavāsa*), and always worship the Lord (*Īśvara*). He should always dwell in a cow-pen or a temple, and be free from fear, desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy.

Having practiced such dharmas as these, he will go to the heavenly world. Alternatively, when the Brāhmaṇas have declined, having performed purification as before and having renounced all ritual actions, he consumes only water as his food while uttering the *praiṣa* formulas. By worshipping the Lord alone, he becomes purified; thus said the venerable Āgniveśya. 11

We shall now explain the re-initiation ceremony (*punarupanayana*). [The sections cover: the fire that begins with the taking of the hand in marriage; then, the two wives of a householder; then, the expiations for domestic rites (*gṛhya-prāyaścitta*); then, the case where a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) breaks his vow of chastity; then, the *brahmakūrca* rite following the ritual bath at the end of the menstrual period; then, the occasional rites (*naimittika*); then, the expiations for domestic rites; and from here on, the rules for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and the rules for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the *Āgniveśya-gṛhyasūtra*.
The second question is completed;
now begins the third question,
the first chapter.

On the new moon day, in the afternoon, or on the days of the wind-god (the fourth, seventh, and eighth) of the dark fortnight, having prepared food for the ancestors, he arranges seats of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing south and invites an odd number of pure Brahmins who are learned in the mantras and possessed of all limbs. He should not feed those related by birth, lineage, or mantra, nor those who are motivated by worldly gain.

Having kindled the fire and strewn it around with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the south and the east, he pours clarified butter into a vessel for the clarified butter over which a single purifier has been placed, and having prepared it, he then sprinkles water around the fire while keeping his sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Having added fuel from an *udumbara* tree, he offers oblations with a ladle made of *udumbara*.

Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he invokes the ancestors with the verse: "Come, O gentle ancestors, by your deep and ancient paths, bestowing upon us progeny, wealth, and long life for a hundred autumns. He pours water toward that same direction with the verse: "O divine waters, send forth this fire; may our ancestors enjoy this sacrifice. May those who partake of the seated strength bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons."

Having performed [the rites] up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), offers: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! "The waters that flow eastward and those from the north—with those waters, the sustainers of the entire world, I place a barrier between myself and my father; *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! "I have placed a barrier with the mountains, and a barrier with the great earth."

By day, with infinite directions and protections, I interpose an interval from the grandfather: *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*. With all the seasons, with days and nights together with their junctions, and with half-months and months, I interpose an interval from the great-grandfather: *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*. Then he offers oblations by means of names, saying: "To such-and-such, *svadhā*, homage; to such-and-such, *svadhā*, homage."

"That which my mother, acting without restraint, has caused me to be excited—may my father take that seed; let another, being impotent, fall away. *Svadhā*! *Namaḥ*! *Svāhā*! Thus a second time; likewise a third time. He modifies the mantra as follows: "That which my grandmother... and "That which my great-grandmother... 1.

Those ancestors who are here and those who are not here, those whom we know and those whom we do not know—O Agni Jātavedas, you know them. May they rejoice with the *svadhā* offered by you, according to their desires. *Svadhā! Namaḥ! Svāhā!* That limb of yours which the flesh-eater has consumed, which Jātavedas has carried away to the worlds and brought forth—that I restore for you again. May the ancestors be whole with all their limbs. *Svadhā! Namaḥ! Svāhā!*

"Carry the clarified butter, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors where you know them to be placed in the distance. May streams of clarified butter flow toward them; may their blessings be true according to their desires. *Svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*! He offers the second oblation in the same way, and likewise the third. He modifies the mantra to "to the grandfathers" and "to the great-grandfathers. In this manner he offers the food. He modifies the mantra to "carry the food."

Then he offers the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the formula: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā! Homage! Having offered it in the eastern part of the southern half [of the fire] and having thrown the ladle [into the fire], he then touches the food with the formula: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not fail among the ancestors there in that world. The earth is level on all sides; Agni is the witness so that what has been given may not be lost."

The *ṛc* verses are your greatness; the earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid. I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among my grandfathers in that world yonder, in that other world. May the atmosphere listen on all sides, and may Vāyu be the listener for the non-neglect of what has been given. The *yajus* formulas are your greatness.

"The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not fail for my great-grandfathers in yonder world. The sky is all around, the sun is the witness, for the non-neglect of what has been given; the Sāmans are your greatness. With these words, he causes the Brāhmaṇas to touch [the food]. Having followed them as they have eaten and having asked for permission regarding the remainder...

Taking a water-pot and a handful of *darbha* grass, and having strewn *darbha* grass with the tips pointing southward, he pours out three vessels of water upon them with his hands turned downward, ending toward the south, saying: "May the Soma-loving ancestors purify themselves; may the Soma-loving grandfathers purify themselves; may the Soma-loving great-grandfathers purify themselves. Or, saying "O [Name], pour down! O [Name], pour down! over each, he places three rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) upon them with his hands turned downward, ending toward the south.

He offers the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to the father with the formula, "This for you, Father, N.N."; to the grandfather with, "This for you, Grandfather, N.N."; and to the great-grandfather with, "This for you, Great-grandfather, N.N. The fourth [ball] is offered silently; it may or may not be performed. If he does not know their names, he offers the rice-ball to the father with, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth"; to the grandfather with, "Svadhā to the grandfathers dwelling in the intermediate space"; and to the great-grandfather with, "Svadhā to the great-grandfathers dwelling in heaven."

Here he gives collyrium, ointment, and clothing, following each morsel of food. He applies the collyrium three times, saying, "Anoint [Name], anoint [Name]! He applies the ointment three times, saying, "Anoint [Name], anoint [Name]!"

"O fathers, these are your garments; do not seek anything else from us, O fathers. O grandfathers, these are your garments; do not seek anything else from us, O grandfathers. O great-grandfathers, these are your garments; do not seek anything else from us, O great-grandfathers. Having cut off a fringe or a tuft of wool, he places it [on the garments]; in the earlier stage of life, having cut his own hair, in the later stage. Then, having gathered the vessel, he pours out the water with the verse: "May these honey-sweet waters satisfy our sons and grandsons."

"May the divine waters, yielding *svadhā* and nectar to the ancestors, satisfy both [the gods and the ancestors]. Having turned the vessel face down and crossed his hands, he pays homage with the six salutations beginning with "Obeisance to you, O ancestors, for the sake of the essence (*rasa*)."

Having gone to the edge of the water, he offers handfuls of water by pouring three handfuls of water [with the formula]: "This honeyed wave for thee, O father, is full of sap; as great as fire and the earth are, so great is its measure, so great is its majesty; I give it to thee as such a being. As fire is unexhausted and undecaying, so may it be unexhausted and undecaying for my father, thyself; Svadhā! May you become Svadhā; live on this unexhausted [offering] together with them. The *Ṛgveda* is your majesty. This honeyed wave for thee, O grandfather, of [thy] father...

As great as the wave, as great as Sarasvat, as great as Vāyu and the intermediate space (antarikṣa), so great is his measure; so great is his majesty. So great a being do I bestow upon him. As Vāyu is imperishable and undecaying, even so may you be imperishable and undecaying for my grandfather and father; may you become *svadhā*. May he, [Name], live together with those [ancestors] upon this imperishable *svadhā*. The *yajus* formulas are your majesty.

"This is for you, O great-grandfather, the honeyed wave of your father, [the portion] belonging to Sarasvant. As great as the sun and the sky are, so great is its measure; so great is its majesty. I give it to him as such a being. Just as the sun is inexhaustible and undecaying, so may it be inexhaustible and undecaying for my great-grandfather’s father; may it become *svadhā*. May you live upon that inexhaustible *svadhā* together with them, O Sāmans; this is your majesty."

Having returned, he pours water from a water-vessel onto the established [ground] with the verse: "Depart, O gentle Pitṛs, by the deep, ancient paths, bestowing upon us progeny and wealth; then come back again to our houses in the month, to eat the sacrificial food, being rich in offspring and heroic sons. By this, the ritual procedure for the Arghya-water is explained. Meat is prescribed; in the absence of meat, vegetables.
On the new moon day, in the afternoon, [he offers] to those Pitṛs who are here a water-pot, a handful of Darbha grass, and three...
Thus ends the first chapter in the third book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the second chapter.

One who is about to perform the Aṣṭakā sacrifice prepares either a bull or a barren cow, rice, food, honey, and clarified butter. The purification is as prescribed. Having established the fire under the constellation Anūrādhā and having strewn grass around it, he pours out the rice to the west of the fire using a single strainer, saying: "I offer this cake made from four measures of rice, which removes the suffering of the ancestors in the world beyond."

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour out for you what is acceptable to the Fathers"—saying "for the Fathers, for the Fathers," he thus pours out four spoonfuls. Having sprinkled [the grains] and silently released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he places this cake on the potsherds in the same manner as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); or [he may place] a single potsherd.

When that [milk] has been boiled, having melted the clarified butter and curds and purified them, he then sprinkles [water] around: with "Adite, give your consent," he sprinkles from the south toward the east; with "Anumate, give your consent," from the west toward the north; with "Sarasvate, give your consent," from the north toward the east; and with "O God Savitṛ, impel," he sprinkles all around clockwise. Having poured the two libations (āghāra), he offers the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga). He performs an expiation with clarified butter, [offering] with the verse: "Thou who liest across, the boundary, the upholder."

"I offer you, who belong to Viśvakarman, with a stream of clarified butter, together with desires; *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*! Then, having cut a portion from the middle of this cake and having spread a base [of ghee] and poured [ghee] over it, he offers it with a ladle made of Udumbara wood.

He offers a cake mixed with ghee, saying: "Carry today this oblation, rich in ghee and accompanied by the *svadhā* call, for the gratification of the ancestors; I offer these oblations to the ancestors with desires, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*! Then, having first taken a portion from the front and from the south, he offers a smaller portion from behind, saying: "This is she who first shone forth; she moves within, having entered. As a bride she has been born, the mother of nine. Three majesties attend her. With desires, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*!"

He offers the third oblation with: "The mortars and the pressing-stones have raised their voice, performing the annual waters for the fathers. O Ekāṣṭakā, may we be possessed of good offspring and heroes; may we be lords of riches! With our desires, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*! He offers the fourth oblation with: "The night which people greet with joy as she approaches like a milch-cow, she who is the mistress of the year—may she be auspicious to us! With our desires, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*!"

He offers the fifth oblation with: "O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings. Whatever desire we have as we offer to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches—with our desires, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*! He offers the sixth oblation with: "Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently..."

"May Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all this well-offered and well-sacrificed for me. To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the offerer of the well-offered, the offerer of the all-offered, the fulfiller of desires through the oblations of all expiations—svadhā, obeisance, svāhā! Having washed and set aside the ladle, having wiped it in the same manner and sprinkled water around it, he offers these rice-balls according to the procedure for the *piṇḍas*. Then, with an act of faith, he touches this cake, which contains ghee and honey. 2.

The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; do not perish for the ancestors there in yonder world. The earth is level on all sides; Agni is the witness to ensure that what has been given is not lost. The *Ṛgveda* hymns are your greatness.

The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among the grandfathers there in that world. The atmosphere is all around you; may Vāyu listen closely for the non-neglect of what has been given. The Yajus-formulas are your greatness.

"The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish for my great-grandfathers in yonder world. The sky is all around, the sun is the witness; for the non-neglect of what has been given, the Sāmans are your greatness. With this [formula], he serves the learned Brāhmaṇas.

Having served the food and gone to the water, he offers handfuls of water with the pouring of water from his joined palms: "This honeyed wave, O Father, is for you; as vast as fire and earth are, so great is its measure, so great is its magnitude. I give this being to you. As fire is preserved and not destroyed, so may it be preserved and not destroyed for my father, your father. Be a *svadhā* offering; may you live together with them upon the imperishable *svadhā*. This *ṛc* is your majesty. (3)

This, O Grandfather, is the honeyed wave for your father, Sarasvān. As great as the wind and the intermediate space are, so great is its measure; so great is its majesty. I give this being to you, so that it may be undecaying and imperishable, just as the wind is preserved and remains undecayed. Thus, let it be an undecaying *svadhā* for my grandfather and father. May you, O *svadhā*, live upon this undecaying [offering] together with them. The *yajus* verses are your majesty.

"This is for you, O great-grandfather, the honeyed wave of your father, Sarasvān. As great as the sun and the sky are, so great is its measure; so great is its majesty. I give this being to you of such magnitude. Just as the sun is undecaying and inexhaustible, so may it be undecaying and inexhaustible for my great-grandfather’s father. *Svadhā* be to you! You are *svadhā*; live on with them, O [Name], for the Sāman hymns are your majesty. This much constitutes the ritual of that day.

Knowing this, the ancient seers indeed prepared this *aṣṭakya* cake in four dishes; with it they satisfied the ancestors, and the ancestors, being satisfied, in turn satisfied them with offspring and cattle. Thus they established friendship with the ancestors, for all beings were their friends. Whoever, knowing this, prepares this *aṣṭakya* cake in four dishes in this manner—

By that very [offering], he satisfies the ancestors, who, being satisfied, satisfy him with offspring and cattle. Thus, indeed, he makes friends with the ancestors; for all beings become his friends, he who, knowing this, prepares this eight-day cake (*aṣṭakya-apūpa*) in four dishes in this manner. 4.

On the following day, under the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, having established the fire, strewn it around, and sprinkled water in the same manner as before, he offers the two Āghāra-libations and the two Ājyabhāga-portions. Having offered the expiatory oblation, he offers the introductory oblation with the mantra: "This cow I dedicate to the ancestors—full of vigor, full of *svadhā*—may the ancestors who have passed away accept it from me! May she satisfy my ancestors with all their desires in the world beyond; *svāhā*! Then he dedicates the cow to them with the formula: "I dedicate you, who are dear to the ancestors."

Then he sprinkles it with the formula: "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the Fathers. They quiet it right here with its head toward the west and its feet toward the south. When it has been quieted, he satiates its vital breaths with water silently. Then, having extracted its omentum, he spreads it out on a broad skewer silently. Then they extract its heart and the two kidneys, which are well-known [parts]. Having placed these upon those very skewers, they cook them on this very fire.

When the [meat] has been boiled, he cuts the omentum into three parts and offers it with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, having first spread a base of ghee and then poured ghee over it, saying: "Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the fathers where you know them to be placed in the distance; let streams of fat flow toward them; may their blessings be realized according to their desires! Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! Then, with the same *udumbara* ladle, he offers portions of this meat, having first spread a base of ghee and poured ghee over each portion. 5

"Behold the Ekāṣṭakā being milked—food rich in meat, rich in ghee, and rich in *svadhā*. May that, purified by the Brāhmaṇas, become infinite, inexhaustible, and abundant through [the fulfillment of] desires; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*! He offers the second oblation: "The Ekāṣṭakā, performing penance, the swelling wife of the year, has yielded her milk. O Fathers, live upon that milk as it is released in a thousand ways through [the fulfillment of] desires; *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*!"

He offers the third oblation with: "Ekāṣṭakā, performing penance, gave birth to a child, the greatness Indra; through him the gods overcame the Dasyus; he became the slayer of the Asuras by his powers. Through desires, Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! He offers the fourth oblation with: "The mortars, the pressing-stones... He offers the fifth oblation with: "Whom people greet with joy... He offers the sixth oblation with: "O Prajāpati... He offers the seventh oblation with: "Whatever I have done in excess of this rite..."

Having washed the ladle and set it aside, and having sprinkled water around in the same manner as for the rice-balls, he offers these rice-balls according to the ritual for the rice-balls and touches them with the formula for touching with faith: "The earth is your vessel," and so forth. He serves learned Brāhmaṇas. Having served them and gone toward the water, he offers a handful of water with the formula: "This for you, O father [or grandfather]. This much constitutes the ritual of that day.

Knowing this, the ancient teachers indeed prepared the cow in this manner for the Aṣṭakā; with it they satisfied the ancestors, and they, being satisfied, satisfied them in turn with offspring and cattle. Thereby they established a friendship with the ancestors, for all beings were their friends. Whoever, knowing this, prepares the cow in this manner for the Aṣṭakā, truly satisfies the ancestors with it; and they, being satisfied, satisfy him in turn with offspring and cattle.

Therefore, he indeed makes friends with the ancestors; for all beings become his friends, who, knowing this, prepares the cow in this manner at the Aṣṭakā sacrifice. On the third day, having again prepared the Śrāddha food and wealth, having kindled the fire, strewn it around, and sprinkled water as before, having offered the two Āghāra libations and the two Ājyabhāga portions, and having offered the expiatory oblation with clarified butter, he then offers from that food—after spreading a base and pouring butter over it—with a ladle made of Udumbara wood, saying: "Carry the food, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors where you know them to be placed in the distance."

"May the streams of food flow toward them; may their blessings be true according to their desires! Svadhā! Namaḥ! Svāhā! With these words he offers the second oblation: "O Night, you who are the image of the year, whom people worship—you, having made our offspring rich in heroes, may they enjoy a full lifespan according to their desires! Svadhā! Namaḥ! Svāhā! With these words he offers the third oblation: "Whom the people greet with joy... With these words he offers the fourth oblation: "O Prajāpati..."

He offers the fifth oblation with the verse, "Whatever of this rite I have overdone," and having thrown the ladle into the fire and sprinkled water around it in the same manner as before, he gives these rice-balls according to the procedure for the *piṇḍas*. He touches them with the formula for touching with faith: "The earth is your vessel," and so forth. He serves learned Brāhmaṇas. Having served them, he goes toward the water and offers a handful of water with the formula, "This for you, O father. This much constitutes the ritual action for that day.

Knowing this, the ancient Vedic scholars prepared the food for the Aṣṭakā festival in this manner; by it they satisfied the ancestors, and the ancestors, being satisfied, in turn satisfied them with offspring and cattle. Thus they established a friendship with the ancestors, for all beings were their friends. Indeed, whoever knowing this prepares the food for the Aṣṭakā in this way, he satisfies the ancestors by it; and they, being satisfied, satisfy him with offspring and cattle.

Therefore, by means of the ancestors, he makes friends; for all beings become his friends. He who, knowing this, gives food and wealth according to his faith on the third day—verily, from that, his cattle come to possess unlimited food and wealth. But he who, knowing this, does not give food and wealth according to his faith on the third day—for him, his cattle do not come to possess unlimited food and wealth. 7

One intending to perform the Aṣṭakā sacrifice should first cut portions from the front and the south, saying: "The earth is your vessel; this is for your father's grandfather. On the day before the full moon of Jyeṣṭha, on the third day after the Ekāṣṭakā, [he performs] the seven [offerings].
Thus ends the second chapter in the third book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the third chapter.

Now, therefore, we shall describe the remainder of the *śrāddha* rites. On the evening before, having offered the *aupāsana* oblation and restrained his breath, he makes a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying either: "Tomorrow I shall perform the monthly *śrāddha* for the ancestors," or "Tomorrow I shall perform the *nakṣatra-śrāddha* for Yajñaśarman," or "Tomorrow I shall perform the three-fortnightly *śrāddha* for Yajñaśarman," or "Tomorrow I shall perform the six-monthly *śrāddha* for Yajñaśarman," or "Tomorrow I shall perform the annual *śrāddha* for Yajñaśarman. Or [he may say]: "Tomorrow [I shall perform the *śrāddha*] for Yajñaśarman..."

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha," he invites Brahmins who are pure, learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), poor, knowers of the Veda, complete in their limbs, and who do not share his lineage (gotra) or ancestral rishi-lineage (ārṣeya). He invites two for the Viśvedevas and three for the ancestors; however, if it is a Sapiṇḍīśrāddha, one more [than the three] is invited. For the Śrāddhas of the deceased (preta-śrāddha), he should invite only one.

"Tomorrow there is to be a monthly *śrāddha* for the ancestors; may you grant me your favor in this regard. Likewise, "Tomorrow there is to be an *aṣṭakā-śrāddha* for the ancestors; may you grant me your favor in this regard. "Tomorrow there is to be a daily *śrāddha*, an *ekoddiṣṭa*, or a *nakṣatra-śrāddha* for the ancestors"—having said this in each case, and having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having worshipped as far as possible with edible substances such as sesame flour and the like, one should offer betel leaves and other items.

On the following day, having performed the morning *aupāsana* oblation, he digs three pits. In the case of *preta-śrāddhas*, he digs only one. In the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, having dug three pits and scattered sesame seeds and *darbha* grass within them, he invites the Brahmins and offers them the *kṣaṇa*. Having washed the feet of the two Viśvedevas in the northern pit, those of the ancestors in the middle one, and the feet of the deceased in the southern one, and having honored them, he should offer betel nut. He should perform everything according to the sequence of washing the feet, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).

In the afternoon, for the purpose of feeding the Brāhmaṇas, he should prepare a *sthālīpāka* (cooked grain offering) on the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). At the time of the invocation of the ancestors, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and standing facing south, he performs the invocation and, having summoned the Brāhmaṇas, seats them according to the prescribed directions. Having offered oblations according to the rule, he offers these rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) at each of the places specified by the ritual procedure for the rice-balls. At the time of arranging the vessels, he places [the water] in a single vessel with the verse: "O ancestors who have come from the path of the gods, from the oceans, from the waters, and from the heavenly realms..."

"In this sacrifice, may they obtain all desires; let them milk [the earth] inexhaustibly. Saying, "I take this *arghya* for you, O Fathers," he takes it for the fathers; saying, "I take this *arghya* for you, O grandfathers," for the grandfathers; saying, "I take this *arghya* for you, O great-grandfathers," for the great-grandfathers. Then, in another vessel, for the deceased (the *preta*), saying, "I take this for you," he pours water for the deceased. "Thou art sesame, having Soma as thy deity, created by the gods at the *gosava* sacrifice."

"Offered by those of old, come, O Svadhā! Delight these fathers and these worlds for us; Svadhā! Homage!"—with these words he scatters sesame seeds. And [he scatters them] with "Delight these grandfathers and great-grandfathers and these worlds for us; Svadhā! Homage! and for the deceased with "Delight these worlds."

"May the winds blow sweet for the one who follows the cosmic order; may the rivers flow with sweetness; may the plants be sweet for us. May the food be sweet at dawn; may the earthly realm be full of sweetness; may the sky, our father, be sweet. May the lord of the forest be full of sweetness for us; may the sun be full of sweetness; may the cows be sweet for us. With these words, he brings the honey.

Taking the *kuśalava* grass, he says: "Thou art the luster of Soma; may my luster be like thine. Thou art the immortal; protect me from death; protect me from lightning; protect me from the tooth-ache. Having churned [the mixture], he casts away the foam with the words, "The head of Namuci has been cast out. He places [the mixture] upon *darbha* grass, covers it with *darbha* grass, sprinkles water over it with the verse, "May the divine waters be auspicious to us," adorns it with perfumes and other offerings, and deposits it in a place where he considers it to be secure, saying, "Svadhā!"

As before, having performed the washing of the feet and having seated them facing north, he invites the Viśvedevas with the words, "The Viśvedevas, please accept the invitation. Having replied, "Om, so be it," he says, "May you partake. The others reply, "I shall partake."

"The invitation (kṣaṇa) should be offered for the monthly śrāddha," thus [it is said] regarding the monthly [śrāddha]; "the invitation should be offered for the aṣṭakā-śrāddha," thus [it is said] regarding the aṣṭakās; "the invitation should be offered for the obligatory (nitya) śrāddha," thus [it is said] regarding the obligatory śrāddha; "the invitation should be offered for the ekoddiṣṭa-śrāddha," thus [it is said] regarding the ekoddiṣṭa; "the invitation should be offered for the nakṣatra-śrāddha," thus [it is said] regarding the nakṣatra; "the invitation should be offered for the three-fortnightly (tripakṣa) śrāddha," thus [it is said] regarding the tripakṣa; "the invitation should be offered for the six-monthly (ṣaṇmāsa) śrāddha," thus [it is said] regarding the six-monthly; "the invitation should be offered for the annual (saṃvatsara) śrāddha," thus [it is said].

At the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha performed at the end of one year, the response regarding the invitation is: "The moment (*kṣaṇa*) should be made. Having said "Oṃ, so be it," the officiant says, "May you accept it," and the others reply, "I accept it. Having honored them with perfumes and other offerings, and having honored the vessel of *svadhā*, he gives a pair of garments, earrings, and a ring. Then he touches the food with the mantra: "The earth is your vessel. He looks at those who are eating with the mantra: "Seated in the vital breath, I offer the nectar."

"May my self [be established] in Brahman for the sake of immortality. He should cause them to hear the *ṛg* and *yajus* verses characterized by paternal signs. Having offered water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) to those who have sipped water (*ācānta*), and having placed a purifier (*pavitra*) in the hand of the father, he brings the *svadhā* offering, saying: "May there be *svadhā* in the hand for the fathers. The response is: "Let there be *svadhā*. In this same manner for the grandfather, in this same manner for the great-grandfather, and likewise for the deceased. Likewise, having offered pure water, the response is: "Let there be pure water."

Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability and having performed a circumambulation, he asks, "What shall be done with the remnants of the food? The response is, "Let them be eaten together with those who are dear. Having returned, he eats the remainder along with his attendants. If, while performing the daily *śrāddha*, he offers a hare, a deer, or a tortoise, he cooks it, or having purchased it with gold, he performs the rite just as on the second day of the *aṣṭakā* festivals. They perform the *tripakṣa-śrāddha* (the three-fortnightly *śrāddha*) according to the rules for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

They perform the six-month *śrāddha* as they do the three-fortnightly one; they perform the annual *śrāddha* as they do the six-month one. In this manner, until the end of the year, they perform [the rites] exactly so on the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) of the deceased's cremation.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the remainder of the *śrāddha*: "The winds blow honey for the one who follows the cosmic order" (*madhuvātā ṛtāyate*), these two verses.
Thus ends the third chapter of the third book in the *Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Now follows the procedure for cremation. When death is imminent, whether for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), one who has not maintained them, or for a woman, one should smear a clean, level place with cow-dung, sprinkle it with water, scatter sand over it, and spread *darbha* grass upon that sand with its points facing south. Having laid the deceased thereon with his head to the south, one should cause the *brahmans*—accompanied by the utterance of *svadhā*—to recite: "Prolong the life-force of life."

Then, when the vital breaths have departed, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), with his hand turned downwards, having thrown a piece of gold into the mouth, having tied a band around the thumb, having adorned [the deceased] with village ornaments, having covered him with an unwashed cloth with its fringes pointing north, having offered the evening oblation and the morning oblation, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice or the New Moon sacrifice, he then melts clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purifies it, takes four portions in the ladle, goes out toward the northeast, and offers it on the Āhavanīya fire while it is provided with fuel-sticks, saying: "To the abode of Death, svāhā!"

Thus it is said. Having caused four Brahmins to carry [the body] toward the village, having placed it at a crossroads and shown its face, or having carried it toward the cremation ground and brought it out to the cremation ground, one should place the deceased there along with the fires and permit the cremation on ground that slopes toward the south and west, which is not broken, not barren, not hollow, or level. [One should recite: "Depart, go away, and creep away from here—those who are ancient and those who are recent."

"May Yama grant him a resting place by means of days, waters, and distinct nights"—with this verse, having wiped the vessel with a branch of *palāśa* or a branch of *udumbara*, having thrown the branch toward the south, having touched water, and having sprinkled [the ground] with water, and having placed a fragment of gold [therein], he says: "Depart, O ancestors who are here; grant us well-being; let there be no shedding of tears; may [the deceased] not return. Having dug three trenches ending toward the south with either a wooden sword (*sphya*) or an axe, and having sprinkled them with water...

Having filled a handful of sesame seeds and rice, he pours them out on the first [brick] with the formula: "To Yama, lord of the ancestors, and to the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration! He does likewise on the second and the third. If he is one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), he cuts a black antelope skin and spreads it down with the hair facing downward and the neck toward the south. At this time, having bathed and filled a water-pot with water and medicinal herbs, he should bathe [the sacrificer] from head to foot with that [water] while reciting the *Daśahotṛ* formula.

Then, having clothed him in a new garment and adorned him, he places him upon the funeral pyre. Then, having cast seven pieces of gold into the seven openings of the vital breaths, or in their absence, drops of clarified butter into the mouth first, he offers rice-grains and sesame seeds, saying: "This is your body; this is your self. From the body I separate the self of yours as Brahman: Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! To that heaven-world, Svāhā!"

One should recite the *Daśahotṛ* formula, beginning with "Consciousness is the ladle" (*cittiḥ sruc*), exactly as before, excluding the *graha* portions, twice in the two nostrils. The word "was" (*āsīt*) is appended to all the *hotṛ* positions except for the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* positions; the dual form "were" (*āstām*) is used for the dual endings, and so forth. One should recite the *Caturhotṛ* formula, "Earth is the *hotṛ*," twice on the corners of the mouth; the *Pañcahotṛ* formula, "Agni is the *hotṛ*," twice on the ears; the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, "Sūrya is that," twice on the vertebrae (*kīkasā*); and the *Saptahotṛ* formula, "The Great Oblation is the *hotṛ*," [twice].

Then he takes the clarified butter (ājya) as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, silently: ghee in the *juhū* ladle; curd and ghee in the *upabhṛt*; curd, honey, and ghee in the *dhruvā*; and milk in the *agnihotrahavaṇī*. Alternatively, one may take only clarified butter in all of them. At this point, he arranges the vessels: having filled those vessels that have pouring-spouts, he sprinkles water over the others so that they are not empty; thus it is known. He places the *juhū* and the wooden sword (*sphya*) in his right hand.

The *upabhṛt* ladle on the left [hand], the *dhruvā* on the chest, the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*) and the two churning sticks (*araṇī*) in the mouth, the *agnihotrahavaṇī* in the nostrils, the two *sruva* spoons—or the *ājya-sruva*—in the ears, and having broken the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel into pieces, one in each [nostril]; the mortar and pestle in the jaws; the pressing stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*) in the teeth; and the potsherds (*kapālāni*) on the head.

On the forehead, the single potsherd; on the belly, the mixing-vessel for the sight; at the navel, the vessel for the clarified butter; on the feet, the grass-bundle for bringing down [the oblation]; on the head, the grass-bundle for placing [the oblation]; on the two sides, the winnowing-basket—cutting each one separately—or on the two nostrils, the two vessels for the *sānnāyya* milk, if he is performing the *sannayana* rite; on the two testicles, the lower and upper grinding stones; on the penis, the *vṛṣārava* stone and the *śamyā* pin; on the two shoulders, the *agnihotra* vessel and the *anvāhārya* vessel; and on the tuft of hair, the *iḍā* vessel and the *veda* grass-bundle.

Alternatively, he pours out the remaining [ashes] between the two thighs. Having covered it with the remainder of the black antelope skin—its neck-part facing south and the hair facing north—the relatives fan it with *sigvāta* fans. There are three *sigvāta* fans: one in the village, one on the road, and one at the funeral pyre. "May those winds blow upon you on the way—meritorious scents, pleasing to the mind, pleasing to the body, favorable to the limbs. May the Maruts carry you, bringing comfort to the skin, comfort to the flesh, and comfort to the bones, to where the worlds of the righteous are. (2)

If he is one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), [the wife] releases the binding of her thumb with the verse, "May the waters burn away our sin" (*apa naḥ śośucadagham*). Then, taking a water-pot, either the wife or the *adhvaryu* priest, having placed it upon his head, goes around three times sprinkling the water while moving counter-clockwise (*apasalaiḥ*). He strikes it slightly with an axe. Then he consecrates the stream of water with the mantra: "May these honey-sweet waters be milked for you in this world."

When [the altar] has been enclosed for the second time, he strikes behind it with the formula: "May these honeyed waters be milked for you in the intermediate world. When it has been enclosed for the third time, he strikes behind it with the formula: "May these honeyed waters be milked for you in the heavenly world. He breaks the clod. [The teachers say]: "If it falls toward the east, he becomes worse off; if it falls toward the west, he becomes more prosperous."

Then he pours the water remaining in the skull-bowl into the vital points of the deceased, with the mantra: "Born in heaven, born in the waters... Having touched moist plants, he rises; he looks at a cow; he looks at Brāhmaṇas; he touches gold. Here he gives a choice gift to the teacher.

Then the Adhvaryu kindles the Āhavanīya fire for him in the south-eastern direction, the Anvāhāryapacana fire in the south-western direction, the Gārhapatya fire in the north-western direction, and the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires to the north. He should cause them to be maintained with the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*), with the *agniryajurbhiḥ* verses, with the wives [of the gods], and with the verse: "The army of Indra..."

With the formulas: "O Vācaspati, with the planets; O Vidhi, O Nāman, Vācaspati; by the power of speech, Soma [is for] Soma, O Vācaspati; with unimpaired speech, O Vācaspati; established in the heart, O Nāman"—and with the *ṛtumukhīya* hymn, and with the mantra "Vāk is the Hotṛ," and "The Brāhmaṇa is the Ekahotṛ," he performs the worship (*upasthāna*). According to some, there is a potsherd (*kapāla*) at the Āhavanīya fire. The Vājasaneyins record that this is performed with the *santapana* fire.

"Go to that destination which the heat of the fire carries away, the destination which the heroes of battle reach when they have cast off their sins, become free from passion, and are freed from sorrow—go to that destination, O fragrant one, to the back of the firmament; Svadhā! Adoration! If he has not maintained the sacred fires, [say]: "Go to that destination which the heroes of battle reach when they abandon the body, the destination which the wise who know liberation and the doers of good deeds who have offered oblations into the *agnihotra* reach—go to that destination, O fragrant one, to the back of the firmament; Svadhā! Adoration!"

Then, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*), having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the mantra, "I sprinkle you together with the *Yajus*," he worships the sun with the *Jyotiṣmatī* verses: "Up from the darkness," "Up that [sun]," and "The bright one. The sons, brothers, and *sapindas* lie down together. Without looking back, they go to the bathing place (*tīrtha*). Or a royal officer, or someone not of their own lineage (*asagotra*), wards them off with a leafy branch of the *parṇa*, *śamī*, or *udumbara* tree, saying, "Do not cross!"

Having said, "We shall not return," they assume the appearance of the deceased: disheveling their hair, scattering dust [on their heads], and wearing either a single garment or no garment at all; facing south, they bathe once, emerge, place their left knee on the ground, wring out their garments, stand up, and taking water in their joined palms, they offer water mixed with sesame seeds toward the deceased, saying, "O So-and-so, this water is for you. Having performed this a second and a third time, they then return to the village without looking back. The youngest goes first, like ants.

At the door of the house, having chewed a nimba leaf and sipped water, and having touched cow dung, gold, water, fire, and mustard seeds with them, and having touched his head and vital breaths, and having stepped upon a stone and entered the house, they do what women say.

In that house where the breaths have departed, one should smear it with cow-dung, set down a calf, scatter sesame seeds and rice mixed with water, and perform a purification rite by saying, "May there be well-being for the houses; may there be auspiciousness in what remains. From this point forward, the woman shall eat only cooked food and observe celibacy for ten nights. Having poured out water once in the evening and once in the morning, she shall pour out water three times on the tenth day. On the tenth day, she shall take a modified meal.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the collection of the bones. When the *agnaukaraṇa* rite has not yet been performed, on the second, third, fourth, fifth, or seventh day, one should take a new jar, go to the cremation ground, and having gathered the bones together with a stake of *pālāśa*, *śamī*, or *udumbara* wood—using either the thumb and ring finger, or all the fingers—one should drench them in milk and pour clarified butter over them, saying: "This is your body; this is your self. From the body, O Brahman, [I restore] your self."

"I pierce Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar for the sake of the heavenly world; Svāhā! Now, if they should not burn [the body], one should take a firebrand and burn it again, saying: "From this you were born; may he be born from you. To Agni Vaiśvānara, for the sake of the heavenly world; Svāhā! Then, taking the bones, they should carry them away to the banks of rivers or to the shores of the ocean.

Alternatively, having dug a pit equal in size to an elephant or equal to a man, and having placed the jar of bones therein, he should smear it again with earth and fill it up; for as long as that [earth] remains, so long is he honored in the heavenly world. 5. Now, therefore, follows the rule for cremation. Then he takes the clarified butter, if [the deceased] was one who maintained the sacred fires. Then the Adhvaryu [acts] for him. Now, therefore, follows the collection of the bones; [there are] five [verses].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter.

Now, if one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) departs while suffering from illness or due to old age, they should prepare a bed for him in the place of the sacrificer at the *agniṣṭha* fire, or behind the *gārhapatya* fire. They bring him food-remnants (*bhakṣa*) as much as he deems sufficient to eat. If he recovers, he returns; but if he indeed passes away, one does not pour milk [into the fires]. Now, the teachers declare that this *agnihotra* sacrifice begins in the evening and concludes in the morning. Regarding this, they cite the following:

If he should die after the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, one should postpone the morning *agnihotra* and offer it [then]. But if he dies after the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, all is well. Now, regarding these *darśa-pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the teachers state that they are completed on the full moon and the new moon days respectively. In this regard, they cite an example: "If he should die after the full moon day has passed, one should postpone [the sacrifice] and perform it on the new moon day. But if he dies after the new moon day has passed, all is well.

Now, if both *parvan* days should be passed over, one should perform the expiation for the omission. Now, if the *agnihotra* of one who is afflicted should be interrupted, and if he has a son or a pupil capable of performing the rite, he should consign the fire into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*), depart from the dwelling, churn out the fire, spread the fires, and offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat. He gives a shallow cup (*śarāva*) as the sacrificial fee. That sacrifice concludes in the established manner.

If he should die while the ritual has commenced in the *divi* [fire], they should conclude this procedure silently; having performed the final rite (*saṃsthāpya*), they should consume water as their food. It is known from tradition: "They consume water as their food. Then, taking him, they carry him out between the altar (*vedi*) and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) facing north, and then they enclose him. They make the door on its southern side. Then, having shaved his hair and beard, removed the body hair, and clipped his nails, [the rite proceeds].

Then, having drawn out his right side, having made it free of feces, having washed it with water, having filled the intestines with clarified butter, he sews them together with *darbha* grass. However, one should not do it in that manner; for it is known [from scripture]: "His offspring will become hungry. Alternatively, having washed it while still containing the feces, having covered it, and having adorned it, they then take him and lead him between the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and set him down behind the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "Here the oblation is prepared."

Then, taking him, they place him within the sacrificial altar (vedī) with his head toward the east, saying, "Here the oblation is placed. Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he goes out toward the northeast; and having placed a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire, while the sacrificer holds onto his right arm, he makes the offering with the verse:
"Pareyuvāṃsam pravato mahīranu bahubhyaḥ panthām anapaspaśānam | Vaivasvataṃ saṃgamanaṃ janānāṃ yamaṃ rājānaṃ haviṣā duvasyata svāhā ||" With this same formula, he also offers on the Gārhapatya fire.

Having silently offered [an oblation] on the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he then takes [the deceased] and leads him between the Vedi and the Utkara. Having laid him down behind the Gārhapatya fire on a black antelope skin upon a stool, with his head toward the south, he fastens a wreath of Nalada grass upon his head and covers him with a new garment with its fringes pointing eastward, saying: "This garment has now first come to thee. Then he removes it, saying: "Depart, O thou who didst wear this here before!"

"Behold the sacrifices and charitable works, and the sacrificial fee as it was given by you in many ways to your kinsmen. His son, or his pupil, or his wife should take charge of that [fee]. He himself should wear it until he grows old, or until the end of his life. Then he prepares three wooden chips. Now, if there are no wooden chips, he cooks three *caru* offerings on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire from black rice grains that have been threshed away within the altar, or he cooks one; he cooks the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture on the *gārhapatya* fire.

Then he prepares these materials: curds mixed with clarified butter, clarified butter, a water-pot, *darbha* grass for strewing, gold, a goat, a sacrificial knife (*śāsa*), a chopping-knife (*iḍasūna*), a cooking pot (*kumbhī*), a vessel for removing the bones (*pracyāvanī*), sand, cords, and three *parṇa*-branches. How indeed should they cremate him? One view is that if he has been a frequent sacrificer (*bahuyājī*), they should cremate him with his previous sacred fires; this is one method. Another view is that they should cremate him with perpetual fires (*ajasra*); this is another method.

"One [method] is that they should burn him with churning-sticks (*nirmanthya*). Or another is that, having kindled three rows of *ulapa* grass so that the fires meet there, one should take a firebrand from that point and burn him with it."

Now follows the ritual for the Anustaraṇī cow. They bring this black, hornless, aged, and dull-witted cow, bound as the lowest of the animals to be sacrificed. It is known from tradition that she is bound on the left side. At this time, the ministers, with disheveled hair, having gathered dust with three fingers, strew it upon their shoulders, saying: "Verily, let there be no sin for him; verily, let there be no sin indeed."

Then his wives, led by the youngest, should go forth with disheveled hair, scattering dust upon their shoulders, saying, "Verily, let there be no sin for him; verily, let there be no sin! At that time, having heated a piece of *palāśa* wood over the *gārhapatya* fire, they proceed, led by a firebrand: first the axe, then the fires, then the vessels, curd, clarified butter, *darbha* grass, and the royal cow. Then, having wrapped him in this couch, or a mattress, or a mat, slaves or aged men should carry him away.

"Then they carry him away by means of the mind," so say some. If he should yoke the two horses, [he recites]: "I yoke these two, thy bearers, for the sake of leading thee to the world of the living, by which thou shalt go to the abode of Yama and also to the world of those who have performed good deeds. Having thus consigned the fires into the kindling woods, they carry them away; or, having consigned them, they carry the fires away either between the two woods or not.

Then they take it up. As it is being taken up, he recites over it: "May Pūṣan, the wise one, the guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, drive you forth from here; may he entrust you to these fathers, and Agni to the gods who are well-disposed. Having gone a third part of this path, they set it down. Then, of those wood-shavings, he smoothes one with a blade of grass. Now, if there are no wood-shavings, he stirs the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, he becomes one [with the rice]; he mixes the third portion of the cooked rice with the stirring-spoon. Having gathered clods of earth and wiped [the vessel] upon them, those who are the youngest first, with disheveled hair, walk around three times counter-clockwise, fanning [the fire] with winnowing-baskets (*sigs*). In this same manner the attendants and in this same manner the women, having bound up their hair, walk around three times again in the opposite direction. Then they take him up. As he is being taken up, he recites the mantra: "May Pūṣan know all these regions; may he lead us by the most secure path."

"May the giver of well-being, the pitiless one, the hero of all, the unassailable, the wise one, go before us. Having gone half this distance, they set it down. Then, of these wood-shavings (*śakala*), he smoothes one with a blade even without a formal ritual recitation (*aśastreṇa*). Now, if there are no shavings, he stirs the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). Having gathered clods of earth and having wiped [the vessel] upon them, those with their hair disheveled, led by the youngest, walk three times around counter-clockwise (*apasalaiḥ*), fanning [it] with winnowing-baskets (*sigs*).

In this manner the ministers and likewise the women, having restrained their hair, circumambulate him three times in the reverse direction. Then they take him up. As he is being taken up, he recites the mantra: "May Viśvāyu protect your life; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path in front. Where the doers of good deeds dwell, where they have gone—there may the god Savitṛ place you. Having traveled the entire distance of this road, they set him down. Then, from among these wood-shavings, he smoothes one with a knife without using a formal ritual formula.

Now, if there are no wood-shavings, he stirs the *caru* with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). Or, if there is only one [shaving], he stirs the remainder of the *caru* with the stirring-spoon. Having gathered clods of earth and having wiped [the vessel] upon them, the relatives, led by the youngest, with disheveled hair, walk three times around [the site] counter-clockwise, fanning it with *sigs* (winnowing-fans). In the same manner, the attendants and likewise the women, having bound up their hair, walk three times again in the opposite direction as they came.
Then he breaks this pot of cooked rice so that it is well-shattered, so that no water may remain in its shards; and they do whatever women say regarding this.

Then he chooses a site for it: one that has water to the west, is not saline, is uninjured, is not difficult to carry away, is not barren, is not liable to collapse, is free from ant-hills, where wild plants are abundant, and where milky trees and medicinal herbs are intertwined; where waters flow slowly from the south-west, turning to the right and reaching a great river, and then flowing eastward; or, according to some, a place sloping toward the south-west; or even a level and fertile ground.

Therefore, they pull up the plants: the *kālā*, the *pṛśni*, the *paṇī*, the *tilvakā*, the *apāghā*, the *apāmārga*, the *śuṇṭhī*, the *bahuputrī*, the *visraṃsinīkā*, the *rājakṣapaṇī*, and whatever other milky plants there may be. Then, having dug them up and sprinkled [the site] with water, and having purchased [the wood] with gold, he sweeps it away with a *parṇa* branch, saying: "Go away, depart, and creep away from here! They construct a wooden pile facing south-east; for it is known that "this is the eastern direction of the ancestors."

Having prepared the sacrificial ground (vihāra) behind the funeral pyre, facing south-east, and having strewn darbha grass around the fire, the deceased, and the pyre; and having spread darbha grass to the south of the vihāra for the southern fires, he places the vessels one by one upon them with their openings turned downwards.

Having prepared the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī) with a single strainer, and having sprinkled the vessels, he pours out the clarified butter (ājya) for the deceased and the pyre, heats it over the fire, carries it around, takes it down, purifies it, and silently cleans the vessels with darbha blades. Then, silently taking the portions of clarified butter according to the New and Full Moon sacrifices...

Then he dedicates the royal cow with the verse, "O Lord of the world... As she is lying down, they strike their left knees together, saying: "O thou who art full of life, we wipe away the sins of man, so that here no other may come before us until old age. They kill her right there with a weapon. Then he consecrates her vital breaths as they are being released with the formula: "O thou who art full of life, I have not let thy breath go loose."

"With your body [you have entered] the earth; come, O Svadhā, unto the ancestors. Bring us here offspring. Having risen, they touch the dust [of the ground], saying: "Do not grieve for me, O beloved one! Though you, a goddess, have gone to the world of the fathers, you who are all-encompassing, spreading through the sky—turn back toward both our worlds with your moisture."

Then he instructs him: "Cutting pieces of flesh from limb after limb, boneless, without letting [the meat] drip or fall away, cooking it with a single firebrand, set aside the omentum as you recognize it; set aside the heart as you recognize it, the tongue as you recognize it, the skin together with the hair of the head and feet as you recognize it, the two kidneys as you recognize them, and the fat as you recognize it. Then he causes his wife to lie down beside him, saying: "This woman, choosing the world of her husband, lies down beside you, O mortal who has passed away."

"Protecting the universe according to the ancient law, bestow upon her offspring and wealth here. Grasping her by the left hand, he who is intent on his duty makes her rise with the verse: "Arise, O woman, toward the world of the living; you lie beside this one whose life has departed. Come! You have attained this wifehood of your husband, the one who took your hand and desires you. Then he wipes his hands with gold for him [the deceased] with the verse: "Taking gold from the hand for the sake of the dead man’s prosperity, sacred knowledge, splendor, and strength."

"Right here you, and here we, being well-disposed, may conquer all rivals and adversaries"—with these words, taking the bow from the hand of the deceased Brāhmaṇa, for his glory, for his kṣatra-power, for his vigor, and for his strength. "Right here you, and here we, being well-disposed, may conquer all rivals and adversaries"—with these words, taking the jewel from the hand of the deceased Rājanya, for his glory, for the prosperity of the people, and for his strength. "Right here you, and here we, being well-disposed, may conquer all rivals and adversaries"—thus for the Vaiśya.

And whatever women say here, that they do. Then he places him upon the funeral pyre together with this couch. Having pulled out the cords, they cast away the couch. He lies supine upon the black antelope skin and the cords. Into his vital breaths he throws fragments of gold. With two separate four-spoonfuls, he offers oblations into the two eyes; it is known from scripture that he offers with the two half-verses beginning, "The bright face of the gods has risen."

How indeed should one employ his sacrificial vessels? Having filled them with curds mixed with clarified butter, he places the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle in the mouth, the two *sruva* spoons in the nostrils, two pieces of gold or two *ājya-sruva* spoons in the eyes, the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel in the ears, having broken it into single pieces; the mortar and pestle in the jaws; the skull-bones on the head, and the single skull-bone on the forehead; and finally, he places the *praṇītā-praṇayana* cup upon the head [with the mantra]: "O Agni, do not shake this cup; it is dear to the gods and to those who partake of Soma."

"May this cup, the drinking-vessel of the gods, in which the immortal gods may rejoice. [With these words, he places] the *juhū* in his right hand, the *upabhṛt* in his left, and the *dhruvā* on his chest; the *upaveṣa* and the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) on his right shoulder; the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) on his left; the flour-scattering ladle (*piṣṭodvapanī*) on his back; the wooden sword (*sphya*) on his belly; the wooden trough (*dārupātrī*) on his side; the two cups (*camasa*) for the *sānnāyya* offering and the *iḍopavahana* tray between his thighs; the two *sānnāyya* jars on his calves; the *agnihotra* pot and the *anvāhārya* cooking-pot on his feet; and the mortar and pestle on his thighs.

Having cut the two testicles into the *dṛṣad* and *upala*, the penis into the *vṛṣārava* and the *śamyā*, and the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) into the two sides, he places one *kūrca* to be set down near the head. There is another *kūrca* to be brought down for the feet. Then they should throw the remaining parts between the thighs. They should cast the earthen vessels into the water; for it is known from scripture: "They cast the earthen vessels into the water. They should place them right there. They should give the iron and copper vessels to the Brāhmaṇas.

Of those [vessels], he should fill whichever are capable of being filled with curds mixed with clarified butter; he should touch the others. "They must not be empty," so it is known. Right here they place upon them the *upavājina* (the horse's fodder), the *khārī*, and the *nalva*. Then, having taken out a portion of its curdled milk (*āmikṣā*), he should place it in his two hands, saying: "For Mitra and Varuṇa, thee!
