Then, having scraped out its two kidneys (*matasna*), he should place them in his two hands, saying: "For Śyāma and Śabala, thee!"

He covers the right [limb] with the right [limb], the left with the left, the heart with the heart, and the tongue in the mouth; having covered the other limbs with their corresponding limbs, he covers its face with the omentum (*vapā*). It is known from tradition: "He veils the two offering-spoons (*sruc*) with the fat (*medas*). Then he covers it with a skin, complete with head, tail, and feet, with the hair on the outside, [reciting]: "Clothe yourself in the armor of Agni with the cows; cover yourself with fat and marrow. Let not the bold one, exulting in his heat, seize you while intending to consume you and cause you to tremble. (7)

Now, if they do not intend to perform the ritual immolation of the *anustaraṇī* cow, he should either release her or give her away to the Brahmins; for it is known from scripture that by giving her away, they attain spiritual welfare in this very world. Now, if he intends to release her, he leads her around three times counter-clockwise with the three verses beginning, "We beheld a young woman approaching. Having led her around three times, he consecrates her as she stands to the north with the verse, "Those who are living and those who are dead."

Then, having plucked out the hairs from her ears, he should place them on her two hands with the mantra: "With the black and the speckled, thee. He places the right hair on her right hand and the left hair on her left hand. Then he releases her with the mantra: "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality—I have proclaimed this to the discerning person: do not slay Aditi, who is sinless and free from guilt. Let her drink water; let her eat grass. Om! Release her!"

Then he causes him to fast, [surrounded] by the Āhavanīya fire in the east, the Anvāhāryapacana fire in the south, the Gārhapatya fire in the west, and the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires in the north. In this regard, there are also prognostications: if the Āhavanīya should first flare up toward him, one should know that he has conquered the world of the gods; if the Anvāhāryapacana, the world of the ancestors; if the Gārhapatya, the heavenly world; and if the Sabhya and Āvasathya, the world of the Seven Sages.

Now, if the entire fire should blaze up together, one should know that he has conquered the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). And they perform here what women say. Now, if one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) has passed away, then follows the ritual for the funeral cow (*anustaraṇī*). Then they take him up; as he is being taken up, he recites the consecratory formula (*anumantrayate*). Then he chooses a place for him. Then he dedicates the royal cow (*rājagavī*) to him. How indeed should one employ his sacrificial vessels? And if there is a funeral cow, [there are] eight.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the *Āgniveśya-gṛhyasūtra*.

Now begins the sixth chapter. Then he sets it on fire. As it is being set on fire, he recites over it: "O Agni, do not burn him up; do not consume him; do not scorch his skin or his body. When you have cooked him, O Jātavedas, then send him forth to the Fathers. When it is blazing, he recites over it: "When you have cooked him, O Jātavedas, then deliver him to the Fathers. When he goes to this path of the departed, then let him become a follower of the will of the gods."

Here he recites the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula: "May your eye go to the sun, your breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to the cosmic law (dharman); or go to the waters, if that is beneficial for you; find firm support in the plants with your bodies. At this point, while the altar is being piled, he binds this goat with a cord of balbaja grass: "The goat is your portion; burn him with heat; let your flame burn him, let your radiance burn him. O Jātavedas, with those forms of yours which are auspicious, carry him to the worlds of the righteous."

If it runs away during the day, he does not bring it back; some, however, do so before the fast-day. They walk around it three times from left to right with a water-pitcher, reciting verses addressed to Varuṇa. Then, having covered it, he offers nine spoonfuls of oblations, dipping with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "To those who are the guardians of this path, svāhā! Then he offers another oblation: "This one indeed [is you]; from us, you are that; this one indeed is that; you are his source."

"Vaiśvānara, the son, having made the worlds for his father, O Jātavedas, carry him where the worlds of the doers of good deeds are; Svāhā! At this very point, he throws the *sruva* ladle after [the oblation]. Having covered these portions with the chest of the funeral pyre, he offers them by striking with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, saying, "To Agni, the possessor of wealth, Svāhā! At this very point, he throws the ladle after [the oblation] behind the pyre. Then he worships him with the nine-verse hymn addressed to Yama, beginning with, "Agni shines with great radiance."

Seated, he recites [the verses] from west to east. Behind the fire-pit, they make three sacrificial furrows toward the south. Then, having flooded them with water and strewn them with sand, they step across; each younger one steps first. With the verse: "O you who possess stones, full of wealth, hold fast! Arise, O friends, and cross over! Here we leave behind those who were unkind; may we overcome auspicious strengths."

Having struck the leafy branches into the trenches with their hindquarters and bound them with a weak cord, they crawl out, [reciting]: "That which is the filter of the god Savitṛ, spread with a thousand streams across the mid-air—by that which he purified Indra from affliction, by that I purify myself, whole in body. The last one throws away [the branches]: "Those branches which creep away from the kingdom, having touched the king and desiring him..."

"May all those elements be purified by the wind; unite us with offspring, wealth, and splendor. They go toward where the water is without looking back. Together with their clothes and carrying earth, they wade through the water facing south, saying, "May Dhātṛ purify us; may Savitṛ purify us. Having thrice poured out water while pronouncing the name [of each person], they emerge, sip water, and worship the sun with the verse, "Up from the darkness... Then they go to the house. Whatever the women there say, that they do.

At this time, those ministers who are present shall have their hair and beards shaved with disheveled hair; for others, there is an option: they may either have them shaved or refrain from doing so. However, according to the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of Bodhāyana, it is the opinion that one who has heard the Vedas (*śrutavat*) must certainly have them shaved even when not present. Some say that those who have returned home (*samāvṛtta*) should not have them shaved, except during a sacrificial session (*vihāra*).

Upon the death of a mother, father, or teacher, one shall observe a three-night period of eating food free from pungent salt, sleeping on the ground, and practicing celibacy; this may last for three days, six days, twelve days, a year, or until the Veda has been mastered; for the highest gurus, the impurity lasts for twelve days, while for others it lasts three nights; the widow remains impure for as long as she lives. Now, if one who maintains the sacred fires should die elsewhere, they shall dwell with the fires being kindled and summoned until his body is united with the fires.

Then, having caused the milk of the *abhivānyā* cow to be milked and having poured it over [the fire] at the *gārhapatya*, he should pour it over [the fire] at the *āhavanīya*. "They bring the fuel from below, for they bring it to the gods from above," so it is known. Then, taking this [milk], having carried it out between the *vedi* and the *utkara* toward the north, they should perform the *upoṣaṇa* in the prescribed manner.

Now, if one who has maintained the sacred fires should die elsewhere, [his relatives] should draw three fire-houses at the water's edge, enter them once, close their eyes, and, restraining themselves, gaze toward the sun from the southern corners of their shoulders; they should also perform the circumambulation. This same procedure applies three times for one who has died in a foreign land. Now, if he has been cremated, they should collect his bones, fashion a human figure out of them upon a black antelope skin within the sacrificial altar, pile the vessels upon them, cover them with young *kuśa* grass, and observe the fast according to the established rule.

Now, if one should not find bones, one should fashion a human figure out of three hundred and sixty leaf-stalks (*parṇatsaru*) upon a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). Having piled the vessels upon these and covered them with young *kuśa* grass, they should observe the fast in the prescribed manner. "They burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires with the fires and the sacrificial vessels," so it is known. For it is said that the "human oblation" (*puruṣāhuti*) is his most beloved; thus they declare this to be the celebrated method of cremation. Moreover, they also cite: "The fires are indeed the heirs to the body."
That too is known from the *Daśataya*: "A hundred autumns, O gods, are near us, wherein you have ordained the aging of our bodies; wherein sons become fathers—do not harm our life-span in its course.

Now, therefore, follows the reconstruction of the funeral mound (*saṃcayana*). When one dawn has passed, or three, or five, or seven, or nine, or eleven—even on non-even days, or after half-months, months, seasons, or years—they may perform the reconstruction once it has been completed.

He prepares a hundred [grains], milk, clarified butter, a water-pot, *darbha* grass for strewing, blue and red threads, a *bṛhatī* fruit, a stone, an *apāmārga* plant, a cane branch, sand, two cords, and three *parṇa* branches. Having extracted embers from that very funeral fire, he offers three *avasarjanīya* oblations with the verses: "Release [him] again, O Agni, go together with the fathers; what the black bird has pecked at thee... and so forth.

When this has been done, having poured in milk and a water-pot and sprinkled [the site] with a cane branch, they prepare it without boiling the bodies, with the six verses beginning, "The fire which we have churned for you. They may repeat either the first or the last verse twice.

Then, having sprinkled this cremation ground with water from water-jars, the principal wife among his wives, having tied a *bṛhatī* fruit to her left hand with blue and red threads, having stepped upon a stone, and having wiped [the bones] once with *apāmārga* grass without looking at them, takes the bones starting from the feet or from the head, saying: "Arise, O body, gather yourself together! Do not abandon this limb, do not abandon this frame! Go where you choose on the earth; there may the god Savitṛ place you."

"This is one for you" is the second; "and another one beyond" is the third; "enter with the third light" is the fourth; "be beautiful for the body's resting place" is the fifth; "dear to the gods in the highest assembly-hall" is the sixth. Then, having piled it up well-piled, he forms it into a lump. He does this so that the dove might not sit in its shadow.

Then he encloses it with an unlimited number of small stones mixed together; he should not, however, enclose it in such a way that a pigeon might perch in its shadow. Then, having washed these bones with water and placed them either in a jar or a vessel, he rises up, saying: "Rise up, go forth, run forward, and make a dwelling for yourself in the highest heaven! In harmony with Yama and Yamī, ascend this highest firmament."

Having placed the water-jar for the entry, then follows the sowing for the *haviryajña*. For one whom he desires, "May he have an infinite world," he places [the seed] upon this [spot] that has been dug out, strewn with sand, and enclosed by a screen, saying: "I set thee on the imperishability of the earth, in the sap of the waters and the plants, in the heavenly world; on the back of the firmament, on the summit of the radiant sun, I set thee, O so-and-so! It is known from scripture: "He indeed becomes one who possesses an infinite world. Behind the water-jar, they make three sacrificial furrows toward the south.

This has been explained previously. Having driven two *parṇa* branches behind the trenches and bound them with a cord made of *abala* grass, they creep out. This has been explained previously. They go to where there is water without looking back. Together with their clothes and carrying earth, they wade through the water facing south, saying, "May Dhātṛ purify us; may Savitṛ purify us. Having thrice splashed water while pronouncing their own names, having emerged and sipped water, he then worships the sun with the verse, "Up from the darkness... Then they go to the house. Whatever women there direct, that they do. 3.

Now, if they are about to cremate [the body], they should set aside beforehand the *juhū* ladle, the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), the black antelope skin, the grinding stones and muller, and the wooden pin (*śamyā*). If these have not been brought forth, one should take the two kindling woods from any *aśvattha* tree, churn out the fire, establish it, and strew grass around it. Having placed the black antelope skin and the wooden pin upon it, and having joined the grinding stones and muller, one grinds the bones with ointment, mixes them with old clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), and offers a libation by pouring it from the *juhū* ladle with the verse: "From him you were born; may he..."

"May it arise from you! To Agni Vaiśvānara, to the heavenly world, svāhā! At this very point, he throws into the fire the *juhū* ladle, the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*), the black antelope skin, the lower and upper grinding stones, and the wooden pin (*śamyā*). Here too, there are prognostications: if the flame should blaze upward, one should know that he has conquered the world of the gods; if it rises for a moment and then whirls about, one should know that he has conquered the intermediate space; and if it flickers along this [earth], one should know that he has conquered right here.

And whatever women say in this matter, they do that. One should not care to prepare a funeral pyre for him beyond this point. One should either scatter the remains of his cremation or cover them with water-rites. The sun shines directly upon him, and the wind blows directly upon him; he is not severed from the touch of the sun, nor from the wind, nor from the waters.

Whomever they might thus establish, and whoever knows him thus—in that very way do the Ahīna sacrifices and the Hāyana sacrifices establish the Aśvattha tree. For him who acts in this manner, these Ahīna and Hāyana sacrifices become ever more excellent and ever more prosperous; his offspring indeed becomes better and more prosperous. Whomever they might thus establish, and whoever knows him thus—it was Kauṣītaki who discovered this.

For him, these followers of the Kauṣītaki school attain ever greater prosperity; for him, as the dawn breaks, there arises offspring that is ever more excellent and more prosperous—provided they place him thus, and provided they know him thus, and provided they know him thus.

Then he kindles him; while he is being kindled, he recites the consecratory formula at this time. At this time his attendants [perform their duties]. Now follows the piling up of the bones (saṃcayana). And furthermore, regarding those who intend to cremate again, there are four [verses].
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Now, one who is about to enter his house prepares the following: a ladle made of *vāraṇa* wood and a dipping-spoon (*sruva*), enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) of *vāraṇa* wood, sacrificial grass (*barhis*) made of *kuśa*, fuel (*idhma*) made of *parṇa* wood, a red ox-hide, fresh clarified butter, collyrium, a stone, a bull, a branch of the *śamī* tree, young *kuśa* shoots, a clump of *darbha* grass, a goat, and barley.

Then, between the village and the cemetery, having kindled a fire on a mound, having spread out sacrificial grass made of *kṛśa* grass, having laid down enclosing sticks of *vāraṇa* wood, and having anointed a fuel-stick made of *parṇa* wood and placed it upon the fire with the utterance "Svāhā," he then spreads out a red bull-hide behind the fire with its neck to the east and the hair upwards. As many of his kinsmen as there are, they mount it, saying: "Mounting long life while praising old age, striving one after another, remain [here]."

"May Tvaṣṭṛ, the well-born, possessor of beautiful jewels, grant long life for living. Then they arrange them in successive order, just as the days follow one another in succession, just as the seasons proceed according to the seasons when they are duly arranged. "Just as the later does not abandon the former, even so, O Dhātṛ, arrange their lifespans. Then, having taken four portions with a ladle made of *vāraṇa* wood into a *sruk* made of *vāraṇa* wood, he offers the oblation: "For no mortal has done anything cruel to your body, O Agni."

"The monkey devours your people, like an old bull [devouring] its own offspring. O Agni, burn away our sin; burn away our sin so that we may obtain wealth. Burn away our sin for Death—Svāhā! Then, dipping the ladle made of *vāraṇa* wood, he offers twelve oblations with the ladle, saying, "Burn away our sin. Then, having risen, they take hold of the ox, saying: "We take hold of the ox for well-being; may you be for us a carrier across, like Indra for the gods."

"These living beings go forward; O you who turn back from death, may our invocation of the gods be auspicious today. Going forward for the sake of truth and laughter, extending our life further and longer, effacing the footprint of death as we go, extending our life further and longer—swelling with progeny and wealth, may you become pure, purified, and worthy of sacrifice. (1)

Then, between the fire and the village, he places a stone with the verse: "I set up this boundary for the living; let no other go beyond this limit. May they live a hundred long autumns; we ward off death with this mountain. Then these wives touch themselves with fresh clarified butter, [saying]: "May these women, not widows and having good husbands, touch themselves with collyrium and clarified butter."

"With young *kuśa* shoots and with *añjana* from Mount Trikakud—he who applies the *añjana* from Mount Trikakud that was produced upon the Himavat; with that root of immortality, we destroy our enemies"—with these words, having gathered these young *kuśa* shoots, he places them upon a clump of *darbha* grass: "As you, O herb, have burst forth from the earth, so may these [people] burst forth with renown, glory, and Vedic splendor."

Having returned home, they ascend the stool with the verse: "Free from tears, free from disease, most gracious, let the women first ascend to the womb. On this day, they cook a goat and barley-rice; he eats the goat with the formula, "The goat has driven away our hatreds," and he eats of the barley-rice with the formula, "Barley art thou; drive away from us sin and hatred. Then they perform the *śrāddha* for him.

One should give [the gift] on one day after dawn, or on three, five, seven, nine, or eleven days, or on even-numbered days, or on half-months. Or, according to one's desire, one may give it every day for eleven months; one must not let it extend into the twelfth month. Or, one may give it on this very day every year. This is the rule established for this. In the same manner, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, or for a woman, the rites involving the piling of vessels and bricks and excluding the shaving of the hair may be performed for a father, a mother, or a teacher.
Or else, it concludes elsewhere with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee. The Pitṛmedha concludes; the Pitṛmedha concludes. 2.

Regarding this matter—that for one who has established the sacred fires and is about to die, one should postpone the morning *agnihotra* and perform it later, and postpone the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) and perform it later—it is said that he should carry out these two rites as if they were intended for one who is still living. If he should pass away before the morning *agnihotra* has been offered and before the new moon has risen, then at that very moment his morning *agnihotra* should be offered silently, in whatever manner and with whatever materials are available; and at that very moment the new-moon sacrifice should be performed silently, in whatever manner and with whatever materials are available.

If, however, it should remain unspoiled, then his morning *agnihotra* must again be offered at the proper time before it has gone bad; and on that new-moon day, he must again perform the sacrifice at the proper time before it has gone bad. As for the statement, "he pours the milk together for the sake of the *āmikṣā*," what is meant is that he should leave some milk remaining. And as for the statement, "on the throne-seat," this is what is meant.

As for this: it is known that one should prepare the forms of human bodies out of black antelope skins within the altar-ground (*antarvedi*), pile the vessels upon them, cover them with young *kuśa* grass, and then observe the fast in the established manner. From the piling of the vessels onwards, the procedure is established; only this much is different here. There is no immolation of a cow at this time; rather, one should perform the covering with young *kuśa* grass, dried *moma* grass, and clarified butter. With the verse, "Clothe yourself in the protection of Agni with cows," one should likewise [cover] those with handles made of *parṇa* wood.

Or rather, according to the *iṣṭikalpa* (the ritual procedure for an offering): "Or indeed, everything may be performed silently, except for the immolation of the cow. Now, it is said: "Prajāpati, having created the creatures, lay down exhausted. The gods, having gathered together the essence and the splendor of the Brāhmaṇa, healed him with that. One should speak thus regarding the *Caturhotṛ* formula.

For him, there is the oblation with the *hotṛ*s accompanied by the planets; the supporting with the hymn of the Sustainer (*bhartṛ-sūkta*); the reclining with the wives; the cleansing with the acceptance of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā-pratigraha*); the scattering of gold chips with the *hṛdaya* hymns and with the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*); the arrangement of the vessels; the fasting with the *vyotiṣmatī* verses; the worship with the two *nārāyaṇa* hymns and the formula "The Brāhmaṇa is the single *hotṛ*"; the clarified butter oblations with "To Prayāsa, svāhā!"; the flesh-oblation with "The mind with the continuity"; the recitation of praise with the *mṛtyu-sūkta*; the immersion with the *saumyā* verse; and the plunging with the *īyuṣṭi* verse.

"The worship of the Sun with the *saurya* [offering]—these they call the Supreme Brahman. One should not employ these for one who is common, nor for a non-teacher, nor for one who is not a *śrotriya*, nor for one who is not a guru. This is the sowing of the sacrificial remains (*havir-yajñiya*) and the re-burning of the path; on whichever day one should pile the funeral mound, on that very day one should perform this. It ends with the jar for one who has not maintained the sacred fires and for a woman. It ends with the sowing for a performer of the *havis*-sacrifices; it ends with the re-burning for a performer of the *soma*-sacrifices; and it ends with the piling of the altar (*cityanta*) for one who has piled the fire-altar."

If it is the other [type of funeral], or if the water has flowed downwards, one should perform purification after observing impurity for ten nights. Now, if the *citis* (funeral mounds) are being piled, there is impurity. Having performed the rites prior to the trenches (*karṣū*) of the *citis*, on the following day one proceeds with the sweeping alone. From this point onward, the procedure is established.

Now, for these sapinda relatives, as well as for the mother’s blood-relations up to the seventh generation on the paternal side, and for the teacher and the pupil—along with their wives and children—the period of impurity for the sapindas is ten nights. For others, it is three nights. Some say that in the case of a child or one who has died in a foreign land, there is immediate purification. Likewise, this same rule applies to the recollection of women, sacrificial priests, and pupils. No cremation is prescribed for those who die before the tonsure ceremony.

For those who perform the *āpaśu* sacrifice, there is the immolation of a cow; for those who do not maintain the sacred fires, there is no *āmikṣā*; for those who have piled the fire-altar, there is no further piling. For women, there is no shaving of the hair, no piling of the altar, no bricks, and no cremation. The vessels of women are made of wood. In the *pitṛmedha* of the Bahvṛcas, one should exclude these mantras concerning women.

Arise, O woman, toward the world of husbands; go toward the world of the living, taking the golden [ornament] from the hand of the dead, taking the bow from the hand of the dead, taking the jewel from the hand of the dead. Do not burn him, O Agni; do not consume him with heat, when you shall make the dead one, O Jātavedas. The goat is his portion; consume that with your heat. Truly, this [body] is yours, and this [soul] is yours. This is one part for you, and the other is beyond. Those two dogs of yours, and that black bird which has pecked at you—arise, go forth, run to your home.

"Perform [the rite]; you are born from him. Go away, depart, and crawl away from here; rise up, O Earth, do not press down. A man whose wife has died, intending to perform the *kratu* sacrifices, should take a wife and establish the sacred fires (*agnīn ādadhyāt*). For it is known: "Therefore, one man may take two wives. The *Pitṛmedha* for a woman whose husband has died is performed with her *aupāsana* fire. Indeed, because she is no longer a widow, a re-establishment of the fires (*punar-agnyādheya*) does not apply to her. And it is known: "Therefore, one woman does not obtain two husbands."

The rule that "they burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) with the fires and the sacrificial vessels" is stated without qualification; thus, it refers specifically to a husband and wife who both maintain the sacred fires. Of those two, if the one who dies first, his *pitṛmedha* (funeral rite) is performed with the three sacred fires and the sacrificial vessels; if the one who dies later, it is performed with the *aupāsana* fire. If they die together, there is a single *pitṛmedha* for both. Furthermore, the *aupāsana* fire is used for the purpose of producing the embers (*ulmuka*). For one who does not maintain the sacred fires and for a woman, [the rite is performed] with the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*). Some authorities prescribe the use of the *uttapanīya* fire.

According to some, one should burn a woman or a young girl with the fire produced by churning. When a wife has been cremated along with the fires of a man whose wife has died, what is the ritual procedure regarding the *aupāsana* fire? If he intends to perform a sacrifice (*kratu*), he should maintain this fire as the *brāhmodanika*. If he intends to retire to the forest, the *aupāsana* alone should be maintained. But if he renounces the world (*saṃnyaset*), he should not attend to it. One who is impure shall not undertake optional austerities, nor shall he sacrifice, nor study the Veda; however, he may give gifts other than those for the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

One should give [the fee] at will to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). As for this statement, "When about to go to his house, he prepares [the materials]," it is said with the meaning that he is about to undertake his own duties as a householder. How indeed should the *pitṛmedha* be performed—with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*) or with it over the left (*yajñopavītin*)? One should say: "With the sacred thread over the right shoulder. For this is the sacrifice (*medha*) of the ancestors (*pitṛ*), while other sacrifices belong to the gods. They should carry [the body] with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, and they should place it upon the funeral pyre;

they should place it upon the funeral pyre. Now, when about to go to his house, he prepares [the materials]. Then, between the fire and the village—as in the case of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
Now, regarding these sapindas by water, there are four [categories];
thus ends the seventh chapter in the third book of the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the eighth chapter.

"One day they should shake it off; three days they should shake it off; five, seven, nine, eleven, half-months, odd nights, half-months, months, seasons, or having completed a year, they should shake it off."

He prepares curds mixed with whey (*vājina*), a hundred-holed jar (*kumbhī*), three *palāśa* leaves for the sacrificial ladles, a red ox-hide for the purpose of beating [the grain], a rope for winding around [the post] twisted to the left, six hundred unbaked bricks, and an unlimited number of *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; two kinds of parched grains—some mixed with sesame and some mixed with *ati-lā* seeds; the milk of a cow that has recently calved; sacrificial grass with its roots; a reed-mat; a garment already worn; four clods of earth from a field that has been ploughed, and five more.

Five *caru* offerings—one with ghee, one with milk, one with curds, and one with honey; four bundles: a bundle of *arjuna*, a bundle of *dūrvā*, a bundle of *kāśa*, and a bundle of *kuśa*; four enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of various trees—of *parṇa*, *vāraṇa*, *vetasa*, and *śamī* wood; two branches of the *vāraṇa* tree; a *kṣetravitṛṇṇī* separating-stick; a *vidhṛti* separating-stick; barley-meal, all-herbs, sand, a cord, and three *palāśa* branches.

Now, if between the village and the cremation ground there is a house, a shed, or a hut that has been built, he should kindle a fire there. To the west of the fire, having fixed three palāśa stakes, and having placed the jar of bones between them, he raises a sieve over it and fills it with curds mixed with whey, reciting the two verses: "In Vaiśvānara I offer this oblation; this ocean, the fountain of a hundred streams. He then consecrates it with the verse: "The drop has fallen."

Then, to the east of this [fire], they walk around it three times from right to left, while beating it with the hide of a red bull, saying, "O skin! O skin! They perform this three times during the night and three times during the day. In the same manner do the attendants, and in the same manner the women; following them, the female dancers should dance along. And whoever is struck down, they settle him together in a pool or a small pond that is suitable for the noble.

They set out in such a way that it would be possible for them to reach the place of their rest before the day on which they might see the moon either in the east or in the west. Having risen at the dead of night and knowing the location of the cemetery, they proceed. Then these four Brahmins, taking spades, go to the north and gather clods of earth or bricks. Then he sprinkles this cremation ground, which has already been sprinkled with its own water-jars, with the formula: "Go away, depart, and creep away from here!"

"He should approach it so as not to crush the living thing; for he would be crushing the vital breaths of one who is alive. Having pressed it with a leafy branch, they go around it with a rope twisted to the left, saying, "Do not moisten this measure."

Its measurement is known to be such that it is neck-high in front and navel-high behind; or knee-high in front and ankle-high behind; or ankle-high in front and level with the ground behind; or one man’s length (puruṣa) in total. Along the two previously described lines, he draws a cord-line. Having removed the cord, they have trenches dug. They raise the earth on the south side of it, making it higher on the west.

Then, with two verses, he takes the fire into himself: "I take Agni first into myself; that Agni who is ours... He mutters the *svayaṃciti* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes... Having touched a white horse, he places this [brick] within the pebbles with the formula: "May Prajāpati settle thee; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit thou firm."

Now, prior to this, a pair of ploughs made of Udumbara wood has been prepared, yoked to either seven oxen or thirteen oxen. With the two verses, "May the draft-oxen be auspicious, may the men be auspicious; may the plough furrow auspiciously; may the thongs be bound auspiciously; may they raise the plough-pole auspiciously; O Śunāsīra, bestow auspiciousness upon us; O Śunāsīra, [accept] this speech," he looks toward the furrow: "O Sītā, we revere you; be favorable to us, O fortunate one."

"May you be fortunate for us; may you be fruitful for us. Then he places the jar of bones in the furrow with the mantra: "Savitṛ has placed these bodies in the lap of Mother Earth; O Aditi, be auspicious through them. Then he unyokes the oxen with the mantra: "Be unyoked, O inviolable ones, paths of the gods! We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; we have reached the light, we have gone to heaven. From this point on, these men become the *adhvaryus* if the Pitṛmedha sacrifice includes sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

If, however, it is a Sattriya fire, he spreads it out according to the oxen: "Where there is an ox, there is a pair of ploughs. Then he causes it to be fanned with the verse: "The winds blow forth, the lightnings fly; the plants rise up, the heaven swells. Nourishment is born for every living being when Parjanya protects the earth with his seed. He sows all the plants like Agni, just as the five sons of Manu sowed the funeral mound for Yama.

"In this way I weave the dwelling, so that there may be many [people] in the world of the living"—with these words he scatters sand. Then he scatters it with six verses according to their meters, beginning with: "O Agni, yours is glory and vigor. Then he lays down the upward-facing bricks (*ūrdhvacit*) with the formula: "You are piled, you are piled around; as upward-facing ones, take your place! O Fathers, you are the deities. May Prajāpati settle you! By that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm! Then he spreads [the sand] over it: for a Brāhmaṇa, with the *gāyatrī* verse, "Swell up... (*ā pyāyasva*).

With the *triṣṭubh* verse, "saṃ te payām̐si," he arranges [the earth] for a *rājanya* according to its natural state and according to the gravel. Then, with two verses—"mayi gṛhṇāmy agre agnim" and "yo no agniḥ"—he takes the fire into himself. He mutters the *svayaṃciti* formula: "yāste agne samidho yāni dhāma. Having touched the white horse, he mutters the two verses for the charging: "apām idam nyayanam" and "namaste."

Then, on the field-ploughing [line], he places four clods of earth: "I push up the earth from around you; placing this world upon you, may I not be harmed. May the Fathers support this pillar; thereon Yama shall establish his seat"—with these words he places one in the east. "Approach this mother, the earth, the wide-extending, the very gracious; may she, young and soft as wool, full of skill, protect you in the lap of Nirṛti"—with these words he places one in the north.

"Rise up, O Earth; do not press down. Be easy of access to him and easy of passage. As a mother her son, so do thou, O Earth, embrace him"—thus [he says] from behind. "Thou standest, O Earth, rising up; let a thousand pillars support thee. May these houses, dripping with honey, be his refuge here for all time"—thus [he says] from the south. Having performed the *tayā devatam* formula, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula.

Then he strews it with parched grains mixed with sesame seeds, [reciting]: "May the parched grains be dark-brown, reddish-brown, and white, serving as milch-cows; may they, with sesame as their calves, yield nourishment for him, and may they be unceasing day by day. Then he places to the south a half-vessel of milk from a cow that suckles another's calf, [reciting]: "This *svadhā* is placed for you in your dwelling, O Yama, in your house; it is your imperishable portion, O so-and-so," [and here] he utters the name of the sacrificer. Having performed the *tad-devatam* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula.

To the south, he lays down the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) together with its roots, [reciting]: "This sacrificial grass we offer for the ancestors; while living, let us bring more excellent [grass] for the gods. Do thou ascend it; become fit for sacrifice. In harmony with Yama, through Yamī, do thou [ascend]. Having performed the *tayā devatam* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula. Then he lays down the reed-stalk (*naleṣikā*), [reciting]: "Mount the floating reed; follow the paths by means of this reed. Having become a floating reed, do thou cross over, ford across, and pass beyond."

Having performed the *tayā devatā* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. Then, having washed this jar of bones with a garment that has already been worn, he piles them according to their respective limbs, saying: "Savitṛ has placed these bodies in the lap of Mother Earth; O Earth, be a source of peace for them. At this point, he recites the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula: "O Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, let your eye go to the sun, your breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to the cosmic law (*dharman*)."

"Or go to the waters, if that is beneficial for you; take your stand among the plants with your bodies," he says, as well as, "Follow the path beyond the two servants. Then he causes it to be fanned: "May the wind be auspicious, may the sun's heat be auspicious; may the plants be auspicious for you. May the quarters be favorable and helpful to me. Then he places these five *caru* offerings along with cakes: "May the *caru* containing cake and ghee sit here, supporting the earth and the sky above."

"Born from the womb, path-maker, honor those who here partake of the clarified butter of the gods! This *svadhā* is placed for you in the dwelling of Yama, in this house—[so saying], he utters the name of the sacrificer. 'Ten-syllabled one, protect her, guard her, I entrust her to you. May the Pitṛs, the deities, and Prajāpati harm you not; may Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!'—with these words, he places it in front."

"Rich in cakes and rich in boiled milk"—thus on the south; "rich in cakes and rich in milk"—thus on the west; "rich in cakes and rich in curds"—thus on the north; "rich in cakes and rich in honey"—thus in the middle. To each direction he adds the formulas, "Hundred-syllabled, thousand-syllabled. Having performed the *tayā devatam* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* rite. Then he strews it with parched grains mixed with sesame, saying, "These I make for you as *svadhā*, as immortals. Having performed the *tayā devatam* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* rite. Then he lays down four bundles of grass.

"Brahmins know you to be the milk of the white *arjuna* plants that are upon the sacrificial porridges (*caru*). From their midst, I take you for the sake of nourishment. [With this,] he brings from the east a clump of *arjuna* grass and a clump of *dūrvā* grass, saying: "Bring this most beloved one of mine; may she grow most abundantly toward this direction of men. From the north, he brings a clump of *dūrvā* grass and a clump of *kāśa* grass for the destruction of the *rakṣases*.

"Those evildoers who have perished from this quarter, so that they shall not exist again"—with these words, he brings a clump of *kāśa* grass from the west, saying: "Bring a clump of *darbha* grass, the beloved herb of the ancestors; may the living one follow its root, its stalk, and also its fruit. He places a clump of *darbha* grass to the south. At the front and the middle of the four clumps, he places the sacrificial pap (*caru*) with these same four mantras. Having performed the *tayā devatam* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula.

Then he places four enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of various trees: "May the two trees not press upon you; O Mother Earth, do not [press]. For you go to Vaivasvata; you shine in the kingdom of Yama. He places those made of cane and *śamī* wood in the east and in the north. Having performed the *tad-devatya* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula. According to some, he then places two *kleṣīka* sticks. Then he deposits clods of earth: "I settle you in the world of the earth."

"May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm"—with these words he places one hundred [bricks] in the east. "I settle you in the world of the atmosphere"—one hundred in the north. "I settle you in the world of heaven"—one hundred in the west. "I settle you in the world of the quarters"—one hundred in the south. "I settle you on the back of the firmament, on the summit of the radiant sun"—two hundred in the middle. Having performed the *tayā devatā* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he lays down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula, "Fill the world, fill the gap. With these *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, the total reaches one thousand. In the case of two-thousand-brick altars and others, he should lay them down again and again until that number is reached. In the *Kāṭhaka Agniciti* as well, he should lay down one hundred and eighty-five. It is known from the *Brāhmaṇa* of the *Kāṭhaka Agnis*: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the *Sautrāmaṇī* or with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa. Having performed the *tad-devata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he causes him to breathe upon it with the mantra: "May the wind be auspicious; may the sun's heat be auspicious; may the plants be auspicious for you; may all the quarters be favorable to you. Then he touches him with the mantra: "May this very [protection] ward off from me any future distress whatsoever; even as that was done by the Aśvins, by Mitra, and by Varuṇa. To the east, he places a branch of the *varaṇa* tree with the mantra: "May the divine tree, the *varaṇa*, ward off this [distress]; may the tree protect us from affliction, from destruction, and from hatred."

To the north, he places a blade of *kṣetravitṛṇṇī* grass with the formula: "Thou art a separator; separate from us sin and hatred. Behind [the fire], he places a branch of *śamī* wood with the formula: "O *śamī*, pacify from us sin and hatred. To the south, he places barley grains with the formula: "O barley, bar from us sin and hatred."

Then he worships it with: "Go to the earth; go to the intermediate space; go to the sky; go to the quarters; go to heaven! Go to heaven; go to the quarters; go to the sky; go to the intermediate space; go to the earth; or go to the waters, if that is beneficial for you there; take your stand in the plants with your bodies. Behind the funeral pyre, they make three trenches running toward the south and east; this has been explained previously.

Having struck down the leaf-branches behind the furrows and tied them with a weak cord, they creep out, saying, "They are creeping out. This has been explained previously. They go toward where there is water without looking back. Together with their clothes and carrying earth, they bathe facing south, saying, "May Dhātṛ purify us; may Savitṛ purify us. Having thrice splashed water while pronouncing her name, and having stepped out and sipped water, she worships the sun with the verse, "Up from the darkness we have risen. Then they return home. Whatever the women say in this matter, that they do.

In this case, they perform the *śānti* (propitiatory rite), as it serves as a substitute for the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice. Here, one should perform it with *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture). The *loṣṭaciti* (the piling of clods of earth) is completed; the *loṣṭaciti* is completed. On the first day, they should shake [the fires]; then, by means of two [verses], he takes the fire into himself after the *caru*s. Three [clods]. Thus ends the eighth chapter of the third book of the *Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Now, if the sacrificer whose fires have been extinguished or whose fires have been stolen should die, and if his son or pupil should be capable of performing the ritual, [the procedure is as follows]: having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), having dug up the ground and sprinkled it with water, having laid the deceased in the place of the sacrificer, and having placed the two churning-sticks (araṇī) in the place of the Gārhapatya fire, he takes hold of the deceased’s right arm and churns [the fire], saying: "Those fires of his who, desiring flesh, have been intent upon me while I was sacrificing—let them arise for the sake of the sacrificer; let them arise for this deceased one, for the oblation tasted [by the gods] and for the heavenly world."

"Let them lead [the body] away. Having spread the fires silently, and having filled the *sruk* ladle with twelve portions of clarified butter, he offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while mentally reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*. He offers in the same manner into the *gārhapatya* fire. Having offered silently into the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he should proceed with the rites pertaining to the funeral of the deceased (*paitṛmedhika*). As for this matter of how one should collect and consecrate the bones of a deceased sacrificer who has passed away from sight: how is the collection performed in this case?

It is known from scripture that he collects thirty-three bones: first taking them from the head, then from the chest, then from the belly, then from the thighs and arms, and finally from the feet; for it is said, "The person consists of thirty-three [parts]. Then, having washed these bones with water, he spreads out a black antelope skin with its neck to the south and the hair upwards, and upon it he collects the bones with this section of the text beginning, "Indra [armed] with the bones of Dadhyañc."

He performs the *tayā devatā* formula: "By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras. Then he performs the *sūdadohas* formula: "Those spotted cows, yielding milk, mix the Soma; they are the clans of the gods at their birth, in the three luminous realms of heaven. They bring [the materials] in earthen vessels on a long pole, having untied them, while consuming food that is neither pungent nor salty. Having placed those [vessels] at the boundary of the village, they should fetch the fires. If they were to carry them beyond [that point], the fires would become mundane.

And it is known from scripture that when departing on a journey, the sacrificer goes to his house after entrusting it to the fires; therefore, they do not go beyond the boundary of the village. For this reason, one should not cross the boundary of the village.

Now, if the sacrificer should die while the fires have been consigned within himself or in the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), and if his son or pupil is capable of performing the ritual, he should place the sacred thread over his right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), dig out the ground, sprinkle it with water, and place the deceased in the sacrificer’s station. Having established a common fire in the station of the *gārhapatya*, he takes hold of the deceased’s right arm from the right side and mutters: "Descend, O Jātavedas; lead this deceased one, knowing the way, to the heavenly world."

"Bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth; accept all these offerings for him who has departed. Or rather, having caused [the fire] to descend into the two kindling woods, he should churn it. Having silently spread out the fires, filled the ladle with twelve portions, and offered the Durgā, Manasvatī, and Mahāvyāhṛti oblations, he offers a full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the two verses beginning "Tad yamo rājā. If there be those seeking wealth, he gives a cow to them. Now, in the case of a sacrificer who has passed away while absent, only his direction is known.

Having designated that direction as the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), having summoned [the deceased] by name, saying "Come hither," and having fashioned a human figure out of *parṇa* and *sarva* grass upon a black antelope skin, having piled the vessels upon them and covered them with young *kuśa* grass, they should observe the fast in the prescribed manner. If, after this has been done, the sacrificer should return because he was obstructed by the fires, how should he act in that case? 2.

Then, having churned fire from sacrificial wood, having established the fire, having strewn grass around it, and having performed the *agnimukha* rite, he offers oblations of cooked food with two verses beginning, "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the *svāhā*-utterances of the section beginning, "Sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ. The procedure from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the granting of the boon of a cow.

To the west [of the fire], having filled a golden vessel, or a new earthen one, or a black antelope skin used as a leather bag, with ghee and water, the father—if the father is still living—consecrates him with the mantra, "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb. Then he causes him to enter with the verse, "O Pūṣan, lead her toward us, the most auspicious one. Having become an embryo in the black antelope skin used as a leather bag, he dwells there for a night. When the dawn has broken, drawing himself out from the hind part [of the skin], he is born.

Having caused the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) to be performed for the newborn son beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), he should observe the ten-night vow (*daśarātravrata*). Likewise, having established the sacred fires (*agnīn*) together with his wife and having sacrificed with the *vrātya* animal sacrifice, he should go to a mountain and perform an offering (*iṣṭi*) to Agni Kāma, consisting of one hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces and intended for long life. He should then sacrifice with the *diśām aveṣṭi*. It is traditionally taught that from this point forward, he should sacrifice with whatever sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) he desires. Once born as a Brāhmaṇa from the Golden Womb (*hiraṇyagarbha*), having fulfilled his obligations, he need not rise to greet anyone; for he is equal to a god.
Thus it is known;
therefore, when the sacrificer has gone abroad, one should maintain the Agnihotra for twenty-four years and then perform the consecration (saṃskāra). This is [the rule].

If he were one who has not studied [the Vedas], or if he should die during the interval between vows before the completion of the Āgrayaṇa, the Iṣṭi, the animal sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya, or the Adhvara sacrifices, then his son or pupil should complete the remaining portions as a single ritual complex (*ekatantra*). He should offer a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) or curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to the same deity for whom the animal was sacrificed. Now it is indeed said: "He enters from darkness into darkness; one should consecrate that deceased Āhitāgni with other fires."

Moreover, they also cite this: "The fires, indeed, are the heirs to the body. There is a loss at death. It is known from scripture: "He who, knowing this, dies during the northern course of the sun goes to the heavenly world by the solar path; but he who dies during the southern course goes to the world of the fathers by the lunar path."

"Those two, the Sun and the Moon, are the supreme sustainers of the universe. Thus, they teach that death is better at the conclusion of a sacrificial rite (*kratu*)—whether by means of oblations during the night, during the waning fortnight, during the sun's southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*); or during the northern course (*udagayana*), during the waxing fortnight, or by day. In other sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) which are characterized by restrictive observances, one should act as prescribed for one who dies while consecrated (*dīkṣita*); likewise in a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) or a multi-day sacrifice (*ahīna*). Now, if the fires have been lost; now, if [the fires] have been absorbed into oneself; now, from a piece of wood used for sacrifice—three [pieces]. Thus ends the ninth chapter of the third book in the *Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Now, regarding the statement, "Some [perform the rites] for the others silently," they cite this as an example: "The woman is designated as 'wife' (bhāryā), and the man is designated as 'Brāhmaṇa'."

These are the purificatory rites for the *hotṛ* priests; others are not consecrated by mantras. We shall now explain them in order: one who has not been initiated (*anupeta*), a madman, one afflicted by water-disease, a blind man, a mute, a deaf man, a leper, one with white leprosy, a hunchback, a lame man, one with missing limbs, one with redundant limbs, a Brahmin who lives in common with his wife, a Brahmin without a protector, a Kṣatriya without sacred fires, a householder, those sons born of a Vaiśya woman, a maiden, a widow, and a barren woman. When their vital breaths have departed, one should bathe them silently. Having carried them to the cremation ground, one should cause them to be burned without mantras.

Having swept with a branch and having scattered sesame and rice grains, and having prepared the funeral pyre, he places the deceased upon the pyre and pours ghee into his mouth [with the formula]: "This is your body; this is your self. From the body, Brahman releases your self: Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! To that world of heaven, svāhā! With this mantra, they fan him with a winnowing basket. Silently, he sprinkles water around [the pyre] from right to left using a water-pot.

One should unite it with the heating fire, saying: "From this you were born; may he be born from you. To Agni Vaiśvānara, to the heavenly world, svāhā! One should then sprinkle [the child] at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).

Now, if the husband of a pregnant woman should die after the third month of her pregnancy has been completed, they should carry him to the cremation ground and cause him to be burned. Having prepared the funeral pyre and placed the deceased behind it, one should scrape [the soil] above the left side of his navel with the mantra: "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre. One then consecrates the child who is being seen with the mantra: "May he live through me, my son! Then they should bathe the child; having placed gold between [his hands], they return to the village alive.

Having offered the breast with the verse, "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible," he offers oblations of clarified butter into that stomach with these five verses beginning with, "To him who has a hundred weapons, a hundred powers," and with this section beginning, "To Prayāsa, svāhā! He should make the opening free from wounds using this section beginning, "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Vyāna, svāhā! Having placed the deceased upon the funeral pyre, he should cremate him according to the prescribed rite. He should give away an Aṣṭakā-cow, a sesame-cow, or a land-cow.

Now, if there should be impurity among men—whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas—due to birth (sūtaka) or death (pretaka), or if others are impure due to a death, one should purify them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), with the *surabhimatī* verses, the *vāruṇī* verses, the *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses, the *pāvamānī* verses, and the section beginning with "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*) up to the end of the *anuvāka*; then, having sprinkled [the corpse] with the *śatarudrīya* and given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one proceeds with the *paitṛmedhika* rites. 2.

Now, if a householder should take many wives and one of them, even a slave-woman, should die, he should perform the *paitṛmedhika* rites with the very same sacred fire. Thereafter, for ten nights, he should observe a vow: sleeping on the ground, celibacy, avoiding ornaments, not eating at night, and not touching or eating the food of those who do not share the same *sapiṇḍa* lineage—such is the vow he should observe. This applies also to other days of impurity. On the eleventh day, they perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.

Having established the sacred fire together with his other wives, the domestic rites are performed upon that fire. If a householder should take many wives, he should not repeat the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *aupāsana* fire; or, if she should die, one should perform the cremation according to the established rule by means of that fire after repeating the ritual procedure. Thereafter, having established the sacred fire together with his other wives, the domestic rites are performed upon that fire.

If among them another should die first, he should kindle the eastern fire, strew grass around it, heat the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, wipe them clean, take four portions of clarified butter into the *sruk*, and while his wife holds on to him, the sacrificer offers the oblation with the mantra: "Homage to thee, O Fever! For non-piercing thee, for the *svadhā*-call thee! May we, unharmed by thee, O Indra, be safe from thy glance! Thus, O Brahman, let this be thine; *svāhā*!"

Then, having consigned this fire into himself with the verse, "This is thy seasonal womb," he places a fuel-stick upon the secondary fire (*aparāgni*) with the two verses, "Being invoked" and "Awake! Having strewn grass around [the fire], melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), purified it, heated the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, wiped them, and taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he—while the deceased is being held by the hand—takes hold of the deceased's right arm and offers the oblation with this hymn: "He who drew forth the Brahman from the Brahman."

Having taken four portions each time from the *praṇītā* water, having prepared four *śarāva*-measures of rice, having cooked it, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having removed it toward the north, he sprinkles the clarified butter over it while it is being attended to. Having performed the rites from the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the *agnimukha*, he offers oblations from the cooked food, reciting the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "O Agni, be united with your portion; may you two agree," and then he offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "O Agni Purīṣya, be our protector; do thou [protect] us. Then, in a pit or on a piece of wood, he offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the verses beginning "Thou art Agni Purīṣya" until the end of the section.

The ritual from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards is established up to the granting of the boon of the cow. He gives a cow to the preceptor. One should cremate [the body] according to the prescribed rule. After ten nights have passed, having established the sacred fires together with his other wives, the domestic rites (*gṛhyāṇi*) are performed therein.
Having prostrated, one should offer salutation with verses to the Supreme Lord known as Sat.
I shall now describe specifically the procedure for the funeral rites of deceased husbands. A pure-souled Brahmin householder should perform the rite of consecration for the ascetic (yati).
Having placed the body—adorned with perfumes and garlands—upon a carrying-pole (śikya), [he should proceed].
Having extinguished the fire of chaff here, the performer of the rite should follow the deceased;
then, having gone toward the east or the north, he should take refuge in a pure place, accompanied by the sound of drums and shouts of victory.
Having dug a site measuring one *daṇḍa* in length with the *vyāhṛtis*,
and having sprinkled it with water while reciting the seven *vyāhṛtis*, one should construct there a funeral pyre of wood suitable for sacrifice, using other woods as well according to one's means.
Then, having cast the body [into the fire], one whose mind is purified by Sāvitrī should cause the oblation to be placed upon it with the words, "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering.
With the mantra "Pavitraṃ te," he should place the purifier (pavitra) in the mouth.
One should place the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) in the right hand with the mantra beginning "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ";
in the left hand, one should cause the sling (*śikya*) to be placed with the mantra "yad asya" ending in *svāhā*;
the bowl (*pātra*) on the belly with the *Sāvitrī* mantra; and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in the secret place.
Then, with the mantra "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," the performer should place the *kaupīna* (loincloth) upon the body,
which is equipped with all the ritual implements deposited therein;
he then stands before it along with the *hotṛ*s and the planets.
One may burn one's body with a fire of chaff; it will perish along with the vital breaths and the wind.
Furthermore, the wise who are skilled in the meaning of the Vedas cite this:
"The rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground have the Brāhmaṇa as their locus."
In that regard, the householder performs the consecration of the ascetic with mantras; having internalized the fire within himself, he who cremates the deceased should,
according to the prescribed rule, cause his son to deposit the fire and cremate him with that fire.
Furthermore, according to the injunctions for the Hotṛ priest, with the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava,

when the father has been closely associated [with these] and has passed away after renouncing the world, the son must perform his cremation, as well as the Śrāddha and the rites of water and rice-balls (piṇḍa).
From the very beginning, one should become a celibate ascetic (*brahmacārī*) through the practice of discernment (*vikalpa*);
in that regard, a householder must perform the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) in the presence of the ascetic;
by carrying, cremating, or even touching the ascetic, one becomes pure merely by bathing.

All [the sons] individually obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) through their sons. However, when a father who was devoted to ritual action has renounced the world and passed away, his cremation must not be performed by them; likewise, the śrāddha, the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa), and the water libations (udaka-kriyā) are not to be performed.
For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the practice of meditation, no cremation, no impurity, and no water libation should be performed thereafter.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). One should fashion a human figure on a black antelope skin using three hundred and sixty palāśa stalks; if the body should perish, they perform the re-consecration. It is known from tradition that for three days they should burn it with fires, increasing the offering by one handful of water each day. He wraps the joints with palāśa bark or *kuśa* grass.

With forty [bricks] he prepares the head; with ten, the neck; with twenty, the chest; with thirty, the belly; with fifty, each of the two arms; and with five of those same [bricks] for each, he provides the fingers. With seventy, each of the two feet; and with five of those same [bricks] for each, he provides the toes. With eight [bricks] he prepares the penis; with twelve, the testicles.

Having bathed them, adorned them, covered them with a new garment (*ahata-vāsas*), and placed them within the sacrificial altar-ground (*antarvedi*), the kinsmen sit around them and consecrate them with the mantra: "This one belongs to Yama; this one belongs to Yama; these belong to Yama. They then commence the preliminary rites (*ādi-karma*). Now, some perform [the rite] silently. Then, when a woman who is pregnant has completed her [period of] purification in the month of Taiṣya; then, when a householder obtains many wives, having bowed down, he performs the salutation (*vandana*). Now, therefore, follows the fivefold re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the *Āgniveśya Gṛhya Sūtra*.

Now begins the eleventh chapter. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *mṛtabali* (the offering for the deceased). Having had the hair and beard shaved and having bathed, the water-rite (*udaka-kriyā*) should be performed. In a south-easterly sacrificial ground, having smeared a square area with cow-dung, having placed three stones in the middle, having scratched [the ground] once, and having sprinkled it with water, one spreads *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south. There, one cuts off a portion of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) mixed once with sesame seeds, measuring either a handful or the size of a hen’s egg. With disheveled hair and having placed his left knee on the ground, he should offer the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) upon a stone.

He should give this ball of rice (*piṇḍa*) to that person. He should also give collyrium, ointment, and clothing. He should pour water from the vessel in a clockwise direction. Here, the *preta*s carry it away like crows.

Having performed [the rites] thus every evening and morning, on the tenth day, having taken a modified meal and offered the evening *bali*, and having poured out water at the time of dawn, he should invite Brahmins—avoiding those with deficient limbs, those with redundant limbs, lepers, those with deformed noses, those with black teeth, the diseased, the husbands of *vṛṣalīs*, the insane, and the sinful; rather, inviting those who are pure, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), of good conduct, accomplished in study, householders, poor, performers of ritual acts, worthy recipients, available immediately, not related by *gotra* or kinship, and designated for the rites—he should say to them: "This for you..."
"O sages, whatever is approved for my deceased father, please partake tomorrow in the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for my father. "It shall be eaten," is the reply.

On the eleventh day, they perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. Before the time has dawned, having invited a Brāhmaṇa and given him something small as an offering, he addresses him with the appropriate mantra. On the following day, having prepared the food and provided a tooth-stick to the Brāhmaṇa whose hair, beard, and nails have been shorn, and having touched a vessel containing wealth and grain, and having placed the vessels in the proper place according to the rules beginning with "In the place [of the vessels]," he should seat the Brāhmaṇa facing north. He should give water mixed with sesame seeds for the purpose of rinsing, except for the final sipping (*ācamana*).

Having poured water into a vessel covered by a single strainer (*pavitra*), having purified it with the strainer, having cast sesame seeds into it, and having placed it upon *darbha* grass, he covers it with *darbha* blades. Having given perfumes and other offerings to the Brāhmaṇa, he says, "I offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). The response is, "Offer the rice-ball. Then he should place the rice-ball upon the *darbha* grass, saying: "May this food, which grants all desires, be infinite, inexhaustible, fragrant, and endowed with all objects of desire!"

"May he, ageless and eternal, attend upon you; may he satisfy the immortals while milking the *svadhā*. Having offered one *piṇḍa*, he sprinkles water with sesame seeds from right to left (counter-clockwise) with the mantra: "Full of vigor, honoring the *svadhā*, may they rest upon you, being pleasant, carrying vigor, providing inexhaustible water as *svadhā*—milk, water, ghee, honey, milk, *kīlāla*, and *parisrut*."

Having adorned the food-ball with collyrium and other substances, having honored the Brāhmaṇa, and having touched the base of his thumb, he says, "Eat. Having been told, "It is eaten," while [the Brāhmaṇa] is eating, he sets aside the remnants of all [the food]. When [the Brāhmaṇa] has sipped water for purification, he scatters *barhis* grass and turns the vessel face down. The Brāhmaṇa should say, "It is well-tasted" (*svaditam*). Then, having placed the purifier (*pavitra*) [on the vessel], he should turn it face up. Having said loudly, "May there be *svadhā*," the response is, "May there be *svadhā*."

Wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*), having sprinkled water, given a fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and caused [the guests] to rise, he asks, "What shall be done with the remnants of the food? The reply is, "Let it be eaten together with those you love. Having circumambulated [them], returned, offered the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) into the water, bathed, entered the temple of the gods, performed the rite without the *dakṣiṇā*, joined his palms in reverence (*añjali*), adorned himself, and gone home, he causes the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*) and so forth; then, together with his attendants, he eats the remnants of the food.
"He sees a son, he sees a grandson, and he is not born as one who has the leavings of a Śūdra"—thus says Kuśahārīta. 2.

In the course of a year, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), having kindled the fire and strewn it around with *darbha* grass blades pointing southward and eastward, he places four water-vessels upon them. Having prepared the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*) with a single strainer (*pavitra*) and sprinkled the vessels, he places one of them to the south as the vessel for the deceased (*pretapātra*). Having brought a vessel half-filled with water, purified it with the strainer, added sesame seeds, and set it down upon the *darbha* grass, he covers it with *darbha* blades.

In the other three [vessels], he pours water with the mantra: "ūrjasvatīḥ svadhayā vandamānāḥ. Having placed the ointment for the eyes and the ointment for the body, as well as the water-pitcher, to the south, and having seated all the Brāhmaṇas—who have thoroughly washed their hands and feet—on seats of *darbha* grass to the south, facing east, and having seated the others facing north, he says, "May you receive [the guest-offering]," and they reply, "I receive it. Having performed worship for them, excluding incense and lamps, he then sprinkles water around [the site] with his sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

Having placed a fuel-stick of *audumbara* wood upon the fire, he offers with a ladle made of *audumbara* wood. Having offered with ghee fit for oblation using the six mantras beginning with "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs," he then offers with the names: "Svadhā, obeisance to such-and-such; svadhā, obeisance to such-and-such"—these are eight oblations. He offers these eight.

Having thus offered of the food to Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt with the formula, "Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā!", and having made the offering in the eastern part of the southern half, he should throw the ladle after it, sprinkle water around it from right to left, spread *darbha* grass with its points directed southward to the south, and upon them he should place one funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased with the words, "This rice is a cow that milks all desires."

Having sprinkled water with sesame seeds while moving counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) with the verse, "Full of vigor, honoring with the *svadhā* call," and having offered these rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) according to the ritual for the balls, he touches them with the formula for touching with faith (*śraddhābhimarśana*). He then serves learned Brāhmaṇas, saying, "Eat! While they are eating, he looks at them and recites: "Seated in the vital breath, I offer the nectar; may my self be established in Brahman for the sake of immortality. He should cause them to hear the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* verses characterized by the ancestors (*pitṛliṅga*).

Having given water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) to those who have sipped water, and having caused them to say "May there be *svadhā*," the response is "Let there be *svadhā*. Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, he should then pour the vessel of the deceased (*pretapātra*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*), repeating the verse: "And our intention is common" (*samānī ca ākūtiḥ*). Then he should place the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) of the deceased among the cakes of the ancestors, using the two verses: "Come together, communicate together; the mantra is common, the assembly is common. He worships them with the two verses: "Those who are common, those who are kinsmen... (*ye samānāḥ ye sajātāḥ*).

At this point, he mutters the ancestral *anuvāka* beginning with "We call upon you who desire [us]" (*uśantas tvā havāmahe*). The ritual for the father should take place thereafter. Having collected the remnants from all [the portions], he should eat them. This concludes the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *Nārāyaṇabalih*. It should be performed on the twelfth day of the waning fortnight during either the sun's southern or northern course. He invites twelve or six Brahmins who are endowed with learning and good conduct.

In a temple or on a riverbank, having performed the rites beginning with the drawing of lines for the sacrificial ground and ending with the *praṇītā* water, he stands up and invokes the deity in front of the fire: "Om bhūḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Om bhuvaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Om svaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa; Om bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, I invoke Puruṣa. Having thus invoked with "Om," and having performed the rites beginning with the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*), and having worshipped the deity with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ," [he proceeds].

Having performed the purification with the four verses beginning "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" and with this Anuvāka beginning "Pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," he should offer unbroken grains, perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps with the verse "Sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ" or with the eight-syllable mantra. Having seated [the deity] facing the western direction, he offers the principal oblations: having recited the Puronuvākyā, "Viṣṇornukaṃ vīryāṇi pravocam," he offers with the Yājyā, "Paro mātrayā."

Then he offers twelve oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, saying, "To Keśava, svāhā," and so forth. He presents the offering of rice-pudding mixed with sugar and ghee to Mahāviṣṇu with the mantra, "I dedicate thee to the God" (*devasya tvā*). Having summoned the Brāhmaṇas with the twelve salutations beginning with "To Keśava," and having seated them facing north on seats prepared with *darbha* grass, he should give them a garment and a ring as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He satisfies the Brāhmaṇas with food consisting of three kinds of grain. Having caused them to pronounce blessings and having obtained their permission, he should restrain his speech.

Having brought together clarified butter, sesame seeds, and sacrificial oblation, and having taken up the *iḍā* vessel with his hand, he should offer them, saying: "To the fathers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the great-grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the mothers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the great-grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*."

To the maternal grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-great-grandfathers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the maternal grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the maternal great-great-grandmothers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the teachers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*.

To the wives of the teachers, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the gurus, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the wives of the gurus, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the friends, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the wives of the friends, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the kinsmen, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the wives of the kinsmen, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To the attendants, *svadhā*, obeisance; to Viṣṇu, *svāhā*.

"Oblation and homage to the wives of the ministers; Svāhā to Viṣṇu! Oblation and homage to all; Svāhā to Viṣṇu! Oblation and homage to all women; Svāhā to Viṣṇu! To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, oblation and homage; Svāhā to Viṣṇu! From the Sviṣṭakṛt offering onwards, the ritual is established as usual up to the granting of the boon of a cow.

To the south of the fire, having strewn *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward, he offers an oblation (*bali*) upon them, saying: "Homage to the Viśvedevas! Homage to the Sādhyas! Homage to all the gods! Homage to all the deities! This is for you; homage! Homage to the Brāhmaṇas! Homage to the Beloved of Brahman! He who performs this offering to the ancestors and to Nārāyaṇa attains everything. The procedure for the deceased (*preta-vidhāna*) has been described above.

In the same way, one should avoid the ritual purification of the body for one who has been killed by weapons, ropes, water, serpents, wind, trees, stones, or by being crushed; or for one who has killed himself, or for one who has fallen upon a cow, a Brahmin, a widow, or an outcast. If someone dies in another land, or is killed in battle, or killed by a tiger, one should bring the body back and cremate it according to the prescribed rite. If even a single limb or two limbs are visible, one should touch the earth and perform the half-cremation rite. Having anointed the remains with honey and clarified butter, one should cremate them according to the rite. This is done with the hope that he might perhaps return to life.

Now, therefore, on the eleventh day they perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* offering of the *amṛtabali*; after one year, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Now, therefore, follows the *nārāyaṇabali* consisting of four [offerings].
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the third book of the *Āgniveśya-gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Having eaten a Śrāddha meal that is blameless and in accordance with the scriptures,
the learned man should then properly vomit it up and drink water mixed with Kuśa grass.
Then, having bathed in a body of water, he should mutter the *mānastoka* verse.
Having recited the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times and performed sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas),
one who has eaten at a monthly śrāddha is purified by a Prājāpatya penance;
however, having eaten at an Aṣṭakā thereafter, one is purified by the previously mentioned [penance].
Having eaten at an *ekoddiṣṭa* thereafter, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance;
having eaten at a *nakṣatra-bhojana*, a learned man should perform the *atikṛcchra*;
and for eating at [the end of] six months or three fortnights, he should perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* and the *taptakṛcchra* respectively.
Likewise, having eaten at a Śrāddha for the deceased of one year, or similarly at a Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, a wise man should perform one Kṛcchra penance after eating the Nārāyaṇa-bali;
however, if he is unable, the wise man should likewise perform one Kṛcchra for all such instances.
Alternatively, one may remain for three nights or even for a single day if one is weak; therefore, by every possible effort, one should not go to the house of a *śrāddha* feast.
Through cooked food, the giver saves [the ancestors], but through uncooked food, the non-giver [saves] the knotted [ancestors].
Therefore, with every effort, one should accept the *āmaśrāddha*;
taking all the materials, he should bring them into the presence of the Brahmins, saying:
"Accept all these from me, desiring the prosperity of my father."
"O Blessed One, please accept my offering; for indeed, alms should be given in my house. Having said, "I shall offer the alms," and being permitted by the Brahmin, he went toward his own home.
Having offered the rice-ball according to the scriptures and likewise an añjali of water, he should take the *svadhā* and, having gone there, place it into the hands of the Brāhmaṇa; then,
after saying "May there be *svadhā*," he spoke with the words beginning "May there be no *svadhā* for me."
When this had been said, he then gave a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇa;
having performed a circumambulation and likewise joined his palms in reverence,
he first offered the oblation according to the prescribed rite before the distribution of the materials.

Having reached his own home, he should go there and feed [the guest] together with his sapinda relatives. Then he offers the universal expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). He should take eight splinters—either of *palāśa* wood, or of *audumbara* wood, or other sacrificial woods. Having performed the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), having strewn grass around the fire, having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*) and purified it, he performs the sprinkling of water all around. Having offered oblations first and last with the *vyāhṛtis* both separately and combined, he should anoint the splinters with clarified butter and offer them one by one, [with the mantra]: "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods; svāhā!"

You are the expiation for the sin committed against men; svāhā! You are the expiation for the sin committed against the ancestors; svāhā! You are the expiation for the sin committed by oneself; svāhā! You are the expiation for the sin committed by another; svāhā! Whatever sin we have committed by day and by night, you are its expiation; svāhā! Whatever sin we have committed knowingly or unknowingly, you are its expiation; svāhā! Whatever sin we have committed while sleeping or while waking, you are its expiation; svāhā!

"Thou art the expiation for sin from sin, svāhā! Having sprinkled water around in the same manner, and having thus offered the *śakala-homa* every day at evening and morning, one becomes purified from all evil; "one becomes purified from all evil," so said the venerable Āgniveśya.
[End of] the twelfth chapter in the third book of the *Āgniveśya-gṛhya-sūtra*, concerning the performance of all expiations after eating at a *śrāddha*.
The third question is completed;
the Āgniveśya Gṛhyasūtra is finished.
May there be auspiciousness.
